appletons-cyclopaedia-american-biography:
Volume Two of Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography came out in 1888, running from Crane to Grimshaw. Editors Wilson and Fiske kept the pace of a life for nearly every notable name. The set was sold by subscription across the country.

This volume's span covers many founders, Civil War officers, and men of letters of the young republic. Each entry gives birth, career, works, and death in tight, factual prose. Steel portraits mark the most famous names. Read across the six volumes, Appletons' forms a portrait gallery of the nation as the Victorian age wished to remember it.

Volume Three of Appletons' Cyclopaedia, also from 1888, continues the alphabet from Grinnell to Lockwood. Wilson and Fiske's dictionary was halfway done, with thousands of American lives already in print. The work's scale was unmatched in its day.

Governors, judges, explorers, and divines fill these pages, each weighed in a column or two. The editors include Canadians and Latin Americans whose lives touched the United States. Family details and lists of writings make the entries useful for tracing kin and careers. The volume carries the national biography through the middle letters with steady, encyclopedic calm. The print is dense, but the facts are laid out in a steady, clear order.

Volume Four of Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography appeared in 1888, covering Lodge to Pickens. The dictionary had become a fixture in American libraries. Wilson and Fiske drew on family papers and earlier collections for their facts.

This stretch of the alphabet holds many Revolutionary officers, senators, and college presidents. Entries balance public deeds with private character sketches drawn from obituaries and memoirs. A few lives were polished by the families themselves, a flaw later readers learned to discount. Even so, the volume preserves facts about hundreds of figures that survive nowhere else in print. Many entries rest on obituaries clipped from the newspapers of the day.

Volume Five of Appletons' Cyclopaedia came out in 1888, running from Pickering to Sumter. The set was nearing its end, and the editors' net had caught most of the nation's notable dead and living. Subscribers received the volumes year by year.

Revolutionary statesmen, Civil War generals, and leading clergy crowd this part of the alphabet. The entries keep the house style: dates, posts, battles, books, and a closing judgment. Charles Sumter's contemporaries and Charles Sumner both appear in these pages. For students of nineteenth-century America, the volume is a dense quarry of names, dates, and careers.
army-letters-from-an-officer-s-wife-1871: Frances Roe's letters home from frontier army posts paint a vivid woman's picture of the post-Civil War West — long marches, isolated forts, and encounters with a vanishing frontier. Candid and observant, they preserve daily life that official reports never captured. A gem of Western Americana.
arxiv-2510-00088:
Sagnik Basu and six colleagues published this 2025 audit of AI models that judge bail cases using photos. Courts already test text models on case reports, and new image-and-text models can also see a defendant's face. The team asked whether such models decide fairly when appearance enters the picture. Their worry is that looks could sway a legal choice that should rest on facts.

The audit found weak results across all the models and social groups tested. Worse, models often denied bail to people who deserved it, and did so with high confidence. The team then tried fixes, adding past court rulings as context and fine-tuning the models in new ways. Both fixes raised accuracy by large amounts in their tests. The authors stress that such models should only assist judges, never replace the human decision.
arxiv-2510-00288:
Lubos Kris and colleagues at the Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies published this 2025 paper on choosing explanation methods for AI models. Transformer language models are powerful but opaque, and dozens of explainability techniques compete to open them. Picking the right method and settings usually demands rare expert judgment. Their tool, o-MEGA, automates that search through hyperparameter optimization.

The team tested o-MEGA on a fact-checking pipeline that matches social media posts with refuting claims. The dataset pairs posts with claims that answer them, drawn from the MultiClaim collection. The tool swept across explanation methods and their settings in the semantic matching task. Occlusion, which hides input parts and watches the output shift, came out best there. The authors argue automated selection makes transparent systems deployable without deep explainability expertise. That matters most in misinformation detection, where trust is the product.
arxiv-2510-00488:
Mirai Ikebuchi wrote this 2025 mathematics paper comparing two ways to measure the shape of abstract algebraic structures. Cohomology assigns algebraic invariants to categories, much as it does to spaces. Quillen's version and the Baues-Wirsching version grew from different traditions. Ikebuchi proves the two coincide for small cartesian closed categories.

These categories are the home of typed computation and logic in algebra. The theorem extends earlier work by Dwyer and Kan on plain small categories. It also extends Jibladze and Pirashvili, who handled categories with finite products. A corollary says the richer structure changes nothing: the cohomology is the same either way. Computing it in the bare setting or with products included gives identical answers. Such matches let researchers import tools across frameworks without re-proving foundations each time.
arxiv-2510-00688:
Milani builds a non-singular bouncing cosmology inside f(R,G,T) modified gravity in this 2025 arXiv paper. Bouncing models replace the Big Bang singularity with a contraction that turns around into expansion, but they must stay stable and ghost-free. Milani couples the modified geometry, which depends on curvature, the Gauss-Bonnet term, and the trace of matter, to a quintom scalar sector with two fields. That pairing produces a double crossing of the phantom divide line during the bounce.

A Hamiltonian analysis shows the flat universe symmetry tames the higher-derivative instabilities that usually haunt such theories. The scalar field equation confirms the pathological modes cancel out. Numerical reconstruction of five versions of the model produced non-singular bounces with positive effective density and a non-negative squared sound speed. The framework also unifies the early bounce with late-time dark energy behaviour.
arxiv-2510-00888:
Mazumdar and Premoselli prove compactness results for conformal metrics with constant higher-order Q-curvature in this 2025 arXiv paper on differential geometry. Q-curvature generalizes scalar curvature, and prescribing it leads to a nonlinear equation of order 2k on a closed manifold. Compactness asks whether solution families can blow up without limit, and for general k the governing GJMS operator has no explicit formula, which blocked earlier attempts.

The authors overcome that obstacle with Juhl's recursive formulae for the operator, driving a refined blow-up analysis. They establish compactness under three regimes, combining local conformal flatness, positive mass, dimension ranges, or a nonvanishing Weyl tensor. Their result is the first compactness theorem covering every order between one and half the dimension. It also suggests the threshold dimension for compactness grows without bound as the order increases.
arxiv-2510-01388:
Zhang and co-authors steer robots by having an image diffusion model paint the path before the robot drives it. Language-conditioned navigation suffers because vision-language models were never trained to output wheel commands. Their system, Ventura, instead generates a path mask, a visual plan drawn in image space.

A light behavior-cloning policy converts the painted plan into executable motion. Training labels come from self-supervised tracking paired with model-written captions, avoiding hand annotation. Real-world trials beat specialized baselines across varied instructions and places. Internet image priors, repurposed, proved surprisingly fluent at planning. The diffusion backbone arrives pretrained on internet images, not robot data. Novel environments tested generalization beyond the training rooms. Limited on-robot training data makes the transfer result striking. Visual plans are inspectable, which low-level commands never are. Language diversity in instructions is handled by the same single policy.
arxiv-2510-01488:
Carmeli and Luecke apply their theory of Tate-valued characteristic classes to orientation questions for highly structured ring spectra. Complex orientations organize how a spectrum sees complex vector bundles, and higher commutativity levels make them scarce and precious. Their construction manufactures orientations of Tate fixed-point objects with usable formulas.

A formula for Frobenius maps on Thom spectra such as the bordism spectrum follows. A rigidity property of that spectrum as a cyclotomic base is proved. A general obstruction theory then yields non-existence results for highly structured orientations at small primes. Miscellaneous applications close the second installment of the program. Thom spectra and bordism anchor the motivating examples. Small primes and low commutativity levels are where obstructions bite. Frobenius lifts receive formulas alongside the maps themselves. Stable homotopy theory is the home discipline throughout. Part two cashes the first part's theory.
arxiv-2510-01688:
Lim and six co-authors name a new failure mode for medical chatbots in this 2025 paper. Large language models are often fine-tuned to run pre-consultation talks with patients. Training data for that task contains mostly short dialogues and few long ones. The authors show that this skew teaches models a habit they call Format Inertia.

A model with Format Inertia keeps asking tidy, well-formed questions in long talks. Those questions repeat familiar patterns instead of gathering new diagnostic facts. The visit looks polished, but it teaches the clinician little. The fix the authors test is simple and data-focused. They rebalance the training set so long and short dialogues appear evenly. Experiments showed that this rebalancing sharply reduced the failure in long medical dialogues.
arxiv-2510-01788:
Courtès and four co-authors tackle a subtle failure in learning physical dynamics from data in this 2025 paper. Their systems are non-canonical Hamiltonian systems, which cover many plasma and fluid models. Long-time simulation needs both a structure-preserving learned model and a matching numerical scheme. Combining a potential-based network with degenerate variational integrators can, however, break down badly.

The team traces the failure to a gauge freedom in the learned potential. The integrator is not invariant under shifts of that potential, so a well-learned model can still simulate unstably. They propose two training strategies that sidestep the clash. One learns the vector field directly, and the other learns the time-discrete dynamics through the scheme itself. Several test cases check both strategies on complex dynamics. They include the guiding center motion from gyrokinetic plasma physics, a demanding long-time benchmark.
arxiv-2510-01888:
Banerjee, Laverick, and Wiseman build a quantum version of counterfactual reasoning in this 2025 physics letter. Counterfactuals ask what would have happened under one changed condition, with everything else held fixed. David Lewis gave the classic analysis, but he built it on deterministic classical physics. Whether the idea survives in random quantum theory stayed an open question.

Their formalism makes the changed condition a choice of measurement setting. It can then answer questions that mix actual and hypothetical detectors in a nontrivial way. One example asks what a field-quadrature detector would have shown, given that a photon detector clicked while watching an atom's glow. The framework conditions on the full record of what actually happened. It then picks a characteristic alternative history rather than averaging over all of them. The result gives quantum causal reasoning a firmer logical base.
arxiv-2510-01988:
Możejko and twelve co-authors navigate peptide space along its true curved geometry in this 2025 paper. Antimicrobial peptides are needles in an astronomical haystack of possible sequences. Generator models map that space continuously, but flat distance measures distort the map. The decoder's own geometry bends the space, and fixed-dimension manifold fixes fail on real peptide data.

Their framework, PepCompass, builds a union of stable curved manifolds from the decoder itself. One sampler follows curved-space Brownian motion to explore locally. Another translates tangent directions into concrete amino-acid substitutions. Combining both yields a local Bayesian optimization method for boosting activity. A geodesic search then walks between prototype peptides along paths biased toward promising seeds. Wet-lab validation closed the loop convincingly. The pipeline found four novel seed peptides, then twenty-five highly active ones with broad-spectrum action, including against resistant strains.
arxiv-2510-02288:
Bogli and Petpradittha prove sharp bounds for quantum operators with complex potentials. Their 2025 mathematics paper extends Lieb-Thirring inequalities. Those inequalities cap the total size of bound state energies. The cap depends on the strength of the attracting potential. Real potentials cover many textbook systems. Complex potentials model systems that gain or lose energy. The complex case needs a new kind of weight. Each energy term is weighted by its distance from the main spectrum. The authors find exactly which weights can work.

Their bounds hold when the weight function is integrable. For weights that fail that test, the sums can blow up. They prove that blow-up directly with divergence estimates. The divergence even beats classic semiclassical predictions in rate. Results cover both Schroedinger and Jacobi operators. Optimal here means no stronger bound of this form exists. Spectral theory gains a finished answer for this family.
arxiv-2510-02388:
Bai and co-authors route each question to the source that answers it best. Their 2025 paper improves retrieval augmented question answering. Documents and databases hold different kinds of truth. Databases shine on exact facts and numbers. Documents handle open, descriptive questions better. Mixing both sources blindly wastes tokens and time. The team first mapped where each source wins. They then built a rule driven routing agent. Explicit rules choose the retrieval path for each query. An expert agent refines those rules from feedback. A meta-cache speeds repeated path decisions.

Experiments ran across three question answering benchmarks. The router beat static and learned routing rivals. Accuracy rose while cost stayed controlled. Interpretable rules let operators audit each choice. Hybrid retrieval needs traffic control, not just more sources. This framework supplies that control with clear logic.
arxiv-2510-02588:
Talipov proves that odd geodesic nets fill space densely for typical curved geometries. His 2025 mathematics paper concerns stationary geodesic nets. A geodesic net is a web of shortest path pieces meeting at junctions. Closed geodesics are the tidy loops inside that family. Nets that are not closed loops look messier and stranger. The question was whether such nets are rare curiosities. For a generic metric in dimension three or more, they are not. Their union forms a dense set in the manifold. Baire category language makes the generic claim precise.

The result confirms a conjecture by Nabutovsky and Parsch. The proof leans on perturbing metrics near any chosen region. A bumpy metrics theorem for nets finishes the density argument. Geodesic theory dates back to Poincare era questions. Generic abundance results reshape what geometers expect to find. Closed loops may be the exception, not the rule.
arxiv-2510-02788:
Nguyen and co-authors present XTRA, a new method for finding shared themes in texts written in more than one language. The task is called cross-lingual topic modeling. Older methods often produced topics that were muddy or poorly matched across languages. XTRA mixes a classic word-count model with modern multilingual embeddings. Embeddings place words with close meanings near each other.

XTRA aligns the two languages in two ways at once. It pulls document topic mixes into line with contrastive learning. It also maps topic word lists into one shared space. Tests on corpora in several languages followed. XTRA beat strong rival methods on topic clarity. It also won on topic variety and on match quality across languages. The code is public, so other teams can check the results.
arxiv-2510-03288:
Duan and a large team present a 2025 arXiv paper on finding faults in software from system logs. Their system, LogAction, learns to spot odd log lines on a new system with very little hand labeling. Labeling logs is slow and costly, so most teams cannot mark enough of them. LogAction borrows training from an older, mature system to get started. It then asks people to label only the most telling new log lines.

The team tested LogAction on six pairings of log data sets. With only a small share of logs labeled by hand, it reached a strong average score for fault finding. It beat leading rival methods by a wide margin in those tests. Smart sampling picks lines near the edge between old and new data, where labels teach the most. The result points to cheaper, safer upkeep for large software systems that must run around the clock.
arxiv-2510-03388:
Sharma, Collins, and White present a 2025 arXiv paper from Los Alamos on computing how warm dense matter carries electric current. Warm dense matter fills planet cores and fusion fuel as it compresses toward ignition. Its conductivity shapes both planet models and fusion behavior, yet the regime is too hot and dense for easy lab checks. Their method mixes exact and random sampling tricks inside density functional theory. That blend keeps accuracy while scaling to bigger, hotter systems.

The team computed light absorption spectra for carbon, hydrogen, and beryllium mixes in two matching ways. They also split the transport totals into parts from exact states, random states, and crossings between them. The split shows which transitions carry current at each light energy. Combined, the parts rebuild the full conductivity across low and high frequencies. Fusion designers and planet scientists both need such numbers to test their models against reality.
arxiv-2510-03688:
Karapetian and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper reporting that stars near the Milky Way's center are drifting outward, based on Gaia DR3 measurements. Standard models treat galaxies as systems in equilibrium, with no expansion. The team computed radial velocities for stars within five kiloparsecs of the Galactic center, splitting the region into twenty seven sectors. They checked disk and halo populations. A driver is feedback from the black hole's phases, pushing material outward.

Twenty one of the sectors showed significant motion, at speeds from three to fifty kilometers per second. Disk and halo stars averaged a significant expansion. Earlier results pointed the same way. The authors call the interpretation preliminary, since one quadrant moved inward and the Galactic bar may distort the picture. If real, central expansion could help explain why the Webb telescope sees massive galaxies early. Galaxies may assemble faster than equilibrium models assume.
arxiv-2510-04388:
Adrian Odenweller and ten coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on the energy shift in Europe. Cheap wind and solar power are growing fast, but supply swings with the weather and the seasons. Planners need models that cover both long term investment and hourly power system detail. The team linked two models so each feeds the other. One model maps multi decade pathways, and the other works out hourly operation.

The linked system was tested on two paths for Germany that reach climate neutrality by 2045. One path allowed flexible demand, and the other did not. The runs showed a power system with nearly all renewable electricity is workable and can pay for itself. Flexible users, such as smart charging cars, paid below average prices. Heat pumps paid almost twice the average price, since they peak on cold winter days. Without flexible demand, prices rose for all users, though batteries softened the rise.
arxiv-2510-04688:
Joann Ching and Gerhard Widmer wrote this 2025 paper on why music emotion systems fail on new styles of music. Programs that judge the mood of a song learn from ratings, which vary by listener and culture. Studies train and test inside one style, such as rock or classical. The authors gathered five data sets with emotion ratings on two scales, pleasantness and energy. Styles ranged across the sets. They then tested models trained on one set against the others.

Performance dropped across those boundaries, a distribution gap. Feature types carried genre bias that made the gap worse. The team built a simple fix from two ingredients. They paired embeddings from a music model called Jukebox with chroma features of harmony. Training on several sets helped as well. Together these choices improved cross dataset results. The lesson is that emotion tools must prove themselves across genres, not inside one.
arxiv-2510-04888:
Ermilova and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on mapping how diseases connect. Doctors know diseases travel together, but charting the links across medicine by hand is slow and disputed. The team compared seven methods for discovering links. Sources were hospital records from a database and the disease code list, with and without text descriptions. Methods ranged from counting co occurrence to masked language models and text encoders.

Four language models joined the comparison as well. Methods produced a web of links between disease codes. The authors compared the webs by graph shape, since no ground truth list exists. Language models produced the least diverse webs, tying codes to fewer kinds of partners. That narrowness held against record based and text based rivals. The authors conclude that language models have limited power to find disease links. The resulting ontology is offered as a base map for clinical research.
arxiv-2510-04988:
Kristi Topollai and Anna Choromanska question a fixed habit in deep learning in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most training runs set the momentum coefficient once, usually at 0.9, and never change it. Momentum controls how much past gradients steer each new step. The authors argue that a fixed setting is needlessly weak.

Their method adjusts momentum online as training proceeds. It approximates the objective with two planes, one from the current gradient and one from accumulated memory. Variants built on SGD and AdamW beat the standard versions across many tasks. Gains were clearest at high learning rates and early in training. The approach needs no extra assumptions and no new tuning knobs.
arxiv-2510-05088:
Ola Carlsson and six co-authors propose steering quantum materials with empty space itself in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Casimir effect means vacuum energy depends on a material's surroundings. Some electronic orders, called nematic, can point in several equal directions. Heat scrambles those directions into small domains, so no order survives at large scales.

The authors show the Casimir energy can favor one orientation over the others. Their example pairs a birefringent crystal with a quantum Hall stripe system. The induced preference came out about ten thousand times stronger than known stabilizing mechanisms. Feasible plate distances kept the effect large enough to matter. The result suggests real experiments could lock fluctuating stripe order into place.
arxiv-2510-05288:
Ruoxing Yang works on fine-tuning language models without leaking private data in this 2025 arXiv paper. Big models usually run on remote servers, which exposes users to network attacks. Fine-tuning on sensitive data creates a second risk: attacks that reconstruct training examples. Yang targets models small enough to run on local devices.

The proposed optimizer, DP-Adam-AC, adds adaptive gradient clipping to differentially private Adam training. Adaptive clipping stabilizes short, noisy training runs. Yang fine-tuned two localizable designs: the small Qwen2.5-0.5B model and the 1.58-bit BitNet model. Experiments on two synthetic datasets showed promising loss improvements across privacy settings. The work shows private, on-device fine-tuning is practical for sensitive deployments.
arxiv-2510-05888:
Abian and colleagues build insect sorting with design search over mixed data. Naming insects drives crop health and field research alike. Huge, skewed biodiversity data sets defeat fixed hand-built networks. Their 2025 BioAutoML-NAS framework searches designs while fusing images with metadata.

Stacked search cells learn the best step for every link. A fusion module merges image codes with label data about each species. Weights and design settings update in turns, a two-level tuning loop. Zero steps prune weak links, yielding sparse, lean networks. On BIOSCAN-5M, the score reaches about ninety-seven percent correct. A second million-scale data set confirms transfer at about ninety-three percent. Gains over transfer learning and transformer yardsticks run into double digits. Telling pollinators from pests early protects crops and habitats. Green farming is the use the authors stress.
arxiv-2510-05988:
Fitouchi and Chepiga find field-free commensurate-incommensurate transitions in a frustrated spin chain. The chain mixes ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor with antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor couplings. Such Mott-type transitions usually need a magnetic field or doping to trigger. Their 2025 DMRG study works at zero magnetization throughout.

Two successive Pokrovsky-Talapov transitions appear in the strongly interacting regime. First, bound pairs of magnons condense out of a gapped period-four phase. The resulting critical phase carries central charge two. It coexists as single-magnon and quadrupolar Luttinger liquids combined. Second, domain wall pairs condense into an incommensurate nematic Luttinger liquid. The second transition emerges from a gapped phase-separated state. Both transitions arguably involve the same underlying nematic liquid. Frustration alone, with both couplings strong, drives both transitions. Quasi-long-range incommensurate order stabilizes without any doping at all. Textbook expectations about needing external parameters are overturned.
arxiv-2510-06288:
Ghugare and six co-authors introduce BuilderBench, a benchmark for agents that learn by building, in a 2025 artificial intelligence paper. Today's models learn mostly through mimicry, so they struggle with novel problems. The authors argue agents should acquire skills through exploration and experience.

BuilderBench gives an agent a target structure and a simulated robot with blocks. Over fifty curated structures test physics, mathematics, and long-horizon planning. Agents may experiment across episodes, trying strategies and piecing skills together. The tasks demand embodied reasoning expressed in actions, not words. The team evaluated frontier language-model agents and from-scratch reinforcement learners. Soberingly, none solved any non-trivial task. The analysis points to a basic lack of exploration ability in current models. BuilderBench gives the field a yardstick for scalable learning through interaction.
arxiv-2510-06388:
Lu, Wu, Hartline, and Hu develop truthful calibration errors for multi-class prediction in a 2025 machine learning paper. Calibrated forecasts are useful because their numbers read as genuine probabilities. Standard measures can be gamed: distorting probabilities may score better than reporting them honestly.

A truthful measure removes that temptation, since honest reporting minimizes expected error. The authors build perfectly truthful errors for multidimensional linear properties of the label distribution. The framework covers full multiclass, classwise, and corrected confidence calibration. For calibrated predictors, their errors preserve Blackwell dominance, so more informative models never score worse. Experiments expose why this matters. Non-truthful confidence errors can reverse model rankings when bin counts change. Truthful versions keep rankings stable across binning choices. Calibration-based model selection becomes harder to distort.
arxiv-2510-06588:
Danush Shekar leads a large collaboration designing smarter pixel detectors for particle physics. Their 2025 paper concerns tracking detectors at future collider experiments. Those detectors will face record densities of charged particles. Reading out every signal would overwhelm the data systems.

The proposed design puts a neural network inside the readout chip itself. The chip spots low-momentum tracks and rejects them on the spot. That real-time filtering allows finer pixels and faster readout. The team studied how sensor design choices change the network's accuracy. A smaller pixel pitch in the bending direction improved momentum discrimination. A larger pitch could be partly offset by making the detector deeper. Magnetic-field drift, which spreads the charge clusters, also improved performance. Co-designing the sensor and the chip together, rather than separately, is the paper's central message for future detectors.
arxiv-2510-06888:
Arkadeep Acharya leads a team building the first broad benchmark for medical search systems. Their 2025 paper introduces M3Retrieve, a test suite for multimodal retrieval in healthcare. Retrieval-augmented generation now feeds many medical tools, yet nobody had a standard way to grade the retrievers. Medical data mix text and images in ways generic benchmarks ignore.

The benchmark spans five domains, sixteen medical fields, and four task types. It holds over 1.2 million text documents and 164 thousand multimodal queries, all properly licensed. Clinicians helped design the data so the tasks stay realistic. Leading retrieval models were then graded across the suite. Dense text retrieval still won in anatomy and physiology topics. Multimodal encoders led on psychiatry content and on PubMed literature search. Orthopedics scores stayed low for every model, flagging a hard subdomain. The public benchmark gives builders a shared yardstick for medical retrieval.
arxiv-2510-07188:
Dewansingh and colleagues demonstrate a laser whose core is a liquid dye inside plastic tubing. Their 2025 paper builds the device from Rhodamine B dye dissolved in glycerol. A tube of fluorinated plastic guides the light along the liquid core. The team searched for dye strengths and tube sizes that lase most easily.

Two dye strengths gave the lowest starting thresholds for laser action. Narrower tubing confined the light modes more tightly and sharpened the emitted spectrum. Adding mirrors at the ends improved the coherence of the beam. The spacing of the emitted modes did not match a simple mirror cavity pattern. That mismatch points to complex mode coupling and internal reflections inside the rod. Scattering losses and stray feedback still limit the device. Better waveguide materials and output coupling are the suggested next fixes.
arxiv-2510-07288:
De Teran and Dopico simplify the standard forms that classify real matrices under congruence. Their 2025 paper concerns congruence, a reshaping of a matrix by a change of basis and its transpose. Every real matrix can be reduced to a canonical form built from simple blocks. Two new forms are presented. The first uses blocks of four types, adapted from a known complex classification. The second uses only three types and arranges them in a block tridiagonal pattern.

The authors compare the two forms in detail. They also connect both to the Kronecker form of the matrix pair behind the scenes. An older form needed eight block types, and the paper maps each onto the new blocks. Leaner forms shorten classification arguments and serve the study of bilinear forms.
arxiv-2510-07488:
Muralidharan, Kwak, and An ask whether lessons from human team science transfer to teams of language model agents. Their 2025 paper builds a framework varying three factors from organizational research. Structure can be flat or hierarchical. Teams can be diverse or uniform in their makeup. Interaction dynamics govern how agents exchange and revise views. Four tasks test the teams, spanning commonsense questions, strategy questions, social intelligence, and detecting implicit hate. Post-task interviews with the agents add a reflective layer rarely present in agent benchmarks.

Flat teams tended to beat hierarchical ones across the tasks. Diversity's effect was nuanced, helping in some configurations and hurting in others. In interviews, agents sounded overconfident about their team's performance. Their reflections praised collaboration yet admitted coordination failures and poor integration of each other's reasoning. The study treats multi-agent systems as organizations, not just pipelines.
arxiv-2510-07588:
Li, Geringer-Sameth, and Golovich hunt near-Earth asteroids in old survey images, before anyone knew the asteroids existed. Their 2025 paper automates prediscovery: finding a newly discovered object in archival frames to stretch its observed arc and pin down its orbit. The pipeline refits the official astrometry, propagates the full orbital uncertainty to past survey epochs, and defines search regions on the sky. It builds low-threshold source catalogs for candidate images, then tests every source as a possible prediscovery.

Applied to Zwicky Transient Facility imaging, about three thousand recent near-Earth asteroids show prediscovery potential. For roughly five hundred, the observational arc would double. Two demonstrations shine. A potentially hazardous asteroid's arc extends by two and a half years, collapsing its future sky uncertainty from degrees to arcseconds. Another object is recovered nearly seven years before its first known sighting.
arxiv-2510-07688:
Lu and six coauthors wrote this 2025 photonics paper on tiny optical ring devices called microresonators. A high quality factor means light circles inside for a long time with little loss. Such devices serve communications, sensing, and precision measurement. The team built a racetrack-shaped resonator from a chalcogenide glass rich in sulfur. They shaped its curves with Euler bends to cut losses where straight and curved sections meet.

Careful modeling of laser scans let them separate the loss sources. The finished device showed an intrinsic quality factor near four and a half million. Its absorption loss was low, and the waveguide stayed under one square micrometer in cross-section. Those numbers set a state-of-the-art mark for nonlinear microresonators. The authors argue the material is now a serious low-loss platform for photonic chips. Strong performance also opens efficient access to scattering effects used in narrow-linewidth lasers.
arxiv-2510-07988:
Jia and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on phone agents that ask the user for help instead of guessing. Most mobile agents act alone and assume tasks are clear and fixed. Real requests are ambiguous, grow new details, and sometimes conflict. Guessing wrong wastes the whole run. The authors propose ReInAgent, a multi-agent framework built around a shared memory and continuous user collaboration.

Three specialist agents divide the work. One manages task information in slots and proactively queries the user. One plans with conflicts in view. One reflects and checks that stored information stays consistent. On tasks riddled with information dilemmas, ReInAgent's success rate beat a leading rival by a quarter. Outcomes matched users' true preferences more closely. The authors admit that very complex screens can still hide key details from the system. Asking at the right moment, they argue, beats silent autonomy.
arxiv-2510-08088:
Li and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper presenting a quantum algorithm for energy levels that bunch too tightly for standard methods. Low-energy states often form nearly degenerate manifolds that decide physical behavior. Phase estimation assumes a lone ground state with a comfortable gap. The authors instead diagonalize the manifold directly, solving an effective Hamiltonian problem inside a small reference subspace.

The reduced problem is exactly equivalent to the full one. A block-encoded wave operator lifts its solutions back to full eigenstates. The analysis bounds eigenvalue accuracy, subspace fidelity, and query cost, assuming nothing about the splitting inside the manifold. Benchmarks on the Fermi-Hubbard model, lithium hydride, and a ruthenium complex showed robust resolution of degeneracies. The algorithm treats degeneracy as structure to exploit rather than noise to out-resolve.
arxiv-2510-08388:
Jasmin Orth, Philipp Mondorf, and Barbara Plank ask how language models judge conditional statements in a 2025 arXiv paper. People rate a statement like 'if A, then B' by two cues. One is the chance of B given A. The other is whether A feels relevant to B, not just linked by chance. Such judgments shape how readers weigh arguments and hypothetical claims.

The team tested models from several families, sizes, and prompting styles on these judgments. They analyzed results with linear mixed-effects models and ANOVA tests, standard tools for grouped data. Models responded to both probability and relevance, though the balance varied with architecture and prompts. Against human data, models used both cues less consistently than people do. Bigger models did not necessarily match human judgments more closely, a result the authors highlight.
arxiv-2510-08588:
Ritesh Mehta tests a dictionary fix for biomedical entity recognition errors in a 2025 arXiv paper for the BioASQ challenge. Biomedical named entity recognition pulls genes, chemicals, and diseases out of scientific text. Similar types, like genes versus chemicals, are easily confused by models. Mehta evaluates GLiNER-BioMed and adds targeted dictionary-based post-processing for common misclassifications.

On the development set, the dictionary step lifted the micro F1-score from 0.79 to 0.83, a clear gain that did not survive contact with the blind test set. There the post-processed model scored 0.77 against the baseline score of 0.79, actually doing worse than the plain model. Mehta also reports trials with Conditional Random Fields and other alternatives. The paper's lesson is blunt: dictionary refinement can overfit development data badly. Robust generalization, not local gains, decides real-world usefulness.
arxiv-2510-08688:
James Johnson, Diane Feuillet, Ana Bonaca, and Danielle de Brito Silva link a famous galactic merger's orbit to the Milky Way's chemical split in a 2025 arXiv paper. Disk stars divide into two groups by alpha-element abundance at fixed iron content, a bimodality needing explanation. The Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus dwarf galaxy merged with the Milky Way on a strongly retrograde path. The team models how that trajectory reshaped disk chemistry.

Their chemical evolution models include radial gas flows that transport angular momentum during the merger. Retrograde and radial mergers trigger a sinking event, dropping much of the interstellar gas toward the center. The lowered gas supply lets Type Ia supernovae drive alpha-to-iron ratios down rapidly afterward. Retrograde paths thus boost low-alpha populations and shrink high-alpha ones, unlike prograde paths. If enough high-alpha stars form by other routes, the observed bimodality emerges naturally.
arxiv-2510-08988:
Zhang, Valentino, and Freitas build a team of AI agents that translates everyday mathematics into formal language, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Autoformalization turns statements written in natural language into precise formal versions that proof software can check. The gap between the two is wide, and single models often stumble over definitions or syntax. Their framework, MASA, splits the translation work among collaborating agents, each driven by a large language model.

The architecture stresses modularity, so new agents and tools can slot in as the fast-moving field invents them. Agents draft, critique, and repair formal statements, calling on theorem provers to verify their work. The team demonstrates the system on real-world mathematical definitions and on standard formal mathematics datasets. They argue that the interplay between language models and provers raises both the speed and the reliability of translation. Their code and data are public for other researchers.
arxiv-2510-09488:
Tom Braden and Nicholas Proudfoot survey a meeting point of geometry and combinatorics in a 2025 arXiv paper. Intersection cohomology is a refined tool for studying singular spaces, and the sizes of its groups can encode deep counting information. In three settings, those groups have been computed with combinatorial sheaves, diagram-based tools that live on finite ordered sets rather than on the spaces themselves.

The first setting covers Schubert varieties and their Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials, realised through moment graph sheaves and Soergel bimodules. The second covers toric varieties and the g-polynomials of convex polytopes, handled through fans. The third covers arrangement Schubert varieties and matroid polynomials. In all three, the constructions still work when the underlying variety does not exist, giving intersection cohomology without spaces. The authors present the three stories in parallel and highlight applications to KLS polynomials.
arxiv-2510-09588:
Carlos Rito and Xavier Roulleau construct an infinite family of algebraic surfaces in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their starting point is the Cartwright-Steger surface, a famous ball quotient surface, whose fundamental group they probed by computer. From it they build a tower of normal projective surfaces, each a cyclic triple cover of the previous one.

After smoothing their singularities, the surfaces from the second level onward all lie on one line in the geography of surfaces. That line, where the two main invariants satisfy a fixed linear relation, runs parallel to the Bogomolov-Miyaoka-Yau line of ball quotients. The authors compute the fundamental groups of the first cases and find the smoothed surfaces simply connected up to the fifth level. Guided by the geometry of the construction, they conjecture that every surface in the tower is simply connected.
arxiv-2510-09788:
Kristaps John Balodis, the sole author, proves a major hypothesis in representation theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. The p-adic Kazhdan-Lusztig hypothesis concerns the representation theory of the general linear group over a p-adic field, a number system built from a prime. It predicts, in precise terms, how certain standard representations decompose, and its analogues have shaped decades of algebra.

Balodis proves the hypothesis for the group of invertible matrices of any size over such a field. His route follows the affine Hecke algebra approach of Chriss and Ginzburg, which he completes and clarifies here. A newer approach through graded affine Hecke algebras, due to Solleveld, reaches more general results, and the author is frank about that comparison. The paper's stated service is to articulate several results that experts have long treated as known but that were never formally recorded in the literature, fixing them in print.
arxiv-2510-10288:
Mandal, Divyadarshini Karthikeyan, and Manas Paldhe present SAM2LoRA in this 2025 arXiv paper on medical image segmentation. The method fine-tunes the Segment Anything Model 2 for retinal fundus images, photographs of the back of the eye used to screen for disease. Full fine-tuning of such a large model is costly.

SAM2LoRA instead adapts the model with low-rank updates, training only small added matrices, guided by a composite loss. The base model uses a hierarchical vision transformer pretrained as a masked autoencoder, which suits fast inference in low-resource settings. Parameter-efficient tuning lets clinics adapt a foundation model on modest hardware. Accurate fundus segmentation supports screening for diabetic eye disease and other retinal conditions.
arxiv-2510-10388:
Molodyk studies the geometry of bicycle tracks in this 2025 arXiv paper in mathematics. A bicycle is modeled as a fixed-length segment moving in the plane. The rear point's path must stay tangent to the segment, since the back wheel cannot slide sideways; that constraint shapes the tracks a bike leaves.

The paper concerns horizontal unitracks, track pairs with special symmetry. Given the front wheel's path, the rear path is forced, and the pair forms a curve problem with surprising depth. Bicycle geometry links to control theory and the theory of differential equations. Molodyk analyzes the complexity of these unitracks, asking which shapes can occur and how intricate the rear track can become.
arxiv-2510-10788:
Lotfi Berguiga and six co-authors give a complete theory of a tiny sideways shift of light that can sense minute changes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When a light beam reflects, it shifts slightly along the surface: the Goos-Hänchen shift. In resonant photonic structures this shift becomes giant, promising refractive index sensors of extreme sensitivity. Their formalism describes the shift and its sensitivity analytically around the critical coupling regime.

The theory connects the shift to physical parameters: the quality factor, angular dispersion, beam size, and the phase singularity. The authors confirm it numerically in two designs, a surface plasmon resonance sensor and a Bloch surface wave metasurface sensor. Their designed metasurface reaches a sensitivity more than five orders of magnitude beyond the current state of the art. They also show beam size is the main practical limit, and they compute detection limits that still surpass today's sensors.
arxiv-2510-11188:
Reading a protein's function from its amino-acid sequence takes specialized models trained on labeled corpora. Xinhui Chen and co-authors try a linguistic shortcut in this 2025 arXiv paper: treat the protein as a second language for a general large language model. Their framework rewrites amino-acid sequences as sentences in a symbolic language that the model can interpret through examples placed in context, with no further training.

The system adaptively builds sequence-question-answer triples that surface functional cues in a zero-shot setting. To support it, the team curated a bilingual corpus of 79,926 question-answer instances covering attribute prediction, descriptive understanding, and reasoning. Across diverse open-source models and GPT-4o, the method improved ROUGE-L scores by up to 17.2 percent with an average gain near 7 percent. It surpassed fine-tuned protein-specific language models, suggesting generic models guided by protein-as-language cues can beat specialized ones.
arxiv-2510-11888:
Jack Laiho and Kenny Ratliff compute what quantum gravity predicts for the correlations of spacetime itself. At low energies, gravity can be treated as an effective field theory, a systematic approximation that needs no final theory of everything. Their 2025 arXiv paper calculates Euclidean correlation functions of curvature and volume operators through one-loop order, the first quantum correction beyond the classical result.

Two subtleties anchor the work. First, the background spacetime's own quantum fluctuations must be included, or the answers depend on arbitrary gauge choices. Second, the conformal mode, the part of geometry that stretches sizes, needs careful analytic continuation. Once handled, the final formulas are strikingly spare. They involve only Newton's constant and the distance between source and sink. That makes them universal predictions and ideal benchmarks for lattice gravity simulations.
arxiv-2510-12388:
Pereira and a very large team report that the centaur Chiron has a system of three rings that appears to be still forming, in a 2025 arXiv planetary science paper. Chiron, a small body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus, had long been suspected of hosting orbiting material. In an occultation the body passes in front of a star, and dips in starlight reveal surrounding structures.

A multi chord occultation in September 2023 showed secondary events best explained by three confined rings at radii of a few hundred kilometers. The outermost lies beyond Chiron's Roche limit, where tidal forces should tear loose material apart. A broader disk and a new faint feature farther out were also detected. Comparing occultations since 1994 shows these features are not permanent. Chiron becomes only the fourth small body known to host rings, and they may be witnessing a ring system forming and evolving for the first time.
arxiv-2510-12488:
Nilo-Castellón and a large team use the James Webb Space Telescope to find galaxies hidden behind the Milky Way's dust and stars, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. This band of sky, the zone of avoidance, resists mapping because galactic extinction, crowding, and confusion noise hide background galaxies, leaving gaps in our picture of large scale structure.

The team analyzed infrared camera images of the NGC 3324 region with a customized extraction pipeline. They cross matched detections across three filters and validated them against established photometry. Selection criteria and visual inspection produced a refined sample of one hundred two galaxies. About a tenth were bright, while most were fainter. Morphologies ran from compact systems to spirals and lenticulars. Some galaxies shine through the most opaque parts of the molecular cloud. The results show the telescope can probe extragalactic sources through heavily obscured regions.
arxiv-2510-12588:
Botticini and co-authors derive from first principles how pressure drives gas liquid flow through capillaries, a stand in for porous rock, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Intermittent flow, where elongated bubbles form a train separated by liquid slugs, is common in such media. The authors model such a bubble train in a round capillary and map where the model stays valid.

The model extends classical Bretherton theory with film lubrication effects and the interplay of viscous plus capillary forces in the thin film coating each bubble. The total pressure drop turns out nonlinear in the mean liquid slug velocity, changing in discrete steps as the number of bubbles varies. Perturbation theory yields a pressure dependent effective viscosity for a single bubble. Extended to bundles of tubes, the framework shows flow exponents shifting smoothly with pressure, while the smallest pores disrupt that scaling. Deviations from Darcy's law are charted.
arxiv-2510-12688:
Pelletier and Cabau extend Poisson Lie group theory into the infinite dimensional setting needed for operator algebras, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Poisson Lie groups merge group structure with a matching Poisson bracket, a tool from classical mechanics and quantum groups. Their convenient version extends Lie groupoids, objects that behave like groups where multiplying is only partly defined, beyond finite dimensions.

The infinite case brings obstructions that break the finite dimensional theory. The authors name those obstructions and show how an adapted notion of bi algebroid, imported from finite dimensional work, can still be recovered. The paper is self contained and reviews the needed theory of partial Poisson manifolds and Banach Poisson Lie groups. As an example, they develop the circle of results by Odzijewicz and coauthors connecting Lie groupoids with von Neumann algebras. The work supplies a base for geometric methods in infinite dimensional analysis.
arxiv-2510-13088:
Patel, Pountourakis, and Taggart study repeated sales when buyers differ in sophistication in this 2025 arXiv paper on pricing theory. A seller without commitment power who tracks behavior can adapt prices, but a fully strategic buyer anticipates this and starves demand to keep prices low, a bleak prediction of earlier work. Real buyers vary in awareness of tracking, dynamic optimization skill, and patience.

The authors mix forward-looking sophisticated buyers with myopic naive ones, noting sophisticated buyers may fake naivete for lower prices. In a two-period model, strategic demand reduction proved robust, and adding naive buyers could paradoxically hurt the seller further through more intense overall reduction, a phenomenon they prove quite generally. In an infinite-horizon model with discounting, the bleak outcome disappears: equilibria emerge where the seller learns meaningfully and earns revenue approaching the commitment benchmark, even as naive buyers vanish.
arxiv-2510-13188:
Paul and colleagues learn tissue graphs for cancer image classification in this 2025 arXiv paper. In histopathology, how cells arrange within tissue reflects functional state, making graph-based learning natural for whole slide images. Most existing methods, though, fix the graph edges in advance, limiting their ability to capture real biological interaction complexity.

Their framework, ABiG-Net, models tissue at two scales. Locally, patch-level graphs are built from cellular orientation within each patch, yielding structural features. Globally, an image-level graph with sparse, biologically meaningful links between patches is learned through a first-order approximation to bilevel optimization, so the graph itself adapts to classification performance. On a colorectal cancer dataset the system reached accuracy in the high ninety percent range for both three-class grading and binary classification, and it scored similarly on a melanoma tumor-lymphocyte task.
arxiv-2510-13488:
Stasica and co-authors train a quadruped robot to walk steadily on a bridge that oscillates beneath it. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies vertical ground perturbations, a condition legged robots rarely face in training. The team uses the Unitree Go2 robot and a real steel-and-concrete bridge. That bridge stretches over thirteen metres and sways at about two cycles per second.

Training happens in MuJoCo simulation with reinforcement learning and domain randomization. Fifteen policies combine five gaits with three training conditions: rigid ground and two oscillating setups. The oscillating setups differ in whether height is judged against the bridge or the ground. Policies trained on the moving bridge proved more stable and adaptable on the real one. They transferred from simulation to the real bridge with no further tuning. Robust gaits emerged even without prior exposure to the bridge itself.
arxiv-2510-13588:
Xu proves new cases of the Rosenberg-Stolz conjecture, a 1994 claim about positive scalar curvature. This 2025 arXiv paper studies products of a closed manifold with flat Euclidean factors. The conjecture says such products cannot carry well-behaved metrics of uniformly positive scalar curvature when the base cannot. Xu approaches the claim through its contrapositive form.

Under a new angle condition that survives conformal changes, he pulls curvature positivity back to the base. The Riemannian result then yields a parallel statement in complex geometry. For Hermitian metrics on the product with the complex line, he produces a metric of positive Chern scalar curvature. That extends an earlier compact result of Yang to this noncompact setting. Both findings generalize to products with higher-dimensional flat factors. An example shows the angle condition cannot simply be dropped.
arxiv-2510-13688:
Gao and co-authors propose JNE, a metric that measures how nonlinear a brain encoding model truly is. Their 2025 arXiv paper works with models that map artificial network features onto fMRI brain responses. Such models predict blood oxygen signals, yet their inner nonlinearity stayed hard to interpret. A principled gauge of that nonlinearity was missing until now.

JNE reads the spread of local linear maps, called Jacobians, from features to predicted responses. Wide spread means the model's response bends strongly with the input. Tests on varied activation functions and network designs confirm the metric behaves as intended. On real fMRI data, nonlinearity grows from early to higher visual areas. That gradient matches the known layout of the visual cortex. An extension, JNE-SS, further shows stimulus-selective nonlinear patterns in specialized brain regions.
arxiv-2510-13888:
Ma and co-authors build ProofBench and ProofGrader to score natural language math proofs in fine detail. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that proof generation lacks the easy answer checking of ordinary math tasks. Without a reliable grader, better provers cannot be trained or selected. Expert judgement is the gold standard but scales terribly.

ProofBench holds 145 competition problems and 435 model-written solutions rated by experts, drawn from contests like the IMO and Putnam. The team explores evaluator design across backbone models, context, and workflow choices. ProofGrader combines a strong reasoning model, reference solutions with marking schemes, and simple ensembling. Its scores land within a mean absolute error of 0.926 points of the human experts on the benchmark's scale, far better than naive baselines, the authors report. Picking the best of sixteen proofs, it closes most of the gap to a human oracle.
arxiv-2510-13988:
Gareth Arturo Marks and Abdullah Al Zaif construct boson stars in four, five, and six spacetime dimensions and test whether they hold together, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A boson star is a ball of a massive complex field held up by its own gravity. It has been proposed as an exotic alternative to black holes. It is even a candidate for dark matter halos.

The authors build round boson star solutions with two kinds of self-interaction, then generalize the pulsation equations, which govern small radial oscillations, to any dimension and potential. The analysis shows radially stable higher-dimensional solutions exist. To check beyond small disturbances, they ran full nonlinear simulations in spherical symmetry, using a reduction trick that lets one numerical framework evolve any background dimension. The evolutions confirm that solutions flagged as stable by the linear analysis are indeed stable under nonlinear spherical dynamics.
arxiv-2510-14188:
Eric Albers, Paul Marriott, and Masami Tatsuno bring information geometry, a framework for separating interactions of different orders in data, to EEG recordings, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The methods were honed on spike trains, which are binary, but electroencephalography produces continuous signals, so the data must be discretized without destroying the interactions of interest.

The authors compare three binarization strategies, then hunted for third-order interactions, patterns involving three signals, during an imagined motor movement experiment. Significance was judged against phase-shuffled surrogate data that destroy higher-order dependencies while keeping each signal's spectrum. A forward model with planted dependencies showed where information leaks away; the biggest loss came when forcing dependencies onto wave-like signals. Despite sparse data, forty-five trials per condition, the EEG analysis detected significant third-order interactions during the task, showing the geometry-based methods can extract higher-order structure from brain waves.
arxiv-2510-14288:
Dao-He Ma and Jin An realize a new class of topological superconductors that combine gapless Dirac points with higher-order topology, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Topological nodal superconductors host exotic surface states, but in most cases their protected nodes sit only at special symmetric positions, limiting the physics.

Building a general theory for superconductors with several orbitals, the authors construct three-dimensional, time-reversal-invariant Dirac superconductors whose protected gapless Dirac nodes sit at general positions in the momentum space. They then add pairing perturbations that break time-reversal symmetry. Majorana hinge modes appear, ghostly zero-energy states confined to the sample's edges. That is the signature of higher-order topology, where the boundary of the boundary carries the physics. They also propose a family whose Dirac nodes carry nonzero even chiralities and are marked by Majorana arcs, widening the catalog of topological superconducting phases.
arxiv-2510-14388:
Zhe Wu and co-authors present Hi-Agent, a hierarchical vision-language agent that operates phones by splitting the work between a high-level planner and a low-level actor, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier phone agents map screenshots to actions, which generalizes poorly to tasks and app layouts because no reasoning intervenes.

Hi-Agent trains a high-level reasoning model, which sets subgoals, with a low-level model. Training reformulates multi-step decision-making as a sequence of subgoals. A foresight advantage function uses execution feedback from the low-level model to guide the high-level one. This avoids the path explosion that plagues reinforcement learning on long tasks. It enables stable training without a critic network. On the Android-in-the-Wild benchmark, Hi-Agent reached a success rate near eighty-eight percent, above prompt-based, supervised, and reinforcement-learning baselines.
arxiv-2510-14588:
Chen and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a video generation method that keeps objects moving in a coherent way. Modern generators make striking images, but motion and interaction over time often fall apart. The authors blame two bottlenecks. User motion hints, such as small two-dimensional maps, shrink to too few tokens inside the model to guide it well. And training one output head for both looks and motion favors pretty textures over steady movement.

Their framework, STANCE, answers with two components. Instance Cues turn sparse, user-editable hints into a dense motion field that carries depth information for each object. A technique called Dense RoPE then tags a small set of motion tokens so they stay prominent inside the model. The system also predicts helper maps, such as depth, alongside the color video, anchoring a scene's structure while color handles appearance.
arxiv-2510-14688:
Shiraishi, Chen, and Simeone propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a low-power way to watch for anomalies with brain-like wireless sensors. Neuromorphic sensors stay quiet until something changes, then fire a spike. Uses range from brain-machine interfaces to remote environmental monitoring. In their system, a central reader queries a chosen subset of sensors in each time frame, and the sensors answer with short impulse radio bursts encoding what they sensed.

The reader must decide whether conditions are normal or anomalous while keeping false alarms rigorously below a set rate. The authors use an online testing method based on e-values, which controls the false discovery rate without needing to know how often anomalies occur. Choosing which sensors to query is cast as a best-arm identification problem from bandit theory, and optimized as data arrives. Evaluations show reliable detection under strict false-alarm limits, with low delay.
arxiv-2510-14788:
Xu and a large team of co-authors describe, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a recommendation engine that follows users across every corner of a platform at once. On content platforms, people search, browse feeds, and discover material in separate scenarios. Traditional recommenders optimize each scenario in isolation, ignoring the signals users leave elsewhere, and they struggle to absorb large language models at billion-user scale.

Their engine, RED, builds one representation of each user's interests by aggregating behavior from all scenarios. A language-model-powered architecture produces rich, multifaceted user and item representations while staying efficient enough to deploy. A scenario-aware mixing and querying policy fuses the behavioral signals at serving time, expressing fine-grained preferences that depend on context. The team validated the system with online A/B tests on Xiaohongshu, reaching hundreds of millions of users, and report substantial gains in both content recommendation and advertising.
arxiv-2510-14888:
Rebouças and co-authors test, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether a fast approximate simulation method can support cosmology with a dark energy that changes over time. Upcoming galaxy surveys will measure matter clustering on small scales, but full simulations for every cosmology are unaffordable. Recent hints suggest dark energy's equation of state may evolve, which multiplies the models to check.

The team uses COLA, a method that trades some accuracy for great speed, to generate simulation suites under the evolving dark energy model. They graft those results onto an existing high-precision emulator for the standard cosmology, extending its reach into new parameter space. The combined emulator reproduced a benchmark's nonlinear power spectrum boosts with under two percent error. In a mock cosmic shear analysis like the LSST survey's coming first year, its parameter constraints agreed closely with the benchmark's, with shifts under a third of a standard deviation.
arxiv-2510-15088:
Astronomer D. R. Mizuno and six co-authors present an improved atlas of space spectra in this 2025 arXiv paper. The spectra come from the Short-Wavelength Spectrometer aboard the Infrared Space Observatory, a telescope that flew in the 1990s. Their team reworked the full scans, which span light wavelengths from about 2 to 45 micrometers, updating an atlas from twenty-two years ago.

The gain lies in how the twelve bands of each scan are joined into one smooth spectrum. New data from the Spitzer Space Telescope, plus close care given to each scan on its own, helped line the bands up far better than before. That work removed odd negative fluxes, meaning readings below zero that cannot be real, found all through the old products. The new set holds 1,035 reworked spectra, now kept at the IRSA archive for any researcher to use.
arxiv-2510-15188:
Ahmed Aly, Essam Mansour, and Amr Youssef build a security system that both spots stealthy intrusions and explains them in plain story form. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets advanced persistent threats, attacks that hide for months inside system audit logs. Earlier tools flagged odd behavior on graphs of those logs but cried wolf often and gave analysts only coarse alerts.

Their system, OCR-APT, learns what normal behavior around each graph node looks like, using graph neural networks rather than fragile clues like file paths or IP addresses. A large language model then walks through each flagged subgraph stage by stage, drafting the attack story while checking each step before moving on, which curbs invented details. On three public benchmark datasets, including two from DARPA programs, OCR-APT beat leading systems on detection accuracy and on how readable its alerts were.
arxiv-2510-15488:
Davide Laurenzano and John F. Wheater derive a soft theorem inside BFSS matrix theory, a quantum model proposed as a definition of M-theory. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies the effective theory of bound states of D0-branes, which correspond to gravitons in eleven-dimensional spacetime. Soft theorems describe what happens when one particle carries almost no energy.

The effective theory comes from removing heavy degrees of freedom at large distances, keeping a one-loop approximation. The authors show this one-dimensional theory, once given an ultraviolet cutoff, is super-renormalizable, so all its Feynman diagrams stay finite. They identify operators with the right quantum numbers to stand for gravitons in the target space. Their main result is that correlations of those operators factorize in the soft limit at both leading and subleading orders. That matches the behavior expected from eleven-dimensional supergravity.
arxiv-2511-00088:
An NVIDIA-led team introduces Alpamayo-R1, a vision-language-action model for autonomous driving that joins causal reasoning with trajectory planning. End-to-end imitation systems scale well but stay brittle in rare, safety-critical long-tail scenarios where supervision is sparse and causal understanding limited. Their Chain of Causation dataset, built by hybrid auto-labeling with human review, grounds decisions in causal language.

Reasoning traces explain why a maneuver is chosen before the trajectory is produced. Self-driving readers get a model designed for the cases that dominate risk rather than average miles. Decision-grounded reasoning also gives engineers an audit trail when the car acts unexpectedly.
arxiv-2511-00188: Matteo De Berardinis and Silvio Ghilardi offer a short, dense note in mathematical logic. They work with S5 algebras, which mirror a kind of logic where statements keep the same truth across linked possible worlds. Their result links these algebras to actions of finite symmetric groups, the groups that shuffle finite sets. The link uses Kan extensions, a tool from category theory for growing maps between structures. The note suits readers in logic and algebra who already know these terms.
arxiv-2511-00288:
Mao Fabrice Djete opens a new class of mean-field control problems, where a planner steers a huge population of agents. In the classic setup, agents are interchangeable and interact only through average behavior. Djete instead fixes a network pattern, often of graphon type, that encodes who influences whom, and the pattern can be uneven and one-sided.

The novelty is that the interaction pattern itself becomes a control: the planner tunes both each agent's local dynamics and the network that links them. Djete develops relaxed, randomized controls for this setting, proves they match the strong form, and shows existence and continuity of the best achievable value. Finite populations with general interaction matrices converge to the mean-field limit as their patterns converge, with optimal values and strategies matching in the limit.
arxiv-2511-00488:
Jun Gao, Yun Peng, and Xiaoxue Ren study why language models stumble at deductive code reasoning: following a program's execution step by step. Models write code well yet reason about it poorly, and the causes were murky. Their empirical study names three: a built-in gap between generation and reasoning skill, a steady bias toward certain code sources, and weak zero-shot generalization on hard benchmarks.

Their framework, ReMind, answers with three cooperating agents. A mutator creates code variants to break source bias. An executor traces variable states step by step to expose inconsistencies. An inspector flags faulty reasoning steps and refines control flow to close the reasoning gap. Across two benchmarks and five models, ReMind beat baselines and generalized to new problems without examples, a robust pattern for reasoning tools.
arxiv-2511-00588:
Dong Chen and nine co-authors put six leading language models through a safety check for spine surgery decision support. Hallucinations, outputs that sound plausible but clash with fact or context, could endanger patients if a model advises treatment. Their clinician-centered design scores diagnostic precision, recommendation quality, reasoning robustness, output coherence, and knowledge alignment across thirty expert-validated spinal cases.

One model, DeepSeek-R1, led overall, above all in trauma and infection cases. Reasoning-enhanced variants did not always beat their standard versions, a warning that longer chains of thought do not guarantee clinical reliability. Stress tests with amplified complexity lowered advice quality notably, even while surface clarity and coherence held or rose. The authors urge interpretability tools, such as visible reasoning chains, inside clinical workflows.
arxiv-2511-00688:
Mohammadamir Bazrafshan and Thomas Kühne tune graphene's electronic character by confining it in space. Graphite conducts like a gapless semiconductor, a single graphene sheet conducts superbly, and narrow graphene ribbons can open a tunable band gap. The authors stack the two worlds: a layer of graphene nanoribbons laid over one or more graphene sheets, and ask what electronic structure emerges from the interaction.

Using a tight-binding model for graphite, they scan configurations of these heterostructures. The combined system cannot be read as two separate systems at all. Even a gapless armchair ribbon layer opens a local gap near the Dirac point when stacked on graphene in a bilayer. Band steepness, which sets how fast electrons move, also proves tunable. The structures look promising for electronic devices built from carbon alone.
arxiv-2511-00788:
Darshan Kumar, Deepak Jain, and Shobhit Mahajan open a two part study of cosmic expansion built on time delays in strong gravitational lensing. When light from a distant source takes several paths around a massive galaxy, the delays between paths carry information about cosmic distances and geometry.

Joined with the distance sum rule, those delays give a model independent route to expansion history. The team adds supernova data sets and baryon acoustic oscillation results from DESI's second release. Lens plus supernova data alone lean slightly toward an open universe, while adding DESI tightens the bounds and leans slightly closed. A flat universe remains allowed throughout, and the main expansion parameters agree with the standard model.
arxiv-2511-01088:
Arturo Fernandez-Perez and Gustavo Marra prove a normal form theorem for a class of Levi-flat hypersurfaces, special surfaces in complex geometry that are foliated by complex hypersurfaces. Their surfaces are analytic and are defined by the vanishing of the real part of a holomorphic function whose singularity is of Morse-Bott type.

A normal form is a standard coordinate description that makes such surfaces easier to classify and compare. As one consequence, their theorem recovers the known Burns-Gong normal form for Levi-flat hypersurfaces with generic Morse singularities. It also provides a new normal form for a certain class of real analytic quadratic Levi-flat hypersurfaces, extending the list of cases with clean local models.
arxiv-2511-01388:
Sahana Rossler and co-authors grow and measure single crystals of alpha-MnTe, a hexagonal crystal classed as an altermagnet, a newer magnetic class mixing traits of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. The crystals were grown by vapor transport with iodine, and X-ray checks confirmed the expected hexagonal structure.

Magnetization and heat readings show an antiferromagnetic transition near room temperature, and the magnetic entropy matches the spin state theory predicts for the manganese ions. Angle and field readings reveal complex patterns tied to magnetic domains, with an anomaly around one tesla. A fitted domain scale model with higher order anisotropic exchange interactions explains the pattern. The one axis and one way anisotropies seen come from short lived domain setups and one way magnetization processes.
arxiv-2511-01488:
Shunyuan Shang, Emna Zedini, Abla Kammoun, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini propose a three-hop optical chain to reach city users whose direct view of the sky is blocked by buildings and trees. A ground station beams light to a high-altitude platform. The platform relays it onward to an optical intelligent reflecting surface. That surface is a controllable mirror array, and it steers the light down to the user.

The study models the impairments on the reflecting leg, including air turbulence, pointing errors, attenuation, and geometric misalignment losses, and derives a close approximation for the loss distribution. From there the authors get closed-form formulas for outage probability, average bit-error rate, and channel capacity. The formulas cover the reflecting link alone and the full end-to-end path. High-power approximations reveal the system's diversity order.
arxiv-2511-01888:
Cynthia Marcelino, Thomas Pusztai, and Stefan Nastic attack the hidden tax in serverless computing: moving data between functions. Stateless functions must fetch and store data through remote services, and the usual serialization, deserialization, and user-kernel copying inflate latency and resource use on every hop.

Their sidecar shim, Roadrunner, serves WebAssembly-based functions with near-zero-copy, serialization-free transfer. It maps the function's own memory and moves data along a dedicated virtual data hose, bypassing the costly format conversions and context switches. Experiments showed clear gains. Inter-function communication latency improved by between 44 and 89 percent. Serialization overhead was eliminated in 97 percent of transfers. Throughput rose by a factor of 69, compared with the standard path. Latency reached near-native levels for this class of serverless functions.
arxiv-2511-02288:
Cuong Tuan Nguyen and four co-authors teach computers to read handwritten mathematics by treating each expression as a graph. Symbols become nodes and their spatial relations become edges, turning recognition into a structure problem. A deep bidirectional LSTM network first segments and recognises the symbols and classifies their spatial relations, producing an initial rough graph of the expression.

A grammar-based parser then proposes every plausible spatial relation. A graph neural network trained for link prediction prunes away the unnecessary connections, leaving the final symbol label graph that captures the expression's true structure. Experiments reported in the paper show the effectiveness of the approach and show promising performance on handwritten expression structure recognition, a step toward reliable input of handwritten maths into digital systems.
arxiv-2511-02888:
Zhongmin Li, Runze Ma, Jiahao Tan, Chengzi Tan, and Shuangjia Zheng built NABench, a large benchmark for models that predict how DNA and RNA changes affect fitness. A single letter change in a sequence can shift function a lot, and new foundation models claim to predict those shifts from sequence alone. Past data sets were too uneven to compare the models fairly.

NABench gathers 162 high-throughput assays and 2.6 million mutated sequences across many DNA and RNA families, with standard splits and rich metadata. The team tested twenty-nine leading models under zero-shot, few-shot, transfer, and supervised settings. Scores varied widely by task and molecule type, exposing clear strengths and failure modes. The open release aims to set firm baselines for nucleic acid modeling.
arxiv-2511-03288:
Peter Raffai and colleagues make a case that cosmic speedup needs no dark energy at all. Their universe starts as the plain matter-only model, but its matter is lumpy rather than smooth. As lumps grow, the uneven expansion bends the overall history toward a steady coasting state, and that bend mimics acceleration when read with smooth tools.

They fit the lumpy model to microwave background, galaxy spacing, and supernova data. The fit stands close to the standard dark energy model on those tests. It also eases the long clash over the current expansion rate and gives a cosmic age near thirteen point seven billion years, in line with old star cluster estimates.
