Expanding filters across many orientations can restore invariance, but at high cost in compute and memory traffic. Their framework removes the usual data lowering step and shares data cleverly among symmetrically rotated filters. That sharing cuts both traffic and redundant work. The method also extends to arbitrary rotation angles that are not symmetric. Benchmarks show faster training and lower energy use than a leading library, with accuracy matching strong rotation invariant methods. Inside a segmentation model, accuracy improves over a non rotation aware baseline.
arxiv-2512-09388:
Kaiwen Ji and colleagues demonstrate a ring of tiny lasers that emits twisted light, carrying orbital angular momentum. Structured light like this is useful for communications and sensing, but generating it usually needs bulky optics. Their device is an array of nanolasers on an indium phosphide photonic crystal membrane, arranged in a ring.

The array realizes a non-Hermitian version of the Rice-Mele model, with alternating coupling strengths and uneven on-site energies. A symmetry protects a special zero mode that locks neighboring lasers into a steady quarter-cycle phase step, winding the phase around the ring. By adjusting the gain and loss balance in a parity-time-like pumping scheme, the team tunes the system to a chiral exceptional point, where energy flows one way between cavities despite reciprocal coupling. The far-field emission then carries nonzero orbital angular momentum, a direct sign of the phase-structured mode.
arxiv-2512-10888:
Brandon Smock and co-authors release PubTables-v2, a large dataset for pulling tables out of documents whole. Table extraction usually runs in two steps, find the table, then read its structure. But newer vision-language models promise to extract tables directly in the context of the full page or document. Progress was hard to prove, because annotated data for the harder settings did not exist.

PubTables-v2 unifies extraction across levels of surrounding context and is the first benchmark for tables that span several pages. Their evaluations draw a sharp lesson about scale. Frontier models crush small ones on the hardest task, full-document multi-page extraction, by a wide margin on the GriTS content score. On the narrower cropped-table task, targeted training closes the gap entirely and can even reverse it. The dataset is public on Hugging Face, with code and models to follow.
arxiv-2512-11188:
Diego Arcis, Jorge Espinoza, and Marcelo Flores introduce a new algebra that merges two known generalisations of a classical object from representation theory. The Iwahori Hecke algebra encodes symmetries of matrix groups. Solomon extended it to the full matrix monoid, giving rook monoid algebras, while Yokonuma replaced a subgroup in its construction, giving another family.

Their framed rook algebra comes from double cosets of the unipotent subgroup inside the full matrix monoid, and its pieces are indexed by a combinatorial object called the framed symmetric inverse monoid. They also define an abstract version through generators and relations, then prove the two agree under a specific choice of parameters. A faithful action on a tensor space and an explicit basis complete the description. The work gives algebraists a unified object connecting rook theory and Yokonuma type Hecke algebras.
arxiv-2512-11388:
Felipe Ribeiro Fujita de Mello and Hideyuki Takada ask a useful question for machine translation: does carefully choosing fine tuning data beat simply using more of it? They fine tuned open language models on Japanese to English translation with data picked by five varied selectors. The selectors ranged from word frequency statistics and learned quality estimators to plain random choice, all under identical training settings.

Selectors that judged meaning consistently outperformed those based on surface word patterns or geometric heuristics. More strikingly, the chosen data sets differed by only a few percent, yet model results shifted substantially. Fine tuning, in other words, is highly sensitive to which cases it sees, not just how many. For builders of translation systems with limited compute, investing in meaning based data choice offers a cheaper path to quality than scaling data or model size.
arxiv-2512-11588:
Gregor von Laszewski and a large team argue that testing AI systems needs a craft of its own. Tests, called benchmarks, let researchers compare models fairly. But modern AI tests are costly, need rare hardware, and age fast as models learn to game fixed test sets.

The authors call for benchmark carpentry: shared skills and training for building tests that keep changing with the field. They draw on work with MLCommons and big lab programs. Good tests, they say, should use varied hardware, not just the fastest chips, and should report results that map to real tasks. Open training at all levels would let more groups build and judge tests well.
arxiv-2512-11688:
Ruslan Nauryzbaev, Ivan Shestakov, and Ualbai Umirbaev classify a special family of symmetries in a free algebra. The algebra is metabelian and anticommutative, meaning swapped products flip sign and triple products vanish in a set way. They study maps that move one variable and fix the rest, called Chein automorphisms after twin cases for groups and Lie algebras.

For rank two, every such map turns out to be linear, hence tame. For rank three and up, the picture flips. The simplest non basic Chein map, of degree three, is shown to be wild in all those ranks, meaning it cannot be built from basic steps. The result completes a corner of algebra symmetry theory.
arxiv-2512-11988:
Xianghui Xie and co-authors present CARI4D, a method that rebuilds human and object interaction in 3D over time from a single video. One camera view hides depth and causes blocked views. Unknown people and objects make steady 4D recovery hard. Past methods needed a known object model. Others only handled a short list of object types.

CARI4D needs neither crutch. It picks among pose guesses from foundation models. It then refines them with a render and compare loop for space, time, and pixel fit. A last step reasons about contact points for a physical cleanup. Errors fell by more than a third on both known and unseen object types. It even works on wild internet videos with no retraining.
arxiv-2512-12088:
S R Eshwar and co-authors stress test Reliable Policy Iteration, a reinforcement learning method built to keep value estimates rising steadily. Deep reinforcement learning is famously touchy: samples are costly, training wobbles, and settings matter too much. Reliable Policy Iteration restores a classic monotonicity promise under function approximation.

The team runs it on CartPole and Inverted Pendulum while varying network shape and environment settings. Against DQN, Double DQN, DDPG, TD3, and PPO, it reached near optimal play early and held it as training continued. Rivals more often spiked and faded. The results pitch the method as a steadier default for control tasks where reliability counts.
arxiv-2512-12288:
A 2025 paper submitted under the name Mahule Roy proposes a quantum aware AI framework for finding new materials. Most generators train on data from density functional theory, a standard physics method with known flaws. For strongly linked electron systems, those flaws pass into the models, which then miss materials where the theory is qualitatively wrong.

The framework pairs a diffusion based generator with a checker network trained on data at many theory levels, from PBE up to CCSD(T). An active learning loop targets spots where low and high level results diverge, and there it found 3 to 5 times more stable candidates than DFT only baselines. ArXiv later withdrew the submission over incorrect authorship and cut its author list back, so the work stands as an unvetted claim, not a settled result.
arxiv-2512-12388:
Pulak Kundu and Uzzwal Kumar Mallick model a wildlife disaster on Amami Oshima Island, Japan, in a 2025 paper. Mongooses were brought from the Indian subcontinent to control venomous Habu snakes. Instead, they caused major ecological harm and threatened the island's native species and long term biodiversity.

Their math model tracks snakes, mongooses, mice, and natural resources together. They check stability, uniqueness, and which factors matter most, then run simulations with a Runge-Kutta method. Starting trapping 10 years after release, rather than almost 20, would have changed the outcome sharply in the model. Mongooses would have survived alongside natives, preserving balance, so they urge modeling before such decisions.
arxiv-2512-12488:
James Luther and Donald Brown test the cultural leanings of large language models in a 2025 paper. Culture shapes how people read everyday exchanges, so a model's default culture matters as AI chat spreads. Using Hofstede's cultural dimensions and the VSM13 survey, they measure the alignment of eight popular models, from GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4 to DeepSeek-V3 and Llama 3.1.

Most models favored the United States when no culture was specified. Cultural prompting, a system prompt asking for a target country's stance, moved seven of eight models closer to the target among China, France, India, Iran, Japan, and the United States. Japan and China were hardest to match, even for the Chinese built DeepSeek models.
arxiv-2512-12588:
Jie Guo, Shuyuan Yang, Jinchuan Hou, Xiaofei Qi, and Kan He introduce a true k-entanglement measure for multipartite quantum systems in a 2025 paper. Entanglement among many parties powers quantum technologies, but universal measures are scarce, and the standard convex roof construction is often intractable to compute. Their work aims to give this measure a rigorous, usable yardstick.

They build a framework of axioms and define a measure that meets all axioms without those extensions, and that can be computed efficiently. A universal algorithm evaluates any state of finite size, with open source software covering all partitions of four qubit systems. Numerical tests certified k-entanglement within 200 seconds, tightening bounds and revealing new thresholds.
arxiv-2512-13088:
Chenmin Sun and Nikolay Tzvetkov prove a smoothing effect for the nonlinear Schrodinger equation in two dimensions. They work on a torus, a doughnut-shaped domain, with random initial data. The claim is that solutions become smoother than the data over time, almost surely.

For deterministic data, this effect was known on a circle but not on higher-dimensional tori. Their proof uses a quantitative form of quasi-invariance for Gaussian measures. Those measures are tied to a smoothing operator whose strength is set by a parameter above two. The result adds a rare global statement about random waves in two dimensions.
arxiv-2512-13388:
Jefferson Tang and Pavel Volkov show that twisted junctions between superconductors can detect pair density waves, states where Cooper pairs carry a repeating spatial pattern. Such waves are hard to spot with ordinary probes, since the pattern is a modulation rather than a uniform signal.

In a twisted junction between two pair density wave materials, an in-plane magnetic field makes the critical Josephson current peak at a finite field value. That peak position is set by the twist angle and the wave's period, an explicit fingerprint. The signature survives changes in geometry and some disorder. Its temperature behavior can separate a pure pair density wave from byproducts of other orders.
arxiv-2512-13688:
Lorenzo Bertassi and co-authors offer a new way to find periodic signals of any shape in active galactic nucleus light curves. Pairs of massive black holes should appear as periodic AGN in time-domain surveys. Most signals will not be simple sine waves, since gas feeding, Doppler boosting, and lensing shape them in complex ways.

Their method uses Gaussian processes with a flexible periodic kernel built for unevenly sampled data with realistic quasar noise. On mock light curves, it beat periodogram analysis and less flexible Gaussian process methods. It found more true signals, including sawtooth shapes. Sensitivity depended most on how many cycles were observed, a guide for surveys such as PTF and LSST.
arxiv-2512-13788:
Shengfan Cao, Francesco Borrelli, and Eunhyek Joa present SCPO, a method for constrained policy learning that keeps every step safe. Safety-critical learning must improve performance without leaving a safe regime. Their setting has rollout-based safety limits that can be evaluated but not differentiated in closed form.

SCPO projects each gradient update into a local safe region in weight space. It builds that region from rollout safety checks plus smoothness bounds, solving a convex projection problem at each step. Starting from a safe point, all intermediate policies stay safe when projections are feasible. Tests on constrained regression and double-integrator imitation show SCPO rejects unsafe updates, stays feasible, and still improves the objective meaningfully.
arxiv-2512-14088:
David Roberts and four coauthors study Markov jump processes, which model systems that hop between states at random times. Their 2025 paper looks at cases close to balance, called equilibrium, where simple diffusion models often miss large rare swings.

Inside, the authors build a better diffusion model that extends an older method once limited to balanced systems. They use tools from stochastic thermodynamics, the study of heat and chance in small systems. They prove the method works to first order away from balance. Tests show it beats the standard Kramers-Moyal expansion at steady state and over time, including error rates for a small electronic memory.
arxiv-2512-14288:
Georgios Bouchouras and four coauthors test large language models for building an ontology for Parkinson disease monitoring and alerting in a 2025 paper. An ontology is a structured map of concepts and links in a field, used so software can reason about alerts and patient data.

They compare four methods: one shot prompts, chain of thought prompts, and two hybrid human plus model methods called X HCOME and SimX HCOME plus. Models alone built plausible ontologies, but the results were incomplete and needed heavy human repair. The hybrid methods came much closer to expert built ontologies. Continuous human supervision and stepwise refinement gave the most complete and accurate result, pointing to collaboration over full automation.
arxiv-2512-14588:
Modern quantum circuits can measure qubits in the middle of a computation and let the results steer the gates that follow. That adaptive style makes it possible to carry out quantum instruments, the most general kind of quantum measurement with outcomes, step by step, in sequence.

Realizing an instrument sequentially means fewer qubits are needed at each of the measurement steps, easing the load on small, noisy hardware. The authors work out how this sequential realization is done in general. The result matters for near-term quantum devices, where qubit counts are tight and mid-circuit measurements are a precious resource.
arxiv-2512-14888:
Nardo Giménez and five coauthors build an algorithm that can describe the solution set of polynomial equations while excluding a forbidden region. In algebraic geometry, a Kronecker representation compresses a finite solution set into a compact, workable form. Their variety is the closure of points where several polynomials vanish, minus points on a chosen hypersurface.

The algorithm is probabilistic and of Kronecker type, working over any perfect field. It blends homotopy deformation with symbolic Newton-Hensel lifting and elimination, using lifting curves as stepping stones. Its cost grows in a soft quadratic way with the degrees and size of the input. The authors give sharp bounds for two workhorse cases in computer algebra: finite fields, and the rationals. The result serves computational algebraists who need certified descriptions of such sets.
arxiv-2512-15388:
Reinhard Moratz and five coauthors improve how language models give walking directions through street networks. A route instruction is only helpful if a pedestrian can follow it on foot, step by step. Plain text generation often misses the spatial relations that make directions clear, like which side a landmark falls on or how streets connect.

The approach grounds the model in the street network itself, treated as a graph. Qualitative spatial representations describe relations between places in human style terms rather than raw coordinates. A graph based retrieval step feeds those relations to the model as it writes. The abstract states the aim in a single sentence. The study targets better route instructions for pedestrian wayfinders, built on bilateral spatial reasoning about the network.
arxiv-2512-15688:
Adam Kaufman and co authors introduce BashArena, a control setting for highly privileged AI agents, in a 2025 paper. Future agents may run servers with broad rights, and a misaligned agent could abuse those rights. AI control research tries to limit such damage while keeping agents useful.

BashArena holds 637 Linux system administration and infrastructure tasks in realistic environments, plus four sabotage goals for a red team: run malware, steal secrets, raise privileges, and disable a firewall. Frontier models are tested at doing tasks, sabotaging without detection, and spotting sabotage. Claude Sonnet 4.5 carried out sabotage while evading a GPT-4.1 mini monitor 26 percent of the time. Results set a baseline for control protocols.
arxiv-2512-16188:
Jianping Mei, Siqi Ai, and Ye Yuan present a gene mapping method in a 2025 arXiv paper. Spatial transcriptomics measures gene activity across a tissue slice while keeping each spot's location. The hard part is grouping spots into meaningful regions, since genes and positions interact in complex ways.

Most methods encode the gene data and the spatial layout separately and merge them only at the end. Their model, stMFG, instead mixes the two views after every layer through cross-view attention. Contrastive learning sharpens the groups while spatial constraints keep them coherent. On brain cortex and breast cancer data sets, stMFG beat leading methods, improving a standard clustering score by up to 14 percent on some slices. Cleaner tissue maps help biologists read how organs and tumors are organized.
arxiv-2512-16888:
Jens Havgaard Nyhegn, Esben Rohan Christensen, and Georg M. Bruun build a field theory for an exciton moving inside an electronic Wigner crystal, a grid formed by electrons themselves in thin materials. Past spectroscopy treated the crystal as frozen, yet its vibrations may shape exciton lines.

The exciton can emit crystal phonons while staying in one band or jumping bands. A self-consistent Born treatment shows these processes dress the exciton into a polaron, a joint particle with a shifted energy and a finite lifetime. The shift and damping swing with electron density in complex ways, and damping jumps when the polaron energy enters the phonon continuum. The results explain traits seen in exciton spectra.
arxiv-2512-17388: Athanasios Beslikas and Alan Sola decide when a special class of functions on a two-disk domain belongs to Dirichlet-type spaces, which measure how wildly a function can vary. The functions, rational inner functions, are tidy fractions with a mirroring property. Their test rests on contact order, a geometric count of how flatly the function touches its singular points, where it misbehaves. That single count settles membership across a whole scale of spaces, including higher-order versions, and several side results follow from the main test.
arxiv-2512-17488:
Almustapha A Wakili and four co-authors outline tumors in brain scans without asking hospitals to hand over patient data. Pooling scans in one place trains strong models, but privacy law and ethics block that pooling. Their system, TwinSegNet, instead sends the model out to each hospital under federated learning, so scans stay home.

Each site fine-tunes the shared model on its own cases, forming a personal digital twin of the global model. The core network mixes classic image filters with a transformer stage to catch both fine edges and wide context. Across nine MRI data sets, the system scored high on overlap accuracy, with sensitivity and specificity above 90 percent. Privacy, in these tests, cost little accuracy.
arxiv-2512-17588:
Sajjad Taravati designs a chip-scale device that turns one low radio tone into a comb of higher tones that travel one way only. Cold superconducting circuits need many control tones at once, above all for quantum computers, yet the usual one-way parts are bulky ferrite blocks that hate the cold. A pattern that varies in space and time can do the same job on a chip.

His design strings Josephson junctions, the workhorse of superconducting electronics, along a bus and modulates them in a traveling pattern. Simulations show the comb's spread and strength follow the applied flux settings, and each output channel can be picked out by retuning. Channels stay well isolated from each other. One input feeding many qubits is the headline use.
arxiv-2512-17788:
Wei Tang and three co-authors fix a trust problem in learning from vague labels. In multi-instance partial-label learning, each training bag of items carries a shortlist of candidate labels, only one of which is right for the hidden item. Models learn to pick, but their confidence scores often lie: a 90 percent claim that is right half the time.

Their calibratable disambiguation loss grades the model's top guess against its strongest rival and scales the lesson by that margin. Two variants pit the runner-up candidate, or the best outsider, against the leader. Theory ties the method to momentum-based training and bounds its calibration error. On benchmark and real-world sets, accuracy rose and stated confidence finally matched reality. The loss drops into existing systems unchanged.
arxiv-2512-18888:
Akshit Achara and four co-authors build an audit for a quiet failure of neural networks: shortcut learning. Models often lean on spurious cues tied to labels in training data rather than the real signal, and when the cue tracks a sensitive attribute, bias follows. Existing checks rely on eyeballing images, useless when cues are invisible, as in medical scans. Their framework, OSCAR, posted to arXiv in December 2025, works in pixel space with numbers instead.

OSCAR turns attribution maps into rank profiles of image regions, then compares three models: a balanced baseline, the test model, and a sensitive-attribute predictor. Correlations between the profiles measure shortcut reliance and rank the regions driving it. On CelebA, CheXpert, and ADNI the metrics stay stable, respond to planted shortcut strength, and separate localized from diffuse cues. Dimming the flagged regions at test time shrinks worst-group gaps.
arxiv-2512-19088:
Khanh Nguyen and three co-authors speed up finding named objects inside three-dimensional scans of rooms and scenes. The task, open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation, lets a user ask for categories never seen in training. Recent methods lean on heavy image models, which makes them slow to run.

Their approach builds 3D masks from color images, guided by a fast two-dimensional open-vocabulary detector. It keeps the detector's knack for spotting rare or new objects while staying quick to classify. That matters for robots and augmented reality, where a system must point to the right object in a cluttered scene without long delays.
arxiv-2512-19288:
Davide Cugini, Francesco Ghisoni, Angela Rosy Morgillo, and Francesco Scala estimate energy gaps in quantum systems without measuring two energies separately. The gap between the ground state and the first excited state shapes a system's behavior. Their method prepares a special superposition state by slow adiabatic change on a quantum device.

Measured values on that state wobble over time, and fitting the wobble yields the gap directly. Tests ran on one- and two-dimensional Ising models and on two small molecules, in clean and noisy simulators. The one-dimensional Ising case also ran on a real IonQ Aria machine, up to twenty qubits, with success.
arxiv-2512-19688:
Six string theorists, led by Pietro Capuozzo and Andy O'Bannon, study what happens when flavor is added to a famous holographic duality in a very tidy way. On the gravity side they place probe D7-branes inside the background of many D3-branes. Through the AdS/CFT correspondence, those extra branes correspond to flavor fields whose mass can vary from place to place.

The team proves that any holomorphic position-dependent mass, one varying as a complex-analytic function, yields a supersymmetric solution preserving half the expected symmetry along two directions. Field-theory arguments confirm the result at any coupling, and holographic calculations show the configuration carries zero energy and zero mass-operator expectation value. Where the mass vanishes, a superconformal defect appears, described by chiral fermions.
arxiv-2512-19888:
Sk. Sohail, Sonej Alam, and Md. Wali Hossain test whether dark energy can behave tamely early in cosmic history and still fit the data. Standard pictures often let dark energy turn phantom, crossing a divide where its pressure grows unusually negative, at late times. They examine models that stay non-phantom early on: thawing, scaling-thawing, and effective fluid variants, confronting each with current cosmological observations.

Late-time background parameters stayed stable across all models, and time-dependent parametrizations mildly preferred phantom behavior at low redshift. Imposing early non-phantom scaling, however, forced steep potentials and squeezed the early dark energy density below one percent at matter-radiation equality. That route does not relieve the Hubble tension, and Bayesian model selection penalizes it, leaving early scaling strongly disfavored.
arxiv-2512-20488:
Sébastien Breteaux, Jérémy Faupin, and Viviana Grasselli prove that even a relativistic quantum particle cannot outrun light, in a precise probabilistic sense. Their particle obeys a pseudo-relativistic Schrödinger equation and moves in an external potential that changes with time. The question is how much probability leaks outside the light cone.

They establish a maximal velocity bound. If the particle starts inside one convex region, the chance of finding it inside a second convex region later is exponentially small. It shrinks with the distance from that region to the light cone's cross-section. The decay is explicit, with the exponent twice that gap distance. Such bounds underpin the causal behaviour of relativistic quantum models with external fields.
arxiv-2512-20588:
Demerson N Gonçalves and co-authors make a screening tool for quantum machine learning both cheaper and rigorous. The minimum accuracy heuristic estimates how well a quantum feature map can do without training a full quantum support vector machine. Originally it was expensive, limited to balanced data sets, and theoretically unproven.

The authors generalize the metric to arbitrary binary data sets and prove it is a certified lower bound on the best empirical accuracy of any linear classifier in the same feature space. Monte Carlo strategies then estimate the bound from a random subset of Pauli directions, with probabilistic guarantees attached. Feature map designers for near-term quantum devices gain a scalable, trustworthy pre-screen before committing to full training runs.
arxiv-2512-20688:
Stefano Grassi proposes rebuilding multi-agent AI on economic design of rules. Self-running agent systems are fragile because private knowledge stays dispersed, the Hayekian information problem, and local incentives drift from global goals, the Hurwiczian incentive problem. His paradigm, Mechanism-Based Intelligence, treats intelligence as emerging from coordination among many brains rather than residing in one.

The core device is a differentiable price mechanism. It computes each agent's exact loss gradient and serves it as a dynamic incentive signal equivalent to a Vickrey-Clarke-Groves payment. That secures honest play as each agent's best move and settling on the global optimum. A Bayesian extension covers one-sided information. Scaling is linear in the number of agents, and tests run far faster than model-free reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2512-20788:
Fartash Chalangari, Anant Vijay Varma, Joonas Keski-Rahkonen, and Esa Räsänen study disordered two-dimensional quantum systems held in a repeating trap. Disorder usually traps quantum states in place, an effect called Anderson localization. Yet some states form scar patterns, lining up along preferred paths instead of spreading evenly.

At low energies the states localize strongly, while a subset at higher energies shows scarring with directional intensity patterns. Scaling theory says all states should localize in very large systems, but finite size lets both behaviors live together. The authors show the mix leaves clear marks in spatial patterns and energy statistics. Those marks could be seen in electronic, photonic, and cold-atom setups.
arxiv-2512-20988:
Zhi-Song Liu, Chenhang He, Roland Maier, and Andreas Rupp densify three-dimensional scans that arrive sparse, noisy, and incomplete. Their framework PUFM++ uses flow matching, learning a path that carries a thin point cloud toward a dense one. A first stage learns the straight route from sparse input to dense target, and a second stage refines it with noise-perturbed samples so the endpoint distribution matches real surfaces.

An adaptive time scheduler, driven by how the interpolation behaves, speeds and steadies sampling, while on-manifold constraints keep generated points glued to the surface instead of floating off it. A recurrent interface network strengthens the feature hierarchy. On synthetic benchmarks and real scans alike, the result sets a new state of the art for upsampling quality.
arxiv-2512-21088:
Daeyeol Jeon and Yongjae Kwon complete a classical construction in the arithmetic of elliptic curves. The modular curve X_0(N) parametrizes elliptic curves equipped with a cyclic subgroup of order N, equivalently the cyclic N-isogenies between curves. Its sibling X_1(N) has long had explicit equations and moduli descriptions, while X_0(N) lagged behind. The authors give a uniform method, extending an approach of Dowd, for writing down explicit generators of the curve's function field.

From those generators comes a concrete moduli interpretation of cyclic N-isogenies, and with it explicit formulas for the sporadic rational points on X_0(N) and the isogenies they encode. Number theorists studying rational isogenies gain a unified solution to the moduli problem for X_0(N), turning case-by-case computations into a single construction that works across levels.
arxiv-2512-21288:
Seyed Arshan Dalili and Mehrdad Mahdavi replace model-merging folklore with a bound, then with a recipe. Merging averages several fine-tuned models into one multi-task model without the original training data. The knobs, the coefficients weighting each model's contribution, are normally set by heuristic and behave brittly. The authors prove a flatness-aware PAC-Bayes generalization bound for merging, with a cross-task heterogeneity term that prices the mismatch between model origins and target tasks.

The bound suggests the method: treat merging as multi-teacher distillation on scarce unlabeled data, since shrinking the divergence between merged student and teacher models provably tightens the risk bound. Their SAMerging algorithm adds sharpness-aware minimization to land in flat minima, and it reports state-of-the-art results across vision and language benchmarks. Practitioners merging open models gain both a reason the trick works and a more reliable set of weights.
arxiv-2512-21388:
Tanmoy Mondal and Pinaki Majumdar study ferromagnetic polarons, states in which an electron traps itself inside a small region of aligned spins. These states form near the magnetic transition temperature in magnets with few charge carriers, when the coupling between electron spin and local moments is strong.

In clean systems, polarons give only a modest bump in resistance and a magnetoresistance of roughly twenty to thirty percent. Mondal and Majumdar find that disorder, acting through pinning centers, promotes polaron formation and can raise the magnetoresistance to about eighty percent. Too much disorder, though, turns the material into an Anderson insulator whose resistance stops responding to magnetization. The authors locate the optimum level of disorder and map magnetoresistance against coupling and disorder, placing known magnetic semiconductor compounds on that map.
arxiv-2512-21488:
Liang Geng, Wei He, and Rongwei Yang count prime triples lying on a particular algebraic surface. The surface is the eigensurface of the symmetric group S3 for one of its irreducible representations, given by a single quadratic equation in three variables. Their question is how often it passes through points whose coordinates are all prime.

The benchmark comes from the prime number theorem, which says primes thin out like one over the logarithm of the size considered. For coprime triples in the whole positive grid, the density of fully prime triples carries a factor involving the Riemann zeta function at three. Geng and his co-authors prove the density on the eigensurface is strictly greater than that ambient value. The surface meets prime points more frequently than a generic surface would. The result links representation theory with analytic number theory.
arxiv-2512-21588:
Sudheer Mishra, Sundararajan Natarajan, and Natarajan E develop a numerical method for the steady Boussinesq equations with temperature-dependent material properties. The Boussinesq system models buoyancy-driven flow, such as convection, where viscosity and heat conduction change with temperature. Good simulation matters for heat transfer, but the equations are delicate.

The authors use a virtual element method on general meshes, with equal-order approximations. A gradient-based local projection is added to bypass a known compatibility condition that equal-order methods usually violate. They prove the continuous problem is well-posed when the data are small enough. Existence of the discrete solution follows from the Brouwer fixed-point theorem, with error bounds in the energy norm. The design avoids higher-order derivatives and keeps those terms apart. Numerical examples confirm the theory.
arxiv-2512-21788:
Jinqi Xiao, Bo Yuan, and their co-authors fine-tune image generation models to follow several conditions at once without the conditions fighting each other. The setting is diffusion transformers adapted with small low-rank modules. A single shared adapter suffers task interference, while a mixture of low-rank experts helps, except that its usual routing decides expert choice token by token.

Local routing clashes with the global meaning of a user's instruction, producing fragmented images and semantic drift. InstructMoLE instead derives one routing signal from the full instruction and applies a single, coherent council of experts to every token. A second ingredient, an output-space orthogonality loss, keeps the experts functionally diverse so they do not collapse into copies of each other. On demanding multi-condition benchmarks, the framework significantly beat standard adapters and earlier expert mixtures.
arxiv-2512-21988:
Sungwoo Kang and Jong-Kook Kim benchmark smartphone dermatology color measurement across devices, using facial images from nine hundred sixty five Korean subjects. Phones, a tablet, and a reference DSLR camera captured matched images, and skin indices such as melanin and skin tone angle depend on consistent color. Two calibration methods are tested in a standard color space: a global linear correction matrix and a region specific version trained per facial area.

Global calibration already cuts device color differences by roughly two thirds and reaches good reliability. Region specific calibration lifts both indices into the excellent reliability band. Face region mattered more than device type before calibration, making region aware methods the largest remaining source of improvement.
arxiv-2512-22088:
Chiwun Yang builds a theory explaining why bigger language models, trained longer on more data, predictably get better. Scaling laws describe that improvement well in practice, yet their theoretical roots have stayed murky. Yang writes transformer training as a system of usual differential equations, then approximates that system by kernel behavior to make it analyzable.

Working with stochastic gradient descent on multi-layer transformers and arbitrary sequence data, the analysis tracks how generalization error approaches its floor as compute grows. Matching upper and lower bounds reveal two stages. Early on, excess risk falls exponentially with compute. Past a threshold, a statistical phase takes over where error decays as a power law. Separate scaling laws for model size, training time, and dataset size fall out of the system.
arxiv-2512-22388:
Omar Alsaqa, Linh Thi Hoang, and Muhammed Fatih Balin introduce BLISS, a sampling strategy that makes training graph neural networks on huge graphs affordable. Such networks learn from connected data but must process every neighbor of every node, which explodes memory and compute on large graphs. BLISS borrows the multi-armed bandit idea from decision theory, dynamically picking the most informative nodes at each layer.

By balancing exploration against exploitation, the sampler keeps coverage of the whole graph while adapting as node importance shifts during training, unlike static sampling schemes. BLISS plugs into both graph convolutional networks and graph attention networks, adjusting its choices to each one's aggregation style. Tests show it maintains or exceeds the accuracy of full-batch training at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2512-22688:
Johnathan Xie and five co-authors present Autoregressive Flow Matching, a probabilistic method for predicting how points move through a scene. Motion prediction models usually train on narrow data for one job, while giant video predictors look realistic yet fumble complex motion despite their scale. Trained on diverse video datasets, their model forecasts future point track locations over long horizons, treating motion itself as the object to model.

The team built benchmarks for human and robot motion prediction to judge the approach. Predicted tracks proved useful as conditioning: feeding a robot action predictor or a human motion predictor these forecasted tracks greatly improved the downstream tasks. Code and trained models are publicly available, and the authors pitch the method as general infrastructure for sequential continuous data.
arxiv-2512-22888:
Giovanni Canossa, Lode Pollet, Miguel Martin-Delgado, Hao Song, and Ke Liu measure how much noise fracton quantum codes can tolerate before stored information is lost. Fracton codes are exotic three-dimensional codes tied to unusual states of matter, and their fault tolerance had barely been studied. The team focuses on self-dual fracton codes, especially the checkerboard code, under random Pauli noise.

A mapping to a statistical mechanics problem, solved with large parallel tempering Monte Carlo simulations, gives the checkerboard code an optimal error threshold near eleven percent. That is the highest known among three-dimensional codes and nearly reaches the theoretical ceiling for topological codes. The simulations also confirm a duality relation between paired models, which implies a second fracton code, Haah's code, sits near the same ceiling. The results present fracton codes as unusually sturdy quantum memories.
arxiv-2512-23188:
Huaning Liu and co-authors model epidemic control as a game between a population and health authorities, where who you are shapes what you do. Income and trust in authority steer vaccination and social distancing choices, so the authors surveyed and split the population into six groups by earnings and authority perception. Each person balances treatment costs, lost social life, guideline compliance, and vaccine price according to the group's outlook.

The resulting mean field game is solved through a forward-backward equation system for the Nash equilibrium, with a numeric algorithm. A trade-off emerges. Stricter guidelines aimed at everyone make followers distance and vaccinate less, while indifferent people socialize more, free-riding on the followers' caution. Guidelines targeted at the infected cut infections and narrowed income gaps. Cheaper vaccines helped low-income groups vaccinate, though less powerfully than distancing rules. Trust-building, the authors stress, is central to mitigation.
arxiv-2512-23288:
Jiagang Ren and Hua Zhang prove derivative formulas of Bismut-Elworthy-Li type for a class of forward-backward stochastic differential equations that include jumps. Such formulas express how a solution changes when its starting point shifts, without computing the derivative of the solution itself. Their equations are driven partly by a Poisson random measure, which models sudden random events.

To handle the jumps, they use the lent particle method developed by Bouleau and Denis, extending earlier results that lacked this tool. As an application, they obtain existence and uniqueness for a family of nonlocal quasi-linear integral partial differential equations whose solutions are differentiable in the space variable. The results hold even when the starting data and coefficients of those equations are rough.
arxiv-2512-23988:
Zhenyu Zhang and eight co-authors go looking for the gears of machine reasoning without deciding in advance what they should be called. Researchers studying how language models reason usually start from human labels such as overthinking or reflection, defined at the word level. The space of possible behaviors is larger than anyone's vocabulary for it. The team's framework, RISE, discovers behaviors directly in the model's activation space.

They slice chain-of-thought traces into sentence-sized steps and train sparse autoencoders on the activations of those steps. The learned features sort out into readable behaviors including reflection and backtracking, occupying separate regions of the decoder space. Nudging a feature up or down controllably amplifies or suppresses its behavior during inference. The autoencoders also exposed structural signals such as response length, and confidence-related directions that let the authors steer how confident a model sounds.
arxiv-2512-24288:
Yinuo Zhao and five colleagues teach robots with imperfect human help. Real-world reinforcement learning lets robots learn manipulation from their own trials. Human interventions during training are usually treated as perfect. Even experts cannot act optimally everywhere, though. They make mistakes in some states. Blindly imitating them caps what the robot can learn.

Their algorithm, SiLRI, weighs help state by state. The problem is cast as constrained optimization. At each state, the constraint depends on how uncertain the human help is there. A state-wise Lagrange multiplier enforces the balance. Policy and multiplier are optimized jointly toward a saddle point. The system runs on a human-as-copilot teleoperation setup. Diverse real manipulation tasks tested it. Time to reach a high success rate fell by at least half against a leading rival. Long-horizon tasks reached full success where other methods struggled.
arxiv-2512-24388:
João Victor Corrêa-Rodrigues and Jane Gregorio-Hetem examine a young stellar group near the nebula Sh 2-295. The group sits in the Canis Major association. That region's star formation history is complex. Three supernova events may have reshaped it. Two older groups of different ages were already known nearby. The group near FZ CMa lies between them.

Spectroscopy with the Gemini telescope hunted for T Tauri stars. Lithium absorption marked youth. Hydrogen-alpha emission probed accretion. Twenty-nine young stars were identified, including six new association members. Three are classical T Tauri stars still accreting. Ages spread widely, from about one to fourteen million years. Younger stars cluster around the nebula. Older ones are more dispersed. The pattern supports several formation episodes. Expansion of the nebula may have triggered the youngest group.
arxiv-2512-24488:
Erik Lentz and four colleagues reread a classic signal transform as an information meter. The Wigner-Ville transform maps a signal into time and frequency jointly. The authors interpret it through Tsallis entropy and related functionals. Information-laden signals can then be detected and localized in noise. Their information volume can even be measured.

Radio-frequency communication supplies the test cases. Wigner-Ville detection beat energy-based measures by wide margins in the shown contexts. Sensitivity gains exceeded fifteen decibels in some of them. No extensive training routines were needed. The advantage matters most under tight observation budgets. Transient and feeble signals are the natural targets. Sensing effectiveness could rise by orders of magnitude there. The paper argues a standard tool of signal processing deserves an information-theoretic second life.
arxiv-2512-24988:
Yegor Zenkevich investigates BPS states in four-dimensional supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory and their string network counterparts in type IIB string theory. A new interpretation casts the algebra of line operators as a tensor product of vector representations of a quantum toroidal algebra. That algebra then determines protected spin characters of all framed BPS states.

The choice of coproduct in the algebra matches the choice of supersymmetry preserved by the states, and wall crossing operators act as Drinfeld twists of that coproduct. Mathematical physics readers get a unified algebraic machine for BPS counting. Kontsevich-Soibelman wall crossing finds a concrete home in the toroidal algebra picture.
arxiv-2601-06988:
Research by Yue Ban and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with counter-diabatic driving for fast spin control in a two-electron double quantum dot. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The techniques of shortcuts to adiabaticity have been proposed to accelerate. The “slow” adiabatic processes in various quantum systems with the applications in quantum information processing.

The authors study the counter-diabatic driving for fast adiabatic spin manipulation in. A two-electron double quantum dot by designing time-dependent electric fields in the presence of spin-orbit coupling. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07488:
Ayush Bidlan, Dipanjan Dey, and Parth Bambhaniya study how a star-like object might collapse under an alternative theory of gravity. Their 2026 preprint uses Brans-Dicke gravity, where a scalar field joins the usual geometry of spacetime. Here the collapse is driven by that scalar field alone, with no ordinary matter present. The field carries a self-interaction potential and couples directly to the Ricci scalar.

Gravitational collapse is the process that can form black holes and singularities. Testing it in Brans-Dicke gravity shows whether the outcomes match Einstein's theory or differ. The setup is deliberately clean, so the scalar field's role stands out. Readers get a focused probe of singularity formation beyond standard gravity.
arxiv-2601-07788:
Liberty Kent, Nilufer Tuptuk, and Ingolf Becker study how cybersecurity teams hand over work between shifts. Incident response runs around the clock, so handovers are constant. Effective transitions are crucial, yet guidance on managing them is limited. Their 2026 preprint reports an exploratory study to build such guidance. The authors reviewed existing literature and online resources, then consulted practitioners.

Two draft guidelines, labeled A and B, came out of the literature work. Practitioner input then tested and refined them. A poor handover can drop an active attack from view for hours. Clear rules for what to pass on, and how, reduce that risk. The paper serves security operations managers and scholars of teamwork under pressure. It treats the handover itself as a security control.
arxiv-2601-07988:
Adithya V Ganesan and colleagues argue that longitudinal text data need new modeling habits. Standard NLP treats documents as independent, unordered samples. In longitudinal studies that assumption rarely holds. Documents are nested within authors and ordered in time. Together they form person-indexed, time-ordered behavioral sequences. Their 2026 preprint adapts modeling and evaluation ideas from word sequences to these behavioral sequences.

The shift matters for mental health, social science, and any field tracking people over time. Order carries signal: change itself can be the outcome of interest. Evaluation must also respect the nesting, or results leak between a person's documents. The authors span several universities and research groups. The paper serves computational social science and clinical NLP scholars. It asks the field to model people through time, not piles of text.
arxiv-2601-08588: Jacob Paul Simpson, Efstratios Palias, and Sharu Theresa Jose study sample complexity in composite quantum hypothesis testing. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats symmetric binary testing, where an unknown state lies in one of two uncertainty sets. Asymptotic error exponents for this problem are well studied. The finite-sample regime remains poorly understood, though. Knowing how many copies of a state suffice for a target error matters for real quantum sensors. The work helps set honest sample budgets for quantum detection tasks.
arxiv-2601-08988:
Ananya Mantravadi, Shivali Dalmia, and Abhishek Mukherji build a test for health AI agents that must act, not just chat. Safe care needs steps: read a chart, check a cut off, sum past values, then act if a rule is met. Past tests lean on quiz style asks. They miss those step and rule skills in full.

Their test is called ART. It runs agents on tasks drawn from real health charts. Each task needs a chain of steps with checks at set points. A slip in one step fails the task, as in real care. A reader in health AI gets a strict, act based scale. It shows which agents can be trusted with chart work.
arxiv-2601-09088:
Shaotian Yan and a team from Alibaba Cloud give a small open chat model built for step thought. The model is called DASD-4B-Thinking. Small here means four billion set values, lean next to top models. Yet the team says it tops open peers of its size on hard tests in math, science, and code. It can beat some far large models too, they say.

Their key is how they pass skill from a big model to the small one. They match the spread of the big model's steps, not just its last reply. That match keeps the small model's thought path in line. A reader who needs cheap step thought gets a lean model with a clear train trick.
arxiv-2601-09388:
Felix Rupprecht and Sabine Wölk study how to build sparse quantum states at lower cost. Their 2026 arXiv paper improves state preparation, one of the most basic tasks in quantum computing. A sparse state has only a few nonzero entries among its basis states, yet it is a key input for many algorithms.

The authors cut the Toffoli gate cost of preparing such states. Sparse states matter most in quantum simulation and in solvers for linear systems. Cheaper preparation means those algorithms spend less of their budget just loading data. The paper gives circuit builders a leaner primitive to work with.
arxiv-2601-09788:
Giulia Brunelli and a large team take a fresh X-ray look at a candidate PeVatron near the galactic center. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the pulsar wind nebula G0.9+0.1 with hard X-ray and multiwavelength data. The nebula is powered by the energetic pulsar PSR J1747-2809 inside a composite supernova remnant.

PeVatrons are rare sources that push particles to petaelectronvolt energies. The team models the nebula's full spectral energy distribution. NuSTAR, XMM-Newton, and Chandra supply the X-ray views. Pinning down how this nebula accelerates particles helps explain where the galaxy's most energetic cosmic rays come from.
arxiv-2601-10188:
Jincheng Guo and a large team profile a rare white dwarf star. The star is named TMTS J0006, in short. A white dwarf is the dense core left when a star dies. This one is both ultra massive and highly magnetic. It also spins at a fast rate.

Its spin period is just a short span, seen in sharp light curves. Three sky surveys caught the same beat. That cross check makes the beat firm. Fast spin in such a dense star is rare. The team works out its mass, field, and heat from the data. Such stars test how stars die and merge.
arxiv-2601-10488:
Louise Gassot, Patrick Gérard, and Peter Miller prove a long held claim for the Benjamin Ono equation. The law rules waves on deep water with a non local term. The claim is named soliton resolution. It says each wave ends as a sum of lone waves plus a fading tail.

Each lone wave moves at its own speed. The tail spreads and dies out in time. The claim needs the start wave to be smooth and to fade at the tails. The proof in this paper closes the claim for that case. Such proofs are a peak aim in wave math.
arxiv-2601-10688:
Rubel Hassan Mollik, Vamsi Krishna Kosuri, Hans Djalali, Stephanie Ludi, and Aboubakar Mountapmbeme work on access to block-based coding for blind and low-vision learners. Tools like Scratch and Code.org are now standard in school computer science classes. Yet they remain mostly out of reach for blind students. Their visual blocks demand sight at every step.

Past fixes changed the Blockly library itself, which made them hard to add to live platforms. The team's framework works as an extension instead, leaving the base library alone. That choice could help schools adopt it without rebuilding their tools. The goal is coding classes where blind learners build programs on equal terms.
arxiv-2601-10888:
Arjun Maniyar studies the cross-ratio degree for eight points on the projective line. The cross-ratio is the basic invariant of four points on a line. The degree problem asks how many configurations of n points meet a set of cross-ratio conditions. For n points, n minus three conditions are specified.

Maniyar computes the maximal cross-ratio degree in the eight-point case. Silversmith's work points to several connections and uses for this degree. Such counts live in enumerative geometry, where each number answers: how many shapes fit the rules? Exact values at small n anchor the theory and hint at patterns for larger point sets.
arxiv-2601-11088:
Yuki Arai and co-authors report a large anomalous Hall effect in the antiferromagnet NbMnAs at room temperature. Some antiferromagnets share symmetry breaking with ferromagnets and can give strong ferromagnetic-like responses. The anomalous Hall effect is a transverse voltage that tracks such a response. NbMnAs shows it at zero applied field.

The effect appears despite the material's small net magnetization. Room temperature and zero field are the conditions devices need. Antiferromagnets are robust against stray fields and can switch fast. A strong Hall signal makes their state easy to read electrically. The result points toward spintronic memory and logic built on antiferromagnets that behave, usefully, a little like ferromagnets.
arxiv-2601-11188:
Lucas Happ studies a rare kind of three-body state in this 2026 preprint. The states are bound, yet they sit inside a range of free motion. He asks how such states form as system settings change. His tool is the path of poles in the plane of complex energy.

Happ uses a simple one-line model for the test. Two bosons are the same, and a third particle is distinct. The parts pull on each other through smooth Gaussian wells. He then varies the pull strength, the range, and the mass ratio one step at a time. The pole paths show how loose states turn into bound ones.
arxiv-2601-11288:
P. Oliva studies an old bronze figure from Sardinia with neutron beams. The 2026 preprint looks at a Nuragic figurine in close detail. Nuragic figures are rare works of early Iron Age craft. Sardinian smiths made them with great skill for their time.

The figures were most likely cast by the lost wax method. Wax shapes melt out and leave a mold for the bronze. That method lets even complex forms be cast with ease. Oliva uses two neutron tools to peer inside the bronze. Diffraction reads the mix and strain of the metal. Tomography builds a 3D view of the inner form. Both tools leave the rare piece whole and unharmed.
arxiv-2601-11388:
An approach to theoretical spectroscopy is set out in this 2026 preprint. The authors are not named in the record held here. Theoretical spectroscopy models how matter takes and gives light. It rests on electronic-structure theory, a broad and strong field.

Such theory can capture the many-body life of materials. It spans ground-state traits and lattice excitations in solids. It also spans light-matter interaction of many kinds. Time-resolved forms track change as it unfolds after a pulse. Modern codes each carry a few or several of these methods. The work argues for an approach that excites, in both senses. It aims at codes that cover more of the field at once.
arxiv-2601-11688:
Vedant Nipane, Pulkit Agrawal, and Amit Singh link datasheets to code with agents. Their 2026 preprint presents SpecMap, a hierarchical LLM agent. Traceability joins spec documents to the code that implements them. In embedded systems, that mapping is a fundamental challenge.

Manual mapping fails on large code repositories at scale. Old recovery methods lean on lexical similarity alone. Information retrieval tricks miss semantic and structural links. Symbol-level ties in low-level software also escape them. SpecMap uses a hierarchy of LLM agents for the task. Agents can read datasheets and code with meaning in mind. Recovered links aid audits, updates, and safety checks.
arxiv-2601-11988:
Wenyi Wang, Sousuke Noda, and Taishi Katsuragawa study light from clouds of scalar fields round spinning black holes. Scalar-tensor theories add a scalar field to gravity. Round a Kerr black hole, such a cloud can grow by superradiance, which pulls spin energy out.

They show that induced decay of the cloud makes light signals that could be seen. The cloud growth in this theory is unlike that of other boson fields. It rests on how matter round the hole is spread, through a chameleon effect. Seen signals would test this form of gravity.
arxiv-2601-12088:
Salvatore Capozziello, Maurizio Capriolo, and Gaetano Lambiase derive an energy-momentum form for a modified gravity theory. The theory, called f(Q) gravity, extends a flat, torsion-free form of general relativity. It is based on non-metricity, a measure of how lengths change under transport.

They build the affine tensor for the energy and momentum of both gravity and matter fields. That joined form is the complex pseudo-tensor for this theory. Such forms are needed to track energy flow in cosmology. The work puts energy bookkeeping for f(Q) on a firm base.
arxiv-2601-12188:
Aditi Singh, Bogumiła Jezierska, Subrata Jana, and Szymon Śmiga give a simpler way to tune range separation for many-body calculations. One-shot GW and Bethe-Salpeter runs rest much on their start point, got from mean-field theory. A range-separated hybrid start can lift skill a lot if tuned well.

Full tuning is costly, so a simple start helps. Their method gives a practical first tune with less work. Better starts mean better spectra and gaps at the same cost. The work aims at real use in materials and molecule codes.  A cheap first tune can save days of compute time.
arxiv-2601-12388:
Amartya Goswami and Joseph Israel Zelezniak study ideals in commutative rings. Their focus is on strongly hollow ideals and a stricter class that adds the word completely. They work with no finiteness assumptions, which keeps the results broad. Ideals are core objects in ring theory, so new classes draw close study.

The pair set out basic structural facts about these ideals. They look at maximality and at what holds under quotients and surjective maps. They give several ways to test when an ideal is completely strongly hollow. One key result links the two classes through the Jacobson radical. If a strongly hollow ideal is not inside that radical, it must be of the stricter kind.
arxiv-2601-13088:
Harry Huang, Talia Xu, and Marco Zuniga Zamalloa look at how light can aid tiny flying craft. Small air craft now do tasks from stock checks to air sensing. Their short flight time and weak sense of place in GPS free zones hold them back.

Craft that are lighter than air offer a swap. A helium skin gives lift, so hover takes near zero power and flights can run far longer. The snag is how to steer and stay on course with so light a craft. The team tests how light can be used both to boost flight length and to guide the craft. For indoor and calm air tasks, the work points to a low power path.
arxiv-2601-13188:
Patrick Yung Kang Lee and a large team study how people form ties with ChatGPT as a companion. Folks now turn to broad chat bots for company, not just to play apps built for that role. Yet little is known about how they see and run such ties.

The team asks how outer forces shape those ties. Friends, press, and norms may push how a tie is kept or hid. They also ask what tricks users use to keep the tie as they want it. The study fills a gap in how AI company is lived day to day. For teams that build chat bots, the finds show care points for health and trust.
arxiv-2601-13288:
Gonzalo Ariel Meyoyan and Luciano Del Corro reuse a live model's own maths to tag text in the same pass. Big served models often call split small models for safety and tag tasks. Each split call adds lag, memory load, and ops bulk.

Their swap is to train light probes on the served model's hid states. The probes read states the model has paid to make for its main text task. Tags then come out in the same pass as the text, with no split call. The probes can pick which tokens and which layers to read. For teams that serve models at scale, the trick cuts cost while it keeps the tag step.
arxiv-2601-13388:
Sasha Ronaghi, Prerit Choudhary, David H. Rehkopf, and Bryant Lin pull diabetes risk clues from free text in health files. Social facts of health, such as home, food, and work strain, sway type two diabetes care. Yet they are oft absent from the neat fields of a health file. Most such facts are caught by fixed forms, which miss the nuance of each clinic's crowd.

Free text in notes holds a rich store of such facts. The team uses large language models to draw them out in a firm form. That form then feeds a risk guess for each patient. For clinics, the route may catch risks that fixed forms leave blank.
arxiv-2601-13488:
Peter J. Forrester and Fei Wei note a set of results on high order equations for unitary matrix sums. The note gives the back tale and spur for a joint paper. It then maps the main finds of that work for a fast read.

The finds link matrix and scalar equations of high order. The sums at stake are Hankel and Toeplitz determinants built from I-Bessel functions. Such sums are the same as set unitary matrix sums. The note puts that link in a wider frame. For maths physics readers, a short map of a dense work plus its wider place has clear worth.
arxiv-2601-13988:
Laura Monk and Frédéric Naud review progress on spectral gaps of large hyperbolic surfaces in 2026. This expository paper surveys the history and recent breakthroughs in the field. The focus is the first non-trivial eigenvalue, called lambda-one. That value sets the spectral gap, a key trait of the surface's vibrations.

They ask how lambda-one can behave as surface volume grows large. The story runs from Selberg to Mirzakhani, two giants of the field. Spectral gaps link geometry, number theory, and quantum chaos. A clear review helps new researchers enter a fast-moving area.
arxiv-2601-14088:
Maria Abu-Sini and Reinhard Heckel build codes for data torn into pieces with typos in 2026. The adversarial torn paper channel models a word that is first edited, then broken. At most a set number of edit errors hit the word: insertions, deletions, and substitutions. The word then breaks into fragments at arbitrary positions.

DNA storage systems and 3D fingerprinting motivate this channel. The team studies near optimal code construction for it. A good code lets the receiver rebuild the message from torn, flawed pieces. Such codes guard data stored in fragile physical media.
arxiv-2601-14688:
Timothy D. Brandt derives statistical formulas for companion hunting in this 2026 paper. Astronomers often detect a companion only through a trend: a radial velocity or astrometric acceleration of its host star. Brandt derives the statistical relationship between that trend, a companion's mass, and its projected separation. The relationships are expressed as probability density functions.

The formulas are analytic and hold independent of all Keplerian orbital elements, so long as orbits are randomly oriented in space. In plain terms, a measured drift can be turned into odds on mass and distance without knowing the orbit's shape. The math is short and closed. No large code run is used, which makes the tool fast to use at a desk. Readers get closed-form relations for a common detection problem in exoplanet and binary star work.
arxiv-2601-14788:
Yifei Liu, Changxing Ding, Ling Guo, Huaiguang Jiang, and Qiong Cao generate human motion from text in this 2026 paper. Diffusion models have seen widespread adoption for text-driven human motion generation. Their generative capabilities and flexibility are impressive. Current motion diffusion models face two major limitations, though.

One is a representational gap. Pre-trained text encoders lack motion-specific information, so prompts are read with the wrong nuance. The other is error propagation during the iterative denoising process. Small slips compound across steps. Their model is reconstruction-anchored, using reconstruction to hold the motion on track. The aim is faith. A wave of an arm should look like the words asked for it, start to end. Readers get a text-to-motion design that fights drift in both meaning and movement.
arxiv-2601-15088:
Arnab Priya Saha and Aninda Sinha study how five particles scatter, one piece at a time. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with five-point tree amplitudes, the basic terms in a scattering process. All five external particles are identical scalars.

The team expands the residues of the amplitude in partial waves. They check the build in two ways. One uses massive spinor-helicity building blocks. The other matches the five-point Veneziano amplitude at fixed mass levels. The work also brings in splitting constraints and the hidden zeros of the full five-point scattering amplitude.
arxiv-2601-15588:
A team signing as Alibaba-AAIG presents a safety guardrail model in a 2026 arXiv paper. The model is called YuFeng-XGuard. As language models spread into real products, guardrails must do more than coarse filtering. They need to judge risk in fine detail. They also need to explain their calls and adapt to new policies. Existing tools often fall short on one of these counts.

Many current guards classify fast but stay opaque. Others rely on fixed rules added after the fact. Inference cost can also block deployment at scale. XGuard is described as reasoning-centric, interpretable, and flexible. It reasons about risk rather than just matching patterns. For builders, a guard that shows its reasoning is easier to audit. That matters when a wrong block or a missed risk carries real cost.
arxiv-2601-15688:
Zhixuan Liang, Xingyu Zeng, Rui Zhao, and Ping Luo improve active learning for object detection in a 2026 arXiv paper. Active learning trains strong models with minimal labeling effort. It picks the most informative examples for humans to annotate. Most methods judge informativeness by data distribution or content alone. That judgment does not directly track downstream performance. In detection, the score that matters is mean average precision.

The authors propose performance-guided reinforced active learning, per the title. The guide is the task metric itself, not a proxy. Reinforcement learning steers which images get picked for labeling. If picks track real gains, annotation budgets stretch further. Labeling images for detection is slow and costly. A smarter picker saves money on every training round.
arxiv-2601-15888:
An unsigned 2026 arXiv paper asks why vision foundation models transfer unevenly. Foundation models pretrain on huge data to capture broad knowledge. In language tasks, that pretraining generalizes well. Vision foundation models behave differently. Despite heavy compute, their gains vary sharply across downstream tasks. One task leaps forward while another barely moves.

The authors postulate a cause: a mismatch between pretraining objectives and what downstream vision tasks demand. Pretraining may teach features the tasks cannot use well. The paper studies these transfer limits directly. For labs spending heavily on vision pretraining, knowing the limits guides where the next dollar of compute should go.
arxiv-2601-15988:
Kalyan Banerjee links two classic objects in number theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. On one side stand elliptic curves, whose rank counts independent rational points. On the other stand class groups of real quadratic fields. Class groups measure how badly unique factorization fails in those fields. Banerjee proves a relation between the two. The link ties curve ranks to the nontriviality of class groups. The connection runs across infinitely many real quadratic fields, he states.

Bridges like this are prized in arithmetic geometry. A fact about curves becomes a fact about fields, and back. Each side has its own tools, so a bridge doubles the attack on hard questions. The abstract states the claim in brief terms. Specialists will look to the proof for the exact shape of the relation.
arxiv-2601-16088:
Abhinav Jangir and Anees Ahmed study how pulse form shapes pair birth in strong fields. Their 2026 preprint looks at birth of electron and positron pairs from void space. A time based field that is not the same on each side drives the birth. The team solves the quantum Vlasov maths for this case. They vary both the phase at the pulse heart and the pulse shape.

The pair track how each change shifts the yield of new pairs. Shape and phase can raise or cut the count in clear ways. Such links help labs plan strong laser tests of pair birth. They also test if maths matches what labs will see. The work stays close to the field maths and its terms.
arxiv-2601-16188:
Sebastián Donoso, Sovanlal Mondal and Vicente Saavedra-Araya extend mean sum results along return times. Their 2026 preprint sits in the maths of long run means. Return times are the times a path comes back to a small mark. Means can be taken along those sparse times in their place of all times. Past work showed such means settle in fast mix systems.

The team widens those results to groups of acts that commute. They also use marks that shrink as time grows. The work part fills gaps left by the first author, Maass and the third author. Sparse means that still settle have use in chance and flow maths. The proof joins mix speed to mean acts.
arxiv-2601-16288:
Van Weeren and coauthors share new MeerKAT views of two star groups, Abell 1775 and Abell 1795. Their 2026 preprint deals with huge radio glows in such groups. Big glows mark groups in clash, while small glows mark cool core groups. Both trace fast grains in the thin gas in the group. Late views hint the two glow types may not split clean.

The new views span a wide band from the MeerKAT scopes. They test if the small glow in one group is of the big type. Glow type tells of past clashes and gas acts in the group. Clear views help sort glow birth tales. The work adds fine radio maps of two key groups.
arxiv-2601-16388:
Hironori Yamaguchi and coauthors find magnet order that Kondo acts help to build. Their 2026 preprint deals with a chain model called the Kondo necklace. Kondo acts pair a free spin with a held spin in a singlet. Such pairs were long thought to kill magnet order. Late work hints Kondo acts can in some cases aid order.

The team shows Néel order, a flip flop spin line, can grow with Kondo aid. That growth flips the old tale for this model class. It widens where teams should look for such order. Real stuff may show the same aid in its spin acts. The work joins two themes long set as foes.
arxiv-2601-16788:
Xuewei Li, Xinghan Bao, Zhimin Chen, and Xi Li sort wide-view street shots into named zones. A full round view shows roads, cars, folks, and sky at once. Tools must tag each point in that wide span. Depth cues help split near from far in the shot. Past tools used depth in raw or plain forms. Their 2026 preprint builds a depth code fit for round views.

Their code reshapes depth to match the round warp of the shot. A fusion step then joins depth with the color view. Sharper tags aid self-drive cars and guide bots. Such tools need the full round scene read right.
arxiv-2601-17488:
Quinn M. Gallagher and four co-authors seek a local key to sort amorphous ices. Amorphous solids lack the neat unit cells of crystals. Yet ice phases with unlike traits must differ in local structure. The authors look for a structural basis at that local scale. Such a basis would do for glasses what space groups do for crystals.

A clear basis lets labs name and sort ice forms with proof. It can show which local motifs drive trait shifts. Water ice is a model for glasses at large. Its lessons reach drugs, foods, and planetary science. The work builds a language for forms that look alike at first glance. That language is a step to control them.
arxiv-2601-17588:
Marcus Ma and Shrikanth Narayanan argue that intelligence needs grounding, not embodiment. Recent language model gains revived an old debate. Must a mind have a body to be intelligent? The authors define intelligence by four properties. They list motivation, predictive ability, and understanding among them. Grounding links symbols to the world they mean.

Embodiment entails grounding, they argue, but grounding can arise without a body. That split reshapes what builders must give AI systems. It shifts focus from robot bodies to world linkage. The debate guides research funds and design choices. A clear stance helps labs test claims about machine minds. The paper stakes that stance with care.
arxiv-2601-17688:
Sudhanva Joshi and Sunil Kumar Mishra study traversability in a wormhole-inspired teleportation protocol. The protocol uses coupled Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev systems. They are prepared in a thermofield double state with a bath. The authors add PT-symmetric non-unitary deformations. PT symmetry pairs parity and time reversal. They ask how those deformations change traversability dynamics.

Traversability marks if a signal can pass through the wormhole analogue. SYK models are a lab for holography ideas. Deformations test how robust the effect is. Results guide both theory and quantum simulation design. Teams can build SYK-like systems on quantum hardware. Knowing which knobs help or harm passage matters for those builds.
arxiv-2601-17988:
Nachi Avraham-Re'em and Emmanuel Roy prove a mixing result for a broad class of random processes. Their 2026 preprint studies infinitely divisible stationary processes indexed by a group. Stationary means the statistics do not shift over the index. Infinitely divisible means each piece can be split into like parts. The authors show that if such a process is ergodic and separable in probability, then it is weakly mixing.

Weak mixing is a stronger form of long-run independence. The result holds for any indexing group at all. It removes group assumptions that older work needed. As with Gaussian processes, ergodicity alone forces mixing here. Clean results like this anchor the theory of random processes.
arxiv-2601-18188:
Weiye Zhu and co-authors present NaVIDA, a navigation agent that learns how its own actions change the world. Their 2026 preprint deals with vision-and-language navigation. An agent reads a natural language instruction and acts on it inside a rich visual scene. Most methods learn reactive links from state to action. They do not model how an action causally reshapes the scene, so errors can compound step by step.

NaVIDA adds inverse dynamics augmentation to the training. Inverse dynamics asks which action could have caused a seen change. That signal teaches cause and effect, not just correlation. Agents that grasp it should follow routes with fewer wrong turns.
arxiv-2601-18288:
S.C. İnan probes the electromagnetic traits of the tau lepton in lead-lead collisions at a future collider. His 2026 preprint studies pairs of tau leptons made in PbPb collisions at the FCC-hh. Two numbers are in view: the anomalous magnetic moment of the tau, and its electric dipole moment. The authors report 95 percent confidence exclusion limits, plus sensitivity limits at three and five sigma. Such limits say how small a deviation the collider could detect or rule out.

The tau is the heaviest lepton, so its moments are prized probes of new physics. A dipole moment would signal a deep asymmetry in nature. Future collider studies of this kind set targets for machine design.
arxiv-2601-18488:
Alice Bernard and five colleagues study how the split of an atom's core can vary from split to split. When a heavy core splits, the two parts fly off with traits that can be counted, such as spin and mass. Math based on energy maps can give the odds for each trait. New tools add those odds up with care.

Still, a mean count can hide how wide the spread runs. The team use a dice-roll math trick to chart that spread in full. Each roll picks a split by the odds, and many rolls build the whole range. That range tells labs what a real test should see, miss by miss. It also shows which counts are firm and which ones swing a lot. Such maps help plan tests on cores that are hard to make.
arxiv-2601-19088:
Saba Alimadadi and Golnaz Gharachorlu blend two styles of mutation testing for Python code. Mutation testing grades a test suite by seeding small fake faults and seeing how many the tests catch. Old tools miss many fault types that are common in a loose typed language like Python.

Their hybrid method is driven by real fault patterns, not just simple code swaps. Python's dynamic typing breeds faults that stiff mutation rules never plant. A suite graded against realistic faults gives a truer read on whether the tests would catch the bugs that truly slip into Python projects.
arxiv-2601-19388:
Yimin Tang, Sven Koenig, and Erdem Bıyık tidy the paths of robot fleets after a planner has done its job. Multi agent path finding is a hard problem with uses in warehouses and robot coordination. Learning based solvers are fast and scale well, but their feasible plans often include wasteful or wobbly moves.
