Their layer, Judgelight, post optimizes each trajectory by collapsing closed subwalks, loops that return to their start. Cutting dead loops keeps the plan valid while making it shorter and cleaner. A cheap cleanup step can lift any solver's output, which makes it a handy add on.
arxiv-2601-19488:
Yizhao Han and nine co-authors sample video frames with an eye on entropy to keep long clips coherent. Autoregressive models build video step by step, as language models build text. In language, picking from a small top candidate set works well because tokens are dense with meaning and low in redundancy.

Video tokens behave otherwise, so fixed candidate sets falter over long horizons. Their entropy guided k-guard sampling adjusts the guard by how unsure the model is at each step. Long, stable video generation is the prize, since drift and decay grow with every extra second.
arxiv-2601-19988:
Xuankai Zhou and colleagues build quantum sensors that sit directly on a material's surface. Optically addressable spins can sense magnetic fields with atomic resolution and quantum-limited sensitivity. Realising them at surfaces has been a long-standing ambition. The obstacle is depth: stable quantum spins usually must sit some distance below the surface, blunting their sensitivity to what lies above.

The team demonstrates a hybrid molecular and two-dimensional architecture. It places working spin sensors right on top of the surface. Surface placement maximises contact with the sample being measured. Such sensors could image magnetism and currents in new materials at the smallest scales. The work removes a depth limit that constrained the field.
arxiv-2601-20088:
Meng Xin and colleagues distil large models into aggressively compressed versions. Their technical report presents quantization-aware distillation for models squeezed to the NVFP4 format, a four-bit number format. Quantization alone usually costs accuracy. Distillation trains the compressed student to imitate a full-precision teacher, recovering much of the loss.

The report covers both language models and vision-language models. It shares best practices the team found for the recovery process. The distillation loss is a KL divergence between teacher and student outputs. Four-bit inference slashes memory and energy costs for serving models. A reliable recipe for recovering accuracy makes such deployment realistic. The report is written for practitioners facing the same squeeze.
arxiv-2601-20988:
Gabor Lippner and Arturo Ortiz San Miguel ask which regular graphs hold the most copies of a given pattern. Their 2026 paper studies subgraph counts in regular graphs. A regular graph gives every vertex the same number of edges. For a fixed pattern graph H, some regular graphs pack in more H-shaped copies than others. The authors seek the graphs with the highest H-density.

They reframe the hunt as a continuous optimization problem. The new frame runs through the eigenvalues of the graph. Counts of injective homomorphisms link to counts from quotient graphs of H. That link turns a discrete search into smooth math. The result gives extremal graph theory a fresh handle. It may help design networks with chosen pattern densities.
arxiv-2601-21088:
Thomas Blommel and four co-authors compare rival ways to simulate driven quantum systems. Their 2026 paper benchmarks the real-time Dyson expansion against Green's function approaches. Driven, interacting quantum systems are hard to simulate. The team focuses on density matrix dynamics and time-off-diagonal Green's functions. They also study time-resolved photoemission spectra. Those spectra show how a material responds right after a pulse.

Two themes run through the comparison. One is Markovianity: how much the system remembers its past. The other is self-consistency in the calculation. The rivals include Kadanoff-Baym equations, their generalized ansatz, and exact diagonalization for small systems. Second-order perturbation theory supplies the interaction treatment. The study tells simulators which tool to trust for driven materials. It is a careful methods audit for non-equilibrium physics.
arxiv-2601-21388:
Mingyi Wang and Dongling Wang build high-order numerical schemes for a fractional diffusion operator. The tempered fractional Laplacian models spread that is heavier-tailed than normal diffusion but still fades at long range. Accurate schemes for it are hard to design.

The authors base their framework on new generating functions drawn from the discrete symbols. For smooth functions, the schemes reach high orders of accuracy. A general frame matters because each new application otherwise needs its own scheme. Their approach gives later work a ready path to accurate, fast solvers for this class of problems.
arxiv-2601-21788:
C. J. K. Larkin and co-authors ask how one unusual pair of massive stars came to be. Wolf-Rayet stars are hot, stripped stars, and how they form at the Sun's metal content is still unclear. Simple single-star paths are hard to square with the orbit patterns seen in different Wolf-Rayet pairs.

Their 2026 study focuses on Wd1-72, a Wolf-Rayet plus O-star binary inside the young massive cluster Westerlund 1. The pair sits inside the shared wind of the whole cluster. The title poses the question the evidence must answer: is this system a recent case where the two stars interacted and exchanged material? The answer would help pin down how often binary interaction, not solo aging, makes Wolf-Rayet stars.
arxiv-2601-21888:
Alexander Fel'shtyn and Mateusz Slomiany introduce a new object in dynamical systems: the synchronization zeta function. It is attached to a pair of self-maps of a topological space, functions that send the space into itself. Zeta functions in dynamics package counting data about repeating behavior into one analytic object.

The authors also define the growth rate of synchronization points, places where the two maps agree in step. And derive an explicit formula for it in the setting of endomorphisms of compact, connected Abelian groups. Their 2026 preprint then studies congruences and asymptotics tied to the new function. Work like this extends a classic toolkit, Reidemeister theory and dynamical zeta functions, into two-map territory.
arxiv-2601-22088:
Levin Maier puts a young set of equations on firm ground. The set is called the magnetic two-part Hunter-Saxton system. It was first drawn from a path law on a space with no end. That first work sketched the shape of the set and a flow that lasts for all time.

What was missed was a proof from the side of hard sums. Maier gives that proof. He studies weak forms of the law: forms that may grow sharp points yet still hold in a mean sense. Such ground work counts, since kin of this set model liquid glass, thin seas, and magnets. Those fields need laws that can be shown to hold, not just laws that look right on a screen.
arxiv-2601-22288:
Mario Truss presents PersonaCite, a tool that ties fake research users to real proof. Their 2026 work notes that model-made personas can sound sure yet hide where their claims come from. Design teams use such personas to test products and plans.

PersonaCite lets a user ask the persona direct questions in a chat. Each reply stays bound to source proof that can be checked. The tool frames personas as research aids, not as stand-ins for real people. That bound can make fake-user tests more honest and more safe to use. It also shows its work on demand.
arxiv-2601-22388:
Monica Rincon-Ramirez and five co-authors ask if a simple heat rule picks the black hole left after two black holes merge. Their 2026 preprint notes that big simulations predict the final hole with great care. Yet a plain rule from within relativity may do the same job.

They test a maximum entropy claim: the merger settles on the state with the most disorder allowed. If true, the rule would give a fast way to call the outcome. It would also tie black hole physics to heat physics in a deep way. The work checks the claim against known cases.
arxiv-2601-22588:
Zhuochun Li and a large team ask if a small model can judge as well as a large one by reading inner states. Large models are widely used as scorers, but they are costly, opaque, and prompt-sensitive. Their 2026 preprint tests small models that judge from internal representations, not from written verdicts.

The claim rests on a gap in semantic capacity between judge and judged. If it holds, judging gets cheaper and more stable. It could also make scores easier to audit. The work rethinks a costly habit of the field. Small, sharp judges would change many pipelines.
arxiv-2601-22688:
Doyoung Kim, Jaehyeok Doo, and Minjoon Seo let a language model branch its reasoning like a tree, in one pass. Models now reason in a single line, which traps dead-end paths inside the chain. Their 2026 preprint, TSLM, uses special tokens to mark branches in the text itself.

The model can grow several paths and expand only the live ones. Tree search in one pass saves the cost of many full runs. It suits puzzles where the first path often fails. The work rethinks the shape of machine thought. Branches, pruned well, beat a single line.
arxiv-2601-22788:
Jana Gonnermann-Müller and a team built FACET, a multi-agent AI that helps teachers tailor lessons to a mixed class. Classrooms now span wide gaps in skill, drive, language, and learning needs such as dyslexia and ADHD. Their 2026 preprint notes that teachers back tailored teaching, yet workload blocks it.

FACET's agents draft varied materials at scale, under the teacher's hand. That help could make tailored learning a daily fact, not an ideal. The work targets a kind bottleneck in schools. It keeps the teacher as the judge. Scale serves care, here.
arxiv-2601-22988:
Di Zhang and a team at Tongji University teach robots to see scenes in three dimensions. Real manipulation needs a steady grasp of space, even when cameras move to new viewpoints. Policies trained from one angle often fail when the view changes.

Their method learns visual representations grounded in geometry, so scenes read consistently across views. A robot that understands shape, not just pixels, can pick and place objects more reliably. View-proof vision is a step toward helpers that work in messy, real rooms. Robust spatial understanding is the stated requirement, because a manipulation policy must know where things are, not just what they look like.
arxiv-2601-23088:
Zhixiang Zhang and four co-authors attack the semantic caches that speed up language model services. Big providers cache answers by meaning, using embedding vectors as fuzzy keys for similar queries. That saves latency and compute on repeated questions.

Treating cache keys as fuzzy hashes, the authors craft collisions that make the cache serve wrong answers. A poisoned cache can mislead many users from a single planted entry. The work tells providers to harden a component many treated as harmless plumbing. Major providers already deploy semantic caching widely, so a key collision weakness reaches production systems, not just prototypes.
arxiv-2601-23188:
Zhongxiang Sun and five co-authors give deep search agents a way to watch their own thinking. These agents handle multi-step retrieval and long tasks well. Their failures often come from having no mechanism to monitor reasoning and retrieval as the job evolves.

Drawing on cognitive neuroscience, the authors add hierarchical meta-cognitive monitoring. Higher levels check the state of lower-level search and correct course when it drifts. Self-monitoring agents should be more reliable for research, law, and other long-horizon work. Meta-cognitive monitoring is hierarchical, so oversight itself is layered rather than a single checker watching a single process.
arxiv-2603-01388:
Graph neural networks learn from data shaped as nodes and links, but they have clear limits. Asela Hevapathige, Ahad Zehmakan, Asiri Wijesinghe, and Saman Halgamuge take up that problem in this 2026 work. Common models treat all neighbors in the same way and miss how nodes hold different roles in larger patterns.

Their fix, called ISP, groups nodes by shared traits and then passes facts along step by step in layers. A new test and a neural version both come from that one idea. Proofs show the method can tell apart graphs that older tests cannot, and it resists a known flaw where node traits blur. Tests on graph tasks, node tasks, and spread tasks beat strong prior models.
arxiv-2603-01588:
Daniel Biebert, Christian Hakert, Kay Heider, and colleagues make decision forests useful even when time runs out mid-run. Their 2026 work targets small devices where a full forest pass may not fit the time budget. An anytime method should give its best guess so far whenever it is stopped.

Older anytime forests stop between whole trees, yet each step down a tree already sharpens the guess. The team orders single steps across the whole forest to gain accuracy as fast as possible. One exact order costs too much to compute, so they offer two greedy orders that walk down or up the trees. The upward order scores near the exact best and near full runs. That makes forests safer for tight, real-time jobs.
arxiv-2603-01988:
Ilya Gorshkov links a special class of groups to graded non-associative algebras in this 2026 work. He starts from faithful odd transposition groups, where a normal set of involutions generates the group. An involution is an element that is its own inverse, and products of two here have odd order.

His subclass fixes that product order to one prime for every pair of involutions. From any such group plus a scalar parameter, he constructs a non-associative, non-commutative algebra. Each generating involution becomes a primitive semisimple idempotent inside that algebra. Those idempotents define a two-part grading of the algebra, splitting it into even and odd pieces. The construction ties group symmetry to algebra structure, in the spirit of axial algebra theory.
arxiv-2603-02188:
Songtao Liu, Hongwu Peng, Zhiwei Zhang, and colleagues cut memory traffic in large language models in this 2026 paper. During text generation, stored key and value data must be reloaded at each step. A recent design shrinks that store, but its single shared head cannot split across chips. Each chip then reloads the full store for every token, wasting bandwidth.

Their design, MLRA, uses several low-rank heads that can split across four chips. That split restores the gains of parallel decoding. In tests, the model matched top scores on language quality and downstream tasks. It also decoded text almost three times faster than the prior design. Code, weights, and data were released for others to check and build on.
arxiv-2603-02488:
Soham Nagawanshi, Shalini Panthangi, Chen Wang, and colleagues add machine learning help to streaming algorithms in this 2026 paper. Streaming algorithms summarize huge data flows in tiny memory. Learning-augmented versions use a model's predictions to beat classic space limits. Unequal weights break that progress, though, as with sliding windows where old data must expire.

Their oracle flags the heavy hitters, the most frequent items in a data set. With that help, they build algorithms for several core problems in time-decay settings. Targets include norm and moment estimation, frequency estimation, and rectangular variants. Theory is paired with tests on real and synthetic data. Results show the predicted space savings hold up in practice, even as old items fade.
arxiv-2603-02588:
Minseok Choi, Dongjin Kim, Seungbin Yang, and colleagues build a guardrail model for specialized domains in this 2026 paper. Safety filters for language models mostly cover general conversation. Finance, medicine, and law are rich in jargon where harmful content hides more easily. General guardrails leave those domains exposed to adversarial prompts.

Their model, ExpGuard, is trained for those three domains specifically. A curated data set holds tens of thousands of labeled prompts with refusal and compliant replies. Domain experts annotated the high-quality test split. On that test and eight public benchmarks, ExpGuard stayed competitive overall. Against domain-specific attacks it beat leading rivals by clear margins in prompt and response classification. Code, data, and the model are open-sourced for adaptation to more domains.
arxiv-2603-02688:
Izat Temiraliev, Diji Yang, and Yi Zhang argue that robots should look things up before they act. Their 2026 paper defines Retrieval-Augmented Robotics for cases where a robot gets no demonstrations at all. A robot facing a complex furniture kit lacks the exact steps, and its built-in knowledge cannot fill that gap.

Their system loops through three steps: retrieve, reason, and act. The robot searches visual manuals, matches flat diagrams to real three-dimensional parts, and then builds an action plan. On a hard long-horizon assembly test, planning grounded in retrieved manuals beat both unaided reasoning and example-based retrieval. The work extends search from answering questions to driving physical action.
arxiv-2603-02788:
Zhiyu Ni, Yifeng Xiao, and Zheng Liang build an agent whose job is to grade other agents fairly. Their 2026 framework tackles a practical problem: tests of reasoning agents must be repeatable, auditable, and able to survive crashes. The tested agent only needs a standard agent-to-agent interface.

An assessor agent hands out tasks, enforces time and step budgets, parses answers, and logs structured failure types. As a case study, the team graded an agent that turns plain-language logic problems into solver programs. On a cleaned, solver-checked set of first-order logic questions, that agent scored well above a chain-of-thought baseline. The setup shows how automated grading can stay rigorous without trusting the agent's own report.
arxiv-2603-02988:
Barbora Benešová, Malte Kampschulte, and Martin Kružík derive the small-strain laws of springy, flowing solids from the full nonlinear theory. Such Kelvin-Voigt solids both spring back and creep, and engineers tend to write their small-strain laws down at once. The 2026 paper starts from a nonlinear model that obeys frame indifference, the rule that response cannot hinge on how the viewer turns.

The authors show that answers of the nonlinear system tend to answers of the small-strain system as strain shrinks. They prove the same match for step-by-step time schemes on several scales. The gap matters, since codes compute with the small-strain laws while real solids obey the full ones. The proof certifies when the shortcut is safe.
arxiv-2603-03288:

Alexey Zemtsov and a team of co-authors present Dual Advantage Fields in 2026, a way to extract actions from goal-conditioned reinforcement learning value models. Such models can judge how reachable every goal is from every state, yet that alone does not say which action to take now.

A learned action-effect model predicts where each action moves the agent in representation space, and actions are scored by alignment with the goal direction. Harikumar Chandrasekharan maps the limits of phase-only control in 2026. In many wave systems, light or sound travels by many paths at once. Engineers can often adjust only the phase of each path, not its strength.

He shows this limit confines the system to a compact curved space. The shape of that space creates isolated, stable states where the waves lock together. How robust each state is depends on the local curvature. Small flaws merely soften the picture. A trade-off follows: more paths mean more stable states, but focus leaks into the paths left uncontrolled. Tests with a telecom photonic lantern mapped the predicted stable regions directly. No heavy calibration was needed.

Xu, Wu, and Chang build a benchmark for a neglected skill: following complicated instructions about videos, in a 2026 arXiv evaluation paper. Multimodal models have progressed rapidly at video understanding. But existing benchmarks use simple prompts. They say little about whether models can satisfy explicit output constraints. Their benchmark, VCIFBench, constructs constraint-rich instructions from two prompt sources. Some prompts are adapted from benchmarks. Others are directly grounded in videos. The constraints span content, format, style, and structure requirements. A hybrid verification pipeline checks the outputs.

The benchmark holds 306 satisfiable test instructions. It also holds a 540-pair preference dataset for DPO training. A 30-item conflict diagnostic subset makes constraints deliberately clash. It targets the gap between understanding a video and obeying the full set of instructions attached to the answer.

Xu, Zhao, and Shan redesign autoregressive mesh generation around a sparse voxel scaffold, in a 2026 arXiv graphics paper. Their system, MeshWeaver, instead treats generation as surface weaving. It predicts the next vertex directly rather than independent coordinates.

Bedi audits the tools that grade practice data for imitation learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Robots and agents often learn by copying recorded demonstrations. Big structural errors, a wrong move at a key moment, fooled every tool that looked only at actions. Two tools even rated the flawed records above clean ones. Above the cutoff, the dissipation pattern looked much like the single-phase case. Near and below it, the multifractal spectrum widened sharply, resting on sparse intense structures. The analysis shows ReMax reshapes the policy-gradient landscape itself. Gradient directions tilt toward higher policy entropy, so exploration emerges even with deterministic rewards. Gradient sizes shrink, though, damping learning and slowing convergence. The Adam optimizer's adaptive scaling can soften that damping, depending on its stability parameter. The practical version, ReMAC, is an off-policy actor-critic using the new estimator. It raised policy entropy with no entropy bonus at all. Performance matched the strong SAC baseline. Inside the model, each token is carried as a hidden state vector, and its L2 norm is just that vector's length. Ankur Garg and co-authors infer hidden causes behind survey answers in this 2026 arXiv paper on causal representation learning. The goal is to recover the high level concepts, such as cultural values or political opinions, that generate low level measurements like questionnaire responses. Priors encode the field's standard assumptions and the demand that concepts stay interpretable. A sequential Monte Carlo sampler then approximates the tangled posterior distribution. Jiaju Chen and co-authors release a dataset of humans collaborating, annotated thought by thought, in this 2026 arXiv paper. AI agents rarely get trained on that layer, because authentic data with such annotations barely existed. Léo Bigorgne settles how a plasma or galaxy of charged particles settles down in this 2026 arXiv paper on partial differential equations. The Vlasov Poisson system tracks a huge ensemble of particles under their own collective field. Small disturbances are expected to scatter: particles end up streaming freely, with a correction because the field decays slowly. Bigorgne proves this modified scattering with initial data, final states, and convergence all measured in the same topology.

Stronger still, the wave operators mapping initial states to scattering states are homeomorphisms between the data spaces: continuous, with continuous inverses. Nothing is lost in the correspondence. In the repulsive case, large spherically symmetric solutions are therefore asymptotically stable. Big round plasmas disperse predictably instead of blowing up. The proof hinges on coordinates moving with the asymptotic flow.

Marin Girard, Gong Cheng, and ChunJun Cao explain objectivity itself with error correction in this 2026 arXiv paper. Why do different observers agree on measurement outcomes if the world is quantum? Quantum Darwinism answers that the environment copies information about a system many times over, so many observers read the same record. Earlier accounts captured only pieces of this. The authors connect it to operator algebra quantum error correction, where information survives local damage.

Their claim is precise: emergent objectivity is the local recoverability of a quantum code. Applied to stabilizer codes, the framework sharply describes classicality and redundancy. It unifies the older objectivity measures that previously floated apart, and classifies cases with coding tools. It also supports large Clifford simulations of decoherence, letting researchers watch objectivity emerge on a computer. The result is a coding based account of how classical facts form out of quantum dynamics.

balzac-cousin-bette-waring-1888:
Honoré de Balzac wrote Cousin Bette in French, and James Waring made the first English version in 1888. Balzac's dark late masterpiece turns on envy and revenge inside one Paris family. He wrote it fast, in months, near the end of his vast career of fiction.

Lisbeth Fischer, plain and poor, nurses lifelong envy of her fair cousin Adeline. She helps the rake Valmont ruin Adeline's husband, the vain old Baron Hulot, by plots. Debt, disgrace, and theft spread through the Hulot house as Bette pulls her strings. A Polish exile, Wenceslas, stands at the center of love, art, and betrayal in Paris. The book is Balzac at his most pitiless, swift, and hard to put down.
bellamy-looking-backward-1888:
Edward Bellamy imagined the year 2000 in Looking Backward, published in 1888. His hero, Julian West, sleeps in 1887 Boston and wakes in the Boston of 2000. That future city runs on socialist lines he could not have dreamed. A guide explains the new order of work, pay, and goods.

An industrial army organizes labor, and equal credit replaces wages and cash. Shops, music, and meals all run as public services in his design. The novel sold hugely and launched clubs devoted to its program. It became the era's best known utopian classic. Readers still visit its future to test their own hopes. The frame tale stays charming.
blavatsky-secret-doctrine-vol1-1888:
Helena Petrovna Blavatsky published Volume 1 of The Secret Doctrine in 1888, with the subtitle Cosmogenesis. Blavatsky, a cofounder of the Theosophical Society, claimed the book rested on an ancient hidden text, the Stanzas of Dzyan. Volume 1 treats the birth and order of the universe.

Blavatsky described worlds forming in great cycles, guided by spiritual beings, long before human life appears. She set Hindu, Buddhist, and other teachings beside the science of her day and claimed they agreed. Critics attacked her sources, but readers flocked to the system. The volume became the founding text of modern Theosophy and shaped occult thought far beyond her society.
blavatsky-secret-doctrine-vol2-1888:
Volume 2 of Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine, Anthropogenesis, also appeared in 1888. Where Volume 1 treated the cosmos, Volume 2 treated humankind. Blavatsky again built on the Stanzas of Dzyan, which she said held a secret record of human origins.

She described root races, early human forms said to arise on lost lands such as Lemuria and Atlantis. Apes, in her account, came from humans rather than the other way round, a direct clash with Darwin. She mixed myth, geology, and scripture into one vast scheme. The volume completed the work that made Theosophy a world movement and fed later lost-race and ancient-astronaut lore.
boas-central-eskimo-1888:
Franz Boas based this study on his stay on Baffin Land in the far north, and it came out in 1888. He worked for the Bureau of Ethnology in the United States. The book deals with the Inuit groups of the central Arctic coast.

Boas set down food, homes, tools, and trade, then turned to belief. He gave the first full account of the angakok, the Inuit shaman, and of taboos and views of the world. The work helped launch the modern study of peoples as a strict field craft. It is still read by all who study the Arctic past.
bosanquet-logic-vol1-1888:
Bernard Bosanquet's Logic, or The Morphology of Knowledge, from 1888, opens with volume one here. Morphology is the study of forms, and Bosanquet studies the forms of thought itself: how judgment and inference grow, stage by stage. He wrote as a British idealist, in the wake of Hegel, against the dry formal logic of the schools.

For Bosanquet, a judgment is not a label pasted on the world but the mind building its world into a system. Inference, likewise, is the self-development of knowledge toward a coherent whole. Volume one lays that living account of thought from its roots upward. The work remains a summit of idealist logic, exacting and rich.
bosanquet-logic-vol2-1888:
Volume two completes Bernard Bosanquet's Logic, or The Morphology of Knowledge, of 1888. Bosanquet, the British idealist, treats logic not as a rule book for arguments but as the anatomy of knowledge in growth. The two volumes together form his fullest statement on how thought builds a world.

The second volume carries the account of judgment and inference toward the system that all knowledge seeks. Each form of thought, for Bosanquet, corrects the one before it and points beyond itself. Truth lives in the coherence of the finished whole, not in single, severed claims. Readers who finish the Logic hold the British idealist theory of knowledge at its most developed.
brazilian-constitution-1988:
Brazil promulgated its present constitution in October 1988, closing twenty-one years of military rule. A freely elected constituent assembly wrote the text in public, hearing thousands of popular amendments from citizens' groups. Brazilians call it the citizens' constitution, a name its makers prized.

The charter restores democracy in full: direct elections, free parties, and a free press after decades of censorship. Its bill of rights is lavish in the modern Latin American style, promising health, education, and social security as duties of the state. Workers gain detailed protections, and the environment receives its own chapter. Critics call the text unwieldy; defenders answer that its promises were the point. The law of freedom regained still governs the giant of South America, the founding act of Brazil's New Republic.
buchanan-s-journal-of-man-1888: Buchanan's Journal of Man, 1888. The anthropological journal. This book preserves that periodical. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. The paper lived through the years.
catalogus-manuscriptorum-chemico-alchemi: Someone catalogued the occult manuscripts in 1788. Chemical, magical, cabalistic, and medical texts got listed. The old bibliography. Its pages add to the record of the past. This book preserves that 18th-century catalogue for future readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-revol: This 1913 reference piece on the English Revolution of 1688 — the Glorious upheaval. Edwin Burton unfolds its Catholic cost. James fled the Protestant winds. William's ships brought the new order. The fall of the last Catholic king. Its Bill of Rights is famed.
cerebrology-and-the-possible-something-i: Cerebrology and the Possible Something in Phrenology, 1888. The cerebrology. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-0000009688:
American prisoners held in Laos, near Pathet Lao and North Vietnamese military headquarters sites, are surveyed in a March 1969 paper. The heading links the prisoners to the enemy's command presence in Laos. Headquarters areas drew bombing, which made nearby captivity doubly dangerous.

Survey papers tried to state how many Americans were held in Laos and roughly where. The answers stayed rough because the prison system hid inside a secret war. Still, an overview guided where scarce collection effort should go next. This file preserves the 1969 attempt at that overview, with all its gaps plainly showing.
cia-0000011788:
What would happen to France if Charles de Gaulle died or was killed? A CIA paper from August 1962 works through that question in cold detail. De Gaulle had founded the Fifth Republic only four years before and ruled it as a towering, personal figure. Assassins of the OAS, fighting his plan to free Algeria, had already tried to kill him.

The paper weighs who could succeed him and whether his system would survive him. It treats the republic as built on one man and tests how it would stand without him. The study is a striking example of planning for an ally's worst day.
cia-0000012088:
Syria's break from the United Arab Republic in 1961 shattered Nasser's grand union. In February 1962, National Intelligence Estimate 36.1-62 weighed his prospects in the wreckage. Egypt kept the union's name even after Syria walked out, a sign of how hard the blow had landed. The estimate came when the colonel's design for Arab unity lay in pieces.

The community's judgment covers what remained of Nasser's power and plans. It weighs his standing at home, his economy, and his reach abroad after the split. The paper shows Washington recalculating the worth of a leader whose star had just visibly dimmed.
cia-0000012288:
Helms wrote yet again to the Pentagon's front office in August 1961, a third memo in a quickening series. The flow of Penkovsky intelligence ran upward and outward that summer without pause. Each letter moved fresh Soviet military detail toward the planners who measured American strength against it, and each one had to be logged, guarded, and answered.

The series itself is the story: no single memo mattered as much as the tempo they kept together. The files preserve that tempo in letterhead and dates. For readers, the drumbeat shows a case that never left the principals' desks for long.
cia-0000012388:
The U-2 incident of May 1, 1960, still generated paper a year later, and an undated staff study, its year estimated as 1961, re-examines it. An American spy plane had been shot down over the Soviet Union that May Day. Its pilot, Francis Gary Powers, survived, was tried in Moscow, and became the Cold War's most famous prisoner of the sky.

The study revisits Powers's fate and the incident's fallout while both were unresolved. The shootdown had wrecked the Paris summit and taught hard lessons about risk. For readers, the paper shows Langley dissecting its disaster long after the wreckage cooled.
cia-0000013888: Planes, trucks, and helicopters moved North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces, and a CIA report dated October 6, 1967, surveys that transport. Moving men and supplies kept the war in the south alive. The report pulls together general facts on all three kinds of travel. It reads as a broad brief on how the other side stayed mobile.
cia-0000014188: Soviet and Chinese strategy across North Africa, the Middle East, and nearby regions fills a CIA paper dated June 4, 1965. The paper tracks the tactics both powers used far from home. By 1965 Moscow and Beijing were rivals as much as partners. Reading their moves side by side helped Washington plan its own Cold War steps.
cia-0000024488: The fall of Nam Tha, seized by communist forces on May 6, has its implications weighed in a CIA record dated in 1962. Nam Tha was a town in northwest Laos, near the Chinese border. Its fall shook the shaky neutral order in Laos that spring. Analysts had to judge whether one town's loss meant a wider collapse was coming.
cia-0000042788:
Many organizations were left leaderless because of the fighting, a CIA record dated November 2, 1989 reports. The title ties the report to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. El Salvador's war had reached into unions, parties, and civic groups alike.

Inside, the report counts a quiet cost of the war: groups without leaders. Leaders had been killed, jailed, driven abroad, or driven underground. Church groups, unions, and parties all felt the same steady loss of people. A country can lose its civic strength without losing a single battle. The file records that slower damage, in which the middle layers of public life thinned out year by hard year.
cia-0000042888:
Venceremos reported the rector's assassination, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. Venceremos was the radio voice of the Salvadoran rebels. The rector it mourned led the university where the Jesuits taught.

Inside, the rebel station's account of the killing is preserved. Rebel radio told the war as the guerrillas wished it heard. Its grief for the rector was also a weapon in the war of words. The rebels knew the killing hurt the government, and their broadcasts made the most of that hurt. The file lets readers hear the other side's version, set beside the government's statements in the same crowded archive of that autumn.
cia-0000044888:
A church and human rights commission office was bombed in Chile, in a CIA record dated June 1, 1985. The office gathered testimony about abuses under the Pinochet regime. Bombing it was an attack on the witnesses themselves, in plain terms.

Inside, the attack on the office is reported for the record. Rights workers in Chile worked under steady threat and surveillance. Their files of testimony were dangerous things to keep in those years. The record preserves one strike against that work, in a country where the church had become the chief shelter for people with nowhere else to turn.
cia-0000045188:
Reuters judged that Duarte's handling of the kidnapping weakened his government, in a CIA record dated September 3, 1985. A wire service verdict carries weight in capitals around the world. The judgment cut at the president in his hardest personal crisis.

Inside, the agency's analysis of his position is preserved. A president bargaining for his daughter looked, to many, like a state bending. That look cost him authority with soldiers and rivals alike. The file keeps the wire's cool verdict, which is part of how the crisis was understood abroad while it was still unfolding at home.
cia-0000046088: An untitled CIA document dated April 3, 1968, centers on twelve photographs, numbered two through thirteen, of Major Carl D. Miller. cia-0000126888: Dated January 1968, this CIA report relays a Soviet official's comments on the possible renewal of Arab-Israeli fighting. cia-0000132188: Situation report 505, from January 1991, records Moscow denying that it had military advisers in Iraq, the heading breaking off. das-geheimnis-aller-geheimnisse-ex-macro: Das Geheimnis aller Geheimnisse, 1788. The secret of secrets. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
davenport-death-blow-spiritualism-1888:
Margaret Fox Kane confessed her fraud to reporter Reuben Briggs Davenport, and his 1888 book told the world. The Fox sisters' rappings of 1848 had launched modern spiritualism. Kane, one of the sisters, now described how the knocks were made. Davenport, of the New York World, shaped her confession into The Death-Blow to Spiritualism.

The book gives the true story of the sisters, in her account, trick by trick. Toe joints, she said, made the famous rapping sounds. Believers fought the confession, and Kane later withdrew it. Historians still treat the volume as a key insider record. It broke the founding story of spiritualism open.
dellon-history-of-the-inquisition-at-goa:
Charles Dellon, a French doctor, fell into the hands of the Inquisition at Goa and lived to write the tale. His Relation de l'Inquisition de Goa appeared in French in 1687, and this English version followed in 1688. Dellon had spent his youth traveling in India when the Holy Office seized him in 1673.

He tells of the secret arrest, the cells, and the long silence. The charges against him were never shown. At last he walked in the auto-da-fé of 1676 in the procession of the condemned. His book carried the horror of Goa across Protestant Europe. It fixed the Inquisition's image in the English mind for two centuries. Few eyewitness tales of the tribunal match it.
demille-strange-manuscript-copper-cylind:
James De Mille wrote A Strange Manuscript Found in a Copper Cylinder in the 1880s. The book came out in 1888, after his death. Four yachtsmen fish a copper case from the sea. In it lies the tale of Adam More, a castaway of the far south.

More tells of a warm land near the pole and its folk, the Kosekin. Their creed turns our world on its head: they court death and scorn wealth and love. More weds a Kosekin maid and flees with her at great cost. The tale is the chief lost race book of its land, Canada.
donnelly-great-cryptogram-1888:
Ignatius Donnelly turned from lost lands to a lost author in 1888. The Great Cryptogram argues that Francis Bacon hid a cipher in the plays called Shakespeare's, proving Bacon wrote them. The book runs to two fat volumes of counts, tables, and claims.

Donnelly counts words by page and line and draws out a hidden tale of Bacon's life at court. His cipher made him the star of the Baconian cause and a target for its foes. Scholars reject the method, but the book's craft made it hard to ignore. It stands as the founding text of cipher hunting in the plays.
dream-days-pg1288: Kenneth Grahame's 1898 companion to The Golden Age: five dreamy stories of childhood, including the first appearance of "The Reluctant Dragon." Told with exquisite nostalgia, they capture the secret world of children, half real and half imagined. The most poetic of all Victorian childhood books.
europmc-pmc10163288:
Bennett and a large team show how deep learning can improve the design of new protein binders, in a 2023 study. Designing proteins that grip a chosen target is a core skill in drug and sensor development. Energy-based design methods worked, but their success rate was low, so most designs failed in the lab.

The team added deep learning steps to sharpen the design process. Their tests show higher success in making binders that hold their targets as planned. Better design tools mean faster routes to new medicines and research tools.
europmc-pmc10216288:
Clemente-Suárez and colleagues review adipokines in health and disease in a 2023 paper. Adipokines are signaling proteins released by fat tissue. Far from being inert storage, fat acts as an organ that talks to the brain, liver, and immune system, and its signals are tied to low-grade inflammation and many diseases.

The review sorts the main adipokines and what each one does. It traces their roles in obesity, diabetes, heart disease, and joint problems. It also weighs their promise as markers and drug targets. The paper shows fat tissue in a new light.
europmc-pmc10379988:
Thang, Chien, and Cuong reviewed polymer-based hydrogels for drug delivery in 2023. A hydrogel is a net of water-loving chains that can hold much water. Such gels can store a drug and let it out slowly in the body. They are soft, body-friendly, and easy to tune.

New designs release drugs when a trigger fires, such as heat, acid level, or an enzyme. Thang notes that this aim can cut harm to the rest of the body. Some gels can be injected as a liquid and then set in place. Tiny nano gels may load and aim drugs still better. The review sees gels tuned to one patient as a growth path for care.
europmc-pmc10406888:
Bernardi gathered top experts in 2023 to settle a long fight over a pore in cell power units. The pore sits in the wall of mitochondria, the parts of a cell that make energy. When calcium floods in, the pore can open and let small bits pass. If it stays open, the unit swells and the cell may die.

Two parts have each been blamed as the pore itself. One is a mover of fuel bits, called ANT. The other is the cell's energy-making machine, ATP synthase. Bernardi weighs proof for both and seeks points of shared ground. Brief pore openings may be normal and useful, aiding energy balance and calcium flow. Long openings drive injury, such as after a blocked blood vessel reopens.
europmc-pmc10776388:
How much should scientists trust a shape guessed by AI? Terwilliger and co-authors take up that question in this 2024 paper. AlphaFold, a leading AI tool, has changed how biologists study proteins, which are the working parts inside cells. Yet its guesses vary in quality and leave out factors such as small bound molecules and cell conditions.

The team checked AlphaFold outputs against maps from lab tests that use X-ray beams on crystals. Many guesses matched the maps very closely. Others, even some rated as highly sure, were bent or placed whole sections in the wrong spot. The authors urge readers to treat each guess as a strong lead, not proof, and to test key details in the lab.
europmc-pmc11047988:
Maleki Varnosfaderani and Forouzanfar assess how AI is changing hospitals and clinics in this 2024 review. Health systems face rising costs, limited access, and growing demand for care tailored to each patient. AI is cast as a key force that could ease all three pressures. The authors set out to judge where it truly helps today.

Case studies cover four domains: clinical decisions, hospital operations, medical image reading, and patient monitoring through wearable devices. Each domain shows gains and leftover hurdles, the review finds. The authors also cover how to evaluate AI tools before use. Ethical risks get a full treatment, above all data privacy and bias in the data. They call for joint work among researchers, clinicians, and technologists to deploy AI responsibly.
europmc-pmc1112588:
Rastogi and Liberles model what happens to spare gene copies after duplication in this 2005 study. Gene duplication is a key source of new traits in evolution. One fate, called neofunctionalization, gives one copy a wholly new job. Another, subfunctionalization, splits the old job between the two copies. Which fate dominates was unclear.

The authors built lattice model genes, simple simulated proteins that fold and bind two targets. Each gene was duplicated in a small simulated population with no mixing of genes. Models that allowed job splitting reached new functions through it, they found. Job splitting acted as a transition state toward a new function, not as a final fate. No pressure kept both copies identical, they note. The result reframes how duplicated genes are retained.
europmc-pmc1247388:
Whyatt and colleagues measured prenatal insecticide exposure in New York City in 2004. Minority women faced wide insecticide exposure during pregnancy there. An earlier report tied cord blood chlorpyrifos to lower birth weight. The expanded study covered 314 mother and newborn pairs.

Air samples during pregnancy showed no link to birth size. Cord blood told a different story for chlorpyrifos. Each log unit rise cut birth weight by about 43 grams. Birth length fell by 0.24 cm per log unit. Combined chlorpyrifos and diazinon measures showed similar links. Whyatt separates air exposure from blood dose. Head size at birth showed no such link.
europmc-pmc1334188:
Hellens and co-authors built plant gene test vectors for fast experiments in 2005. The vectors use Agrobacterium bacteria to deliver genes into tobacco leaves. New pGreenII vectors were stripped of parts needed only for stable transforms. That trimming suits short-term expression tests.

One test expressed a P450 enzyme to prove the system works. Dual luciferase vectors measure promoter strength and gene regulation. Transcription factors were paired with target promoters to test control. Hairpin vectors probed how silencing constructs should be designed. Hellens gives plant labs a compact functional genomics toolkit.
europmc-pmc1462988:
Bacteria carry odd DNA arrays of short repeats, called CRISPR, next to a set of linked genes. Makarova and co-authors asked in 2006 what this system does. Past work guessed it fixed DNA damage. The tight link between the repeats and the genes hinted at a shared task instead.

Sorting the linked proteins into about 25 families, Makarova saw a pattern. The parts mirror, in role, the RNA interference system that guards complex cells from viruses. She proposes the arrays act as an immune system. Stored bits of invader DNA guide attacks on matching germs and plasmids, small DNA rings. The idea recast CRISPR as defense, not repair.
europmc-pmc1621088:
Treating culture as a checklist for clinicians can backfire. Kleinman and Benson made that argument in 2006, examining cultural competency, a popular approach in medicine. It trains doctors in supposed beliefs of ethnic groups, as in the Mexican patient or the Chinese patient.

Anthropology, where the culture concept began, rejects such fixed group portraits as stereotyping. Culture is not a synonym for ethnicity or language. Kleinman notes culture is not always at the heart of a case, and leaning on it can block a practical grasp of a patient's real problem. They propose fixing the approach rather than teaching lists of do's and don'ts.
europmc-pmc1849888:
Chen, Roos and colleagues ran a head-to-head test in 2007 of programs that find orthologs, genes in different species descended from one ancestral gene. Spotting orthologs underpins gene annotation and genome comparison. No gold-standard dataset existed at genome scale, so the methods had never been fairly graded.

The team used latent class analysis, a statistical trick that infers accuracy from agreement and disagreement between methods, without a truth set. A clear trade-off emerged on the eukaryotic data tested. Methods built on BLAST searches caught more true pairs but admitted more errors, while tree-based methods were stricter and missed more. Two tools balanced best, with sensitivity and specificity both above 80 percent: INPARANOID for pairs of species, and OrthoMCL for grouping many species at once.
europmc-pmc1852588:
Zhang, Jacobsen and co-authors mapped in 2007 a silencing mark across the whole genome of the plant Arabidopsis thaliana. The mark is three methyl tags on one spot of histone H3, a spool protein that DNA wraps around. In animals the mark is vital for development, but its plant reach was unknown.

Using a dense tiling chip that covers the genome, they found the mark on about 4,400 genes. That makes it a major silencing system in plants. Its upkeep proved largely independent of DNA methylation and RNA interference, two other silencing routes. Unlike animals, where the mark spans huge regions, plant marks were confined to the transcribed part of single genes. They also avoided the low-density DNA packaging zones seen in animal genomes.
europmc-pmc2025288:
Hayward and co-authors proposed in 1977 a shared system for judging treatment response in advanced breast cancer. The project came from the International Union Against Cancer, known as the UICC. Different centres were using different evaluation methods, making published results hard to compare. A single uniform system promised fair comparison across trials. Breast cancer was chosen first because agreement seemed within reach.

A draft document was circulated widely to workers in the field for comment. It was then revised before final publication. The guidelines serve trials that assess objective response in locally advanced or spreading breast cancer. Subjective response, how a patient feels, is not covered. Eligibility requires tissue proof of breast cancer available for review. The British Breast Group accepted the system, replacing its earlier method.
europmc-pmc2125288: A medical paper studying Barlow's disease produced in fetal and newborn guinea pigs. The scurvy model. This article preserves that nutrition research. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2126288: A medical paper with a report on antimeningitis vaccination and observations on agglutinins. The meningitis shot. This article preserves that immunology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128088: A medical paper on measurement of the growth of tissues in vitro. The measured growth. This article preserves that cell biology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
europmc-pmc2128188: A medical paper on the effect of induced cellular reaction on cancer grafts' fate. The grafts, rejected. This article preserves that oncology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128288: A medical paper on epinephrine content of the suprarenal glands in anaphylaxis. The shock glands. This article preserves that endocrinology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
europmc-pmc2128388: A medical paper on leucocytic secretions. The white cells' output. This article preserves that immunology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128488: A medical paper on measurement of the inherent growth energy of tissues. The tissues' vigor. This article preserves that cell biology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2128588: A medical paper with studies on oxidation by pneumococcus, oxidation of enzymes. The germ's rust again. This article preserves that biochemistry. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2131088: A medical paper with studies on tumor susceptibility and heredity. The inherited cancers. This article preserves that oncology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131488: A medical paper on the transfer of rat anemia to normal animals. The passed anemia. This article preserves that hematology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2140088:
Pinkas, Strop, Brunger and Khosla solved the active structure in 2007 of human transglutaminase 2, an enzyme that crosslinks proteins. Called TG2, it shapes tissue matrix and drives the gluten reaction in celiac disease. Earlier structures of related enzymes all showed closed forms with hidden active sites. The team trapped TG2 with an inhibitor mimicking inflammatory gluten peptides, then read its structure by X-ray crystallography at fine resolution.

The trapped enzyme sat in an extended shape, dramatically different from earlier structures. Its active site was exposed, revealing a tunnel where the reaction happens. Two tryptophan residues bridge the tunnel and stabilise the reaction steps. Mutations on one side shifted the enzyme toward breaking down rather than crosslinking. The structure grounds new work on TG2's roles and on the celiac autoantibody response.
europmc-pmc2199288:
Calafat and colleagues measured two industrial chemicals in urine from a national United States survey in 2008. Bisphenol A, or BPA, is used in polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins. The second chemical, tOP, is used in surfactants. The team analysed urine from 2,517 participants aged six and older in the 2003-2004 survey, using sensitive mass spectrometry methods.

BPA was detected in 92.6 percent of people, and tOP in 57.4 percent of them. Exposure was near-universal across the general population in the United States. The sample was nationally representative and covered children and adults during the survey years. Children carried higher BPA levels than adolescents, who carried more than adults. Females had higher levels than males. Mexican Americans had lower levels than non-Hispanic black or white participants. Levels were lowest in the highest income group.
europmc-pmc2246288:
Blenkiron and co-workers profiled microRNA expression in human breast cancer in 2007, seeking markers of tumour subtype. MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression. The team profiled 99 primary tumours, five normal breast samples and 33 cancer cell lines with a bead-based platform covering 309 human microRNAs. They combined expression data with genomic changes measured in the same tumours.

The platform detected 133 microRNAs expressed in normal breast or tumours, out of 137 found overall. Results proved reproducible and matched independent PCR checks for a subset. Integrated analysis of microRNA expression and genomic changes classified tumours into their subtypes. The authors present the combined approach as a way to find new subtype markers. Such markers could sharpen diagnosis and point to subtype-specific biology in breast cancer.
europmc-pmc2374988:
Teschendorff and co-authors sorted a hard-to-treat breast cancer group into subtypes in 2007. These cancers lack the estrogen receptor, a hormone sensor, so hormone drugs do not work on them. The team used a feature selection method, a computer routine that picks the most telling genes, across three large gene activity data sets.

Their analysis showed this cancer group is not one disease. It holds at least four main subtypes with distinct gene patterns. One subtype stood out: its tumors carried a strong immune response gene module, meaning a set of immune genes switched on together. Patients with that immune-rich subtype had a good prognosis, a better outlook than the others. The authors presented the module as a marker that could guide how hard to treat these patients.
europmc-pmc2396288:
Eddy tackles a hidden cost in DNA database searches in this 2008 theory paper. Searching compares a query pattern against millions of sequences and scores each match. Judging whether a score could arise by chance needs a statistical formula, and one key constant in it used to require slow computer simulations to pin down.

Eddy proposed that with full probabilistic scoring, the constant takes a simple fixed value: the natural log of 2. He argued the best-match scores then follow a known bell-like curve for extremes, called a Gumbel distribution. The total-evidence scores, called Forward scores, should fade off in a matching simple pattern. Simulations across 9,318 protein family models from the Pfam database backed both claims. The result makes significance values fast and accurate to compute for both score types.
europmc-pmc2491588:
O'Brien and colleagues showed that a hormone receptor inside bone's buried cells controls bone mass in 2008. Osteocytes are former bone-building cells trapped inside the bone itself, long suspected of directing remodelling. Parathyroid hormone, PTH, drives remodelling but can add or remove bone. Whether it acts through osteocytes was unknown.

The team engineered mice whose osteocytes carry an always-on PTH receptor. These mice built higher bone mass with faster remodelling: more bone-eating and bone-building cells, and fewer builder cells dying. Their osteocytes made less sclerostin, a protein that blocks the Wnt growth signal, so Wnt signalling rose. Removing the Wnt partner receptor LRP5 blunted the extra mass but not the faster remodelling. The study splits PTH's osteocyte effects into two routes, one needing LRP5 for mass and one driving turnover without it.
europmc-pmc2553488:
Hotez and colleagues mapped the overlooked diseases of the tropics in Latin America and the Caribbean in this 2008 review. These diseases afflict the region's poorest people. Many patients are indigenous or of African descent. The authors gathered burden data, meaning case counts and healthy years lost, to rank the diseases and chart where they cluster.

Hookworm and other gut worm infections, plus Chagas disease, carried the heaviest burden, ahead of better-known threats in total impact. Then came dengue, schistosomiasis, and leishmaniasis. Trachoma, leprosy, and lymphatic filariasis followed. The diseases cluster in 11 sub-regions with distinct ecologies. The authors judge that schistosomiasis could be eliminated from the Caribbean, while the biggest burdens first need scaled-up resources or new control tools.
europmc-pmc2575188:
Jensen, Jørgensen, Binderup, and Kjaer compared in 2008 three ways of measuring tumour size in cancer drug studies on mice. Researchers judge treatments by tumour volume, usually measured with external calipers, a technique prone to error. The team implanted human breast cancer cells under the skin of 20 mice. They measured each tumour three ways: by caliper, by microCT scanning, and by PET imaging. Then they weighed the true volume after removal.

All three methods tracked the true volume, but microCT showed no systematic bias while calipers and PET both did. Repeated measurements by one observer varied by 7 percent with microCT. With calipers the figure was 14 percent. Two observers also agreed more closely with the scanner. The authors judge PET unsuitable for sizing and recommend microCT over calipers.
europmc-pmc2613888:
Oñate-Sánchez and Vicente-Carbajosa published streamlined protocols in 2008 for extracting pure, DNA-free RNA from the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Gene expression measurement by quantitative PCR demands RNA with no contaminating DNA, yet standard protocols are laborious, use toxic chemicals, and still need an enzyme cleanup step. Seeds and seed pods are especially awkward tissues.

Their two protocols use simple, non-toxic buffers for most tissues. They reserve organic extraction for seeds and siliques, the seed pods. Contaminating DNA is removed before the final precipitation step, skipping extra purification. Starting material can be as small as 10 to 20 milligrams without losing quality. Tests on genes with known expression patterns confirmed the RNA works reliably, and the low cost suits high-throughput work.
europmc-pmc2614188:
Nilsson, Kristiansson, Ryberg, Hallenberg, and Larsson measured in 2008 how much the standard fungal barcode region varies within species across the whole fungal kingdom. The region, called ITS, is the most popular locus for identifying fungi from DNA, and automated identifiers assume variation within a species stays clearly below variation between species. The team mined the international sequence databases for all fungi with enough data.

They found substantial differences across the kingdom that did not track taxonomy or lifestyle in any simple way. Some groups varied little within species, others a great deal. No single ceiling, including the canonical 3 percent threshold, separated within-species from between-species variation throughout the fungi. The authors caution against simplified automated identifications and stress that translating sequences into species names still needs taxonomic expertise.
europmc-pmc2631488:
Langfelder and Horvath published the WGCNA software package in 2008, implementing weighted gene co-expression network analysis in the R language. The method groups genes by how similarly they behave across samples, forming correlation networks whose clusters, or modules, often share a biological job. Earlier descriptions of the method were scattered across papers, leaving users without a single consistent tool.

The package covers the whole workflow. It builds networks and detects modules. It summarises each module by its eigengene, a representative activity profile. It also relates modules to each other and to outside traits such as disease state. It also computes module membership scores, simulates data, and draws visualisations. Applications already span cancer, mouse and yeast genetics, and brain imaging. The package and tutorials are freely available online.
europmc-pmc2845588:
Park, Chyun, Kim, Line, and Chew ran a controlled trial in 2010 of astaxanthin, the red pigment that colors salmon and shrimp shells, in young healthy women. Cell and rodent studies had cast it as a strong antioxidant that calms inflammation and perks up immunity, but human data were missing. Forty-two women took zero, two, or eight milligrams daily for eight weeks.

Blood levels of the pigment rose with dose. A DNA damage marker fell by week four, and an inflammation marker dropped in the low-dose group by week eight. Immune tests improved: killer cell activity rose, lymphocyte growth after stimulation rose, and skin test responses strengthened in the low-dose group. Two immune signals also rose at the high dose, rounding out a broad immune lift.
europmc-pmc2873288:
Diaz de Leon and colleagues studied in 2010 families whose faulty telomerase gene leads to scarred lungs in middle age. Telomerase rebuilds telomeres, the DNA caps that shorten each time a cell divides. Faults in its protein part, TERT, had turned up in some patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, lung scarring without a clear cause.

Across twenty-one families and one hundred thirty-four carriers, cap length shrank with age and shortened further in each new generation. Relatives without the faulty gene still had shorter caps than normal, showing caps themselves are inherited as well. Lung scarring never appeared before age forty but struck about sixty percent of carriers past that age, making the condition a slow countdown written into chromosome ends.
europmc-pmc2876988:
Schultz reviewed in 2010 what single dopamine neurons in the midbrain actually signal about reward, drawing on recordings from awake monkeys. Dopamine cells were long cast as pure pleasure signals based on lesion and drug studies. Fine-grained recordings during behavior tasks reveal a much more precise code.

The cells fire in brief bursts that report reward value compared with what was expected, a prediction error signal that learning theory requires for teaching. The burst size scales with value and probability combined into expected value, and it is measured against the spread of recent outcomes. Far fewer cells respond to punishers or merely startling events, so the signal is not general arousal. Some cells also flag risk, giving the brain a compact value-and-risk report for choices.
europmc-pmc2892488:
Darling, Mau, and Perna released in 2010 progressiveMauve, a program that aligns whole genomes even after evolution has shuffled, gained, and lost large chunks. Simple aligners assume the same parts in the same order, but real genomes rearrange, duplicate segments, and drop genes, leaving a mosaic of shared blocks. Their method finds blocks conserved in only some of the genomes, a case earlier tools missed.

A new scoring rule judges candidate breakpoints, the joints where shuffling happened, and a probability filter strips out chance matches between unrelated stretches. Fresh accuracy metrics measure breakpoint and gap calls separately. On simulated and real bacterial genomes with heavy reshuffling, accuracy stayed high. The tool became a workhorse for comparing pathogen genomes during outbreak tracing.
europmc-pmc2920088:
Steenland, Fletcher, and Savitz reviewed in 2010 the human evidence on PFOA, the persistent chemical once essential to nonstick coatings. It does not occur naturally, yet it sits in the blood of nearly everyone in industrialized countries, with a typical United States level near four nanograms per milliliter. The body does not break it down, and clearing half takes about three years.

Animal studies tie it to tumors and to immune, liver, and hormone effects. Human studies, mostly snapshots that cannot prove direction, most consistently link higher PFOA with higher cholesterol and uric acid, though the cholesterol pattern shifts oddly across exposure levels. Liver enzyme links were weaker and less consistent. Drinking water drives exposure in some communities, but general sources remain poorly mapped.
europmc-pmc2944788:
Hayes and co-authors compared how gene effects are spread for three cattle traits in 2010, asking what that spread means for predicting breeding worth from DNA markers. Holstein cows supplied the test traits: black coat share, milk fat share, and an overall body score.

Coat colour rested on three known loci explaining about a quarter of variation, plus many tiny effects elsewhere. Milk fat had one large-effect locus and a swarm of small ones. The body score showed only small effects throughout. These contrasts, measured over chromosome chunks, explain why DNA prediction accuracy differs between traits.
europmc-pmc2945788:
Goecks, Nekrutenko, and Taylor presented Galaxy, a free web platform for genome analysis, in a 2010 article with the Galaxy Team. Computer-heavy biology raised worries that results were hard for others to repeat or even to run.

Galaxy records where every dataset came from and the exact steps applied, so analyses can be shared, rerun, and checked. Its Pages feature lets authors publish a full analysis as an interactive document mixing data, tools, and explanation. The design targets researchers without programming training who still need careful, transparent computing for sequencing and other large-scale data.
europmc-pmc3103488:
Shahedur Rahman and Rezuanul Islam wrote a 2011 review in Cell Communication and Signaling about Sirt1, a protein found in mammals. Sirt1 removes small chemical tags from other proteins and needs a common cell fuel to do so. Their article gathers what was known about its many jobs in the body.

The review covers Sirt1 in fat tissue, the liver, the heart, and the brain, and links it to weight gain, cancer, aging, and cell wear over time. It also treats stress responses, early growth, and survival of placental cells. For readers, the paper offers a single map of a protein tied to diet, lifespan, and disease.
europmc-pmc3125288:
Cyril Vidau and colleagues tested combined stresses on honey bees in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Bee numbers are falling worldwide, and both gut parasites and farm insecticides are suspects. The team infected young bees with a common gut parasite, then fed some of them very low, non-lethal doses of two widely used insecticides.

Infected bees exposed to either insecticide died at clearly higher rates than bees facing only one stress. Oddly, the two chemicals pushed parasite spore output in opposite directions. Infection did raise activity of one detox enzyme in gut and fat tissue, so simple detox failure does not explain the deaths. The authors argue that parasite spread plus chemical traces in hives together help drive colony losses.
europmc-pmc3125388:
Sandra Thygesen and colleagues checked hospital coding accuracy in Denmark in a 2011 paper in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Researchers often use a standard index of nineteen long-term diseases to adjust hospital studies, trusting that registry codes match real diagnoses. The team audited that trust against patient records.

They reviewed discharge papers and charts for fifty hospital contacts per disease, drawn from a decade of northern Danish admissions. Nearly every coded diagnosis was confirmed on review. Twelve of the nineteen diseases scored perfectly, and the weakest, diabetes with complications, still scored well above four fifths correct. The authors conclude the registry codes are reliable enough for comorbidity adjustment in research, at least in this Danish setting.
europmc-pmc3155788:
Maura Lodovici and Elisabetta Bigagli reviewed how polluted air harms the body through oxidative stress in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Toxicology. Dirty air is tied to more heart and lung disease and death, and the leading explanation runs through unstable oxygen chemicals that inflame and kill cells. The review gathers the evidence pollutant by pollutant.

Fine and ultrafine particles, ozone, nitrogen gases, and metals in particles can all generate those chemicals directly or provoke cells to make them. Traffic exhaust is a major source of the smallest particles, which reach deep into lungs and can enter the blood. How much harm follows depends partly on how well each organ can raise its own protective scavenging systems. The authors stress that particle mix, not just particle amount, shapes the health impact.
europmc-pmc3203188:
Eric Feeley and colleagues investigated how the protein IFITM3 blocks influenza A virus, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. IFITM3 is switched on by interferon, the alarm signal cells release during infection, and it was known to restrict several viruses in the lab. The team wanted to pin down exactly where it stops the virus.

They showed that interferon prevents viral genomes from escaping the cell's endosomal compartments, and that this block needs IFITM3, which by itself can produce it. Test particles could not deliver their contents into the cell interior when IFITM3 was present. The protein sits in late endosomes and lysosomes, right in the path of incoming viruses, which explains why viruses that fuse there are vulnerable while surface-entering ones may slip past.
europmc-pmc3231888:
Laura Lamberti and colleagues pooled the evidence that breastfeeding protects babies and toddlers from diarrhea, in this 2011 review in BMC Public Health. Diarrhea remains a major killer of young children in poorer countries, and feeding practices in the first two years shape the risk. The team systematically gathered studies published over three decades.

Across eighteen studies, breastfeeding protected against diarrhea illness, prevalence, hospital admission, and death, with the strongest protection from exclusive breastfeeding in the first six months and from any breastfeeding thereafter. Not breastfeeding at all carried a many-fold higher risk of diarrhea death for young infants compared with exclusive breastfeeding. The authors say the results back the World Health Organization recommendation of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months as a key child-survival measure.
europmc-pmc3282688:
Shangong Wu and colleagues catalogued the bacteria living in the grass carp's intestine, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. The gut community matters for managing farmed animals, yet basic information for many species is thin. Using gene sequencing of intestinal contents and of the fish's culture environment, the team asked what lives in the gut and where it comes from.

The intestine harbored many cellulose-digesting bacteria, fitting the fish's plant diet, and its most abundant members were tied to feed digestion. Potential pathogens and probiotics were both present as important members. A core community of three bacterial phyla ran through the samples. The gut community resembled those of the culture water and sediment most closely, marking them as major sources, though feed also significantly shaped what lived in the fish.
europmc-pmc3375788:
Van Tu and colleagues investigated hand, foot, and mouth disease in southern Vietnam in 2007, focusing on the 2005 season. The illness brings a few days of fever plus sores in the mouth and a rash on hands, feet, and buttocks. Several related enteroviruses can cause it, but one stood out as dangerous.

Enterovirus 71, the team found, was strongly tied to acute brain and nerve disease, while coxsackievirus A16 was not. Young children under five faced the greatest risk of lasting harm or death. Brain inflammation in the region was shifting toward younger children, which had prompted the study. The results argue for close virus tracking during outbreaks.
europmc-pmc3410788:
Wen, Shen, Shi, and Tang built a software platform in 2012 for tracing how microRNAs evolve across species. These tiny RNAs steer many body processes, and deep sequencing now finds them by the thousand in plants and animals. Few tools, though, could follow their sequence and activity changes across species at once.

Their platform, miREvo, combines three jobs behind a graphical interface. It discovers new microRNAs in sequencing data, finds their counterparts in other species using whole-genome alignments and measures their distances, and profiles how strongly each is expressed in each species. Tests on fruit fly and plant data showed the pipeline working end to end. The free tool targets evolutionary studies of small RNAs.
europmc-pmc3458588:
Gänzle and Follador reviewed in 2012 how lactobacilli, the lactic acid bacteria of food and gut, eat short sugar chains and starch. These chains, built of a few sugar units, are staple food in the bacteria's habitats and central to their ecological success. Two-sugar metabolism is well understood; longer chains had drawn less study until interest in gut ecology and prebiotic foods arrived.

The review walks through five chain families plus starch, using data on where each enzyme sits in the cell and what the transporters accept. Pathways for two-unit sugars often stretch to three and four units too. But nearly all the cutting enzymes stay inside the cell, so import is the choke point. That single constraint, the authors note, sets lactobacilli apart from gut specialists that digest outside.
europmc-pmc3488188: Colon cancer got a pre-op chemo pilot. This 2012 pilot tests chemo before surgery for colon cancer. The authors reveal the feasibility. Their work guides trials. The Foxtrot group led the work. The paper is widely cited. It shaped trial design.
europmc-pmc3558688: Microglia got a fractal measure. This 2013 paper measures brain immune-cell shapes with fractal math. The authors reveal the measure. Their work guides neuroscience. Karperien's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped brain-image analysis.
europmc-pmc3575288: Genome editing got Mojo Hand. This 2013 paper introduces Mojo Hand, a TALEN design tool. The authors reveal the tool. Their work spread through labs. Neff's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide.
europmc-pmc3628788: Pregnancy weight got a baby-weight review. This 2013 pooled study links mom's BMI to baby weight. The authors reveal the links. Their work guides obstetrics. Yu's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. The study shaped pregnancy guidance.
europmc-pmc3716788: Counts got TCC. This 2013 paper launches TCC for count-data comparison. The authors reveal the package. Their work spread through labs. Sun's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3720188: Trials got a what-if tutorial. This 2013 paper teaches what-if analyses in trials. The authors reveal the how. Their work guides researchers. Thabane's tutorial is widely cited. It is a classic. Students rely on it. The tutorial is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3748788: Diabetes got a C-peptide review. This 2013 paper reviews C-peptide tests in diabetes care. The authors map the use. Their review guides endocrinology. Jones's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped diabetes testing. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3812088: Genomes got a history-from-DNA method. This 2013 paper reads population history from DNA. The authors reveal the method. Their work guides genetics. Excoffier's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped population genetics.
