The nation's germ-defense shelves deserved better buying discipline, GAO argues. The report is a plea to run biodefense like lives depend on it, because they do.
geheime-figuren-rosenkreuzer-1785-1788:
Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer, printed at Altona from 1785 to 1788, is the emblem book of the Gold- und Rosenkreuzer order. The German title means the secret figures of the Rosicrucians, drawn from the 1500s and 1600s. The order that issued it was the leading Rosicrucian body of its century.

Sixteen engraved plates carry the book, each plate a dense symbolic image. Around the plates runs the order's own commentary, steeped in alchemy and theosophy, two paths to hidden knowledge of God and nature. The volume became the order's most famous printed work. Its plates still shape how the Rose Cross is pictured today.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-4-1788:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 4 of his Decline and Fall in 1788. Attention turns east to Justinian and the Byzantine Empire. Belisarius, Justinian's great general, reconquers parts of Italy and Africa from the Goths and Vandals. Law receives its classic code under Justinian's direction.

The plague that struck the empire in the 540s gets a chilling account. Gibbon also surveys Persia and the early state of Arabia before Muhammad. His irony spares neither monks nor emperors. The volume shows the History's true scope: a whole civilization's world. Readers admire its learning on law, war, and faith alike.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-5-1788:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 5 of his Decline and Fall in 1788. Muhammad and the Arab conquests enter the narrative in this volume. Gibbon gives a long account of Arabia, the Prophet's life, and the Koran. Arab armies then sweep Persia, Syria, Egypt, and Spain with stunning speed.

Later chapters treat the iconoclast emperors, the Bulgarians, and the state of the Eastern Empire. Gibbon's treatment of Islam was unusually fair for his age. His irony returns in full for monks and relic cults. The volume carries the story to the eve of the Crusades. Its breadth shows why the History is called a world in itself.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-6-1788:
Edward Gibbon completed his Decline and Fall with Volume 6 in 1788. The final volume covers the Crusades, the Mongols, and the last centuries of Byzantium. It ends with the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453. Gibbon closes by surveying the ruins of Rome itself.

His last pages reflect on the whole arc from empire's height to ruin. The siege of 1453 is told with grim grandeur. Gibbon finished the work in Lausanne and recalled sitting in the Capitol as a young man when the idea first struck him. The six volumes form the greatest history ever written in English, by wide consent.
giraldus-cambrensis-topography-of-irelan:
Giraldus Cambrensis tells of wolf priests in The Topography of Ireland, writ near 1188, here in Thomas Forester's English. Giraldus was a Welsh priest who rode with Prince John to Ireland. His book maps the land, its beasts, its saints, and its marvels. One part stands out: a priest in Ossory meets a pair who turn wolf by a curse, and who beg rites for a mate at death's door.

The tale is the first great wolf text of Ireland. It blends awe, faith, and doubt in a rare mix. The whole book is a rich store of that age.
golden-dawn-book-t-tarot-1888:
Hands in the Golden Dawn wrote down their tarot lore in Book T, a set of drafts from near 1888. The Golden Dawn was a small band of mages in London. Their drafts fix what each card means, how cards link to stars and signs, and how to lay a spread for fate.

Waite drew on these drafts for his famed pack of cards. Most packs since then still use their scheme. Few short drafts have shaped an art so much. Here is the source text, plain and terse, that all those packs rest on. The drafts are terse, oft in code and brief hand notes. Waite and his peers fleshed them out in their own packs and books soon past.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-1-1888:
George Grote published his History of Greece in twelve volumes from 1846, here in Murray's 1888 edition. This first volume of the ten-volume 1888 set opens the foundational modern history of ancient Greece in English. Grote, a London banker and radical MP, rewrote Greek history from a democratic point of view.

Volume One treats the legendary age, geography, and early peoples of the Greek world in careful detail. Grote sifts myth from fact, telling the tales while marking them as tales, not sober history of Greece. His preface defends Athens and democracy against the aristocratic bias of earlier English histories of the Greeks. The scale is vast, the style clear, and the learning worn with unusual ease for readers. Later volumes carry the story from early states to Alexander and his successors in turn.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-10-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this tenth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume closes the long work in full. Grote ends with Alexander and the generation of his successors, as his preface promised his readers there.

Alexander's conquests scatter Greek speech and cities from Egypt to the Indus in one brief lifetime. Grote treats the conqueror with respect and reserve, weighing the cost to the free city-states of Greece. The volume also surveys Greek Sicily and the western colonies, completing his wide Mediterranean canvas of Hellenic life. His last chapters take stock of what the Greek experiment in self-government left the modern world as legacy. The ten volumes stand as Victorian scholarship's monument to Greece, still readable and still argued.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-2-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this second volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume presses into early times. Grote writes as a scholar and a democrat, keen to do justice to the Greek people.

The early volumes trace Greece from legend toward record, state by state and colony by colony. Constitutions, lawgivers, and tyrants take shape as scattered tribes grow into the classic city-states of Greece. Grote's method weighs sources openly, so readers see doubt handled rather than hidden in the history's pages. His sympathy for popular government sets the tone that made the work a liberal landmark in England. Read in sequence, the volumes build one vast arc from myth to empire.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-3-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this third volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, retold for the democratic age in England. Each volume advances the long story while keeping Grote's clear style and open weighing of sources.

As the history moves toward the classic age, Persia looms and the Greek states arm and league. Grote gives constitutions and colonies the same care he gives battles and famous men of Greece. His Athens rises in these volumes from one city among many toward the head of a league. The narrative pace quickens as record replaces legend and the great wars come into view at last. Scholars used Grote for a century, and general readers still find him lucid.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-4-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this fourth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and its middle volumes reach the great wars. Grote's democratic reading of Athens was a rebuke to the Tory histories that came before him.

Persian invasion, Athenian sea power, and Spartan land might collide in the world these volumes survey in depth. Grote lingers on institutions as much as battles, for he thinks constitutions make the fate of states. His Marathon and Salamis stand beside his accounts of law, finance, and the Athenian assembly at work. The prose stays measured even as the scale of events swells toward the classic age's height in Greece. For Victorian readers this was Greece made modern, rational, and politically alive again.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-5-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this fifth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume stands near its classic center. Grote brings a banker's head for finance and a radical's heart for the Athenian demos to it.

Athens at her height, empire, tribute, and the building age of Pericles fill volumes of this scope. Grote defends the Athenian empire's energy while he faults its coercion of subject allies in the Aegean world. Sophists, orators, and generals move through a narrative that never loses the thread of institutions and laws. His judgments are argued, not asserted, and readers can follow his evidence page by documented page. The History's fame rests on this union of learning, clarity, and political sympathy.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-6-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this sixth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and by this volume war dominates the tale. Grote wrote with the Peloponnesian War's long shadow over Athens and Sparta in full view here.

The rival leagues harden, speeches sharpen, and the great war grinds the Greek world down year by year. Grote follows campaigns and constitutions together, since in Greece the two were never truly apart in practice. His account honors Thucydides while it checks him against the fuller record available to modern scholarship in London. Readers get plague, faction, and the slow ruin of the Athenian empire as one connected story of power. Few English histories match its patience with causes over the long haul of war.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-7-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this seventh volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume nears the war's grim end. Grote's sympathy for Athens is tested by her crimes and follies, which he does not spare.

Sicily draws Athens to her great disaster, and the tale turns on error, pride, and chance. Grote weighs commanders and assemblies alike, asking who truly chose the fatal course at each hard turn. The narrative keeps its clarity even as expeditions, sieges, and sea fights crowd the Aegean and Sicilian coasts. His democratic faith survives the wreck, for he blames men and systems, not the demos alone, here. In sequence the volume forms the History's tragic center, Greece consuming her own strength.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-8-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this eighth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume covers the war's aftermath. Grote treats defeat and recovery with the same care he gave Athens in her imperial prime years.

Oligarch coups, Spartan victory, and the slow rebuilding of walls and fleets fill these postwar chapters in Greece. Xenophon and the march of the Ten Thousand carry Greek arms deep into the Persian empire's heartland. Grote follows the shifting leagues and the rise of Thebes as Sparta's grip weakens across the Greek world. His interest in constitutions sharpens as democracies and oligarchies trade places in city after Greek city. The volume shows Greece inventing new balances after hegemony's first great collapse.
grote-history-of-greece-vol-9-1888:
George Grote's History of Greece fills this ninth volume of Murray's ten-volume edition of 1888 in London. The set is the foundational modern history of ancient Greece, and this volume nears the Macedonian age in Greece. Grote's narrative slows for philosophy and oratory as the city-state world begins to fail around them.

Demosthenes thunders against Philip of Macedon while Athens debates, delays, and arms too late for her freedom. Thebes rises and falls at Leuctra and Mantinea, and Sparta fades from the first rank of powers. Grote gives the orators and the courts their due as engines of the late democratic city at Athens. His liberal reading finds dignity in Athens' last stand for self-government against a rising military monarchy in Macedon. The volume sets the stage for the History's close in Alexander's vast and brief career.
guyton-de-morveau-method-chymical-nomenc:
Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau led the team that gave chemistry a new set of names in 1787. Their scheme came out in English in 1788 with this title. Old names for stuffs were a mess of trade terms and false hints. One stuff might bear six names, and one name might serve for three stuffs.

The new names tell what a stuff is made of, in a clear scheme of roots and ends. Sulfates, oxides, and acids each fall in their own class by rule. The reform gave the new chemistry the tongue it still speaks, from school rooms to labs.
hartmann-secret-symbols-rosicrucians-188:
Franz Hartmann, a German doctor turned Theosophist, published Secret Symbols of the Rosicrucians at Boston in 1888. The book collects plates from a rare German work of the 1780s, with Hartmann's commentary for modern readers. Through it, the nineteenth-century occult revival received the Rosicrucian emblem tradition in visual form.

Alchemical diagrams, cosmic wheels, and symbolic figures fill the large plates. Hartmann explains each in the revival's own mystical idiom. The source-book shaped how the Golden Dawn generation pictured the old fraternity. Its images have been reprinted ever since, often without credit. Readers who want the visual language of Rosicrucianism, as the revival learned it, start with Hartmann's plates.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol8-1888:
Eight years separated Volume VIII of the Guiding Symptoms from the first, and it arrived in 1888. The delay shows in the care of the editing, as Hering's students worked through boxes of proving notes. Remedies still march in alphabetical order, their symptoms filed under body regions.

Few books in the school carry this much raw clinical memory. A prescriber chasing an odd, precise symptom, the kind that names one remedy alone, would search here first. The marks of rank beside each line keep the search short. Volume VIII keeps the promise of the title: guidance, not mere bulk.
hinton-new-era-thought-1888:
Charles Howard Hinton was a math man who gave the fourth dimension its name in print. His A New Era of Thought came out in 1888. He taught readers to think past length, breadth, and height. The book laid the base of what fans call hyperspace thought.

Cube drills train the mind to picture a form with a fourth reach. Hinton asks what such a space would mean for the soul and for fact. He gives plain steps that a keen reader can work through at home. The book made talk of a fourth reach a set field of thought.
home-d-d-home-life-mission-1888:
Mme. Dunglas Home guards her man's name in D. D. Home: His Life and Mission, out in 1888. Home had died two years past. His wife prints his notes, tales of guests, and words of praise from lords and sages who sat with him. Arthur Conan Doyle adds a warm word at the book's front in her aid.

The tale runs from his youth in the United States to fame in the courts of Europe. She aims to fix his fame as a true seer, not a trick hand. The book is the set life of the age's top seer.
hopkins-scientific-christian-mental-prac:
Emma Curtis Hopkins earned the name teacher of teachers, and Scientific Christian Mental Practice, from 1888, is her textbook. Hopkins trained Charles Fillmore and a generation of New Thought ministers in her Chicago classrooms. Her course builds from a Statement of Being through denials and affirmations, step by ordered step.

Students learn to deny error's power and affirm the good they claim as real. The method is mental, yet Hopkins gives it the shape of a strict spiritual discipline. Her book systematized New Thought teaching, and its structure shaped the movement's churches and classes for decades.
hugo-hunchback-of-notre-dame-hapgood-188:
Victor Hugo wrote Notre-Dame de Paris in French, and Isabel Florence Hapgood made it English in 1888. Hugo's great Gothic novel of medieval Paris stars the cathedral itself as hero. He wrote it in part to save the church from decay and clumsy repair work.

Quasimodo, the deaf bell-ringer, loves the dancer Esmeralda from his tower heights. Archdeacon Frollo's lust for her drives plots of kidnap, trial, and false witchcraft charges. Hugo fills the book with crowds, gargoyles, and a famous bird's-eye view of Paris. The end is grim for nearly all, yet the cathedral stands above their fates. The tale revived care for Gothic art across France and far beyond it.
hutton-theory-of-earth-1788:
James Hutton presented his Theory of the Earth paper in 1788 to the Royal Society of Edinburgh, in its Transactions. Hutton, a Scottish farmer and naturalist, argued that the Earth's features are the work of slow forces still at work today. That claim opened the door to deep time.

Rocks, Hutton said, are worn down, laid down in seas, hardened, lifted, and worn again in an endless cycle. At sites such as Siccar Point, tilted layers under flat ones proved to him a past far longer than the received chronology allowed. His famous line found no vestige of a beginning. The paper is the founding document of modern geology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahler-arthur-1:
Arthur Mahler, an Austrian archaeologist, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Prague on August 1, 1871, he studied at the gymnasium there. He then read art history and archaeology at the universities of Prague and Vienna, taking his doctorate. In 1902 he became a lecturer in archaeology at Prague's German university.

The article lists his scholarly connections and his one named book. He belonged as a corresponding member to the Austrian Archaeological Institute. He wrote for its yearbooks and for French journals of archaeology and numismatics. His book of 1902 studied Polyklet and his school, a contribution to the history of Greek sculpture. He also gave a series of lectures at the American School of Archaeology at Rome. The short entry preserves a young scholar working where art history meets classical digging.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marano-plural-m:
Marano, the name for the secret Jews of Spain and Portugal, is defined in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. The word in Spanish means damned or accursed, and also hog. It was thrown at Jews who had accepted baptism under pressure. The forced conversions followed the massacres of 1391 and Vicente Ferrer's preaching campaigns.

The article explains why the Maranos changed history. More than a hundred thousand converts entered Christian society at once. They grew rich in trade and married into the old nobility. Their children reached high office at court, in law and medicine, and even in the Church. The writers argue that this class brought on both the Inquisition and the expulsion of 1492. They then divide the Maranos into classes, starting with the indifferent. Some converts mocked Judaism for advantage, while others kept the old faith in secret. The entry opens the full story of the crypto-Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matthias-ben-th:
Matthias ben Theophilus is a name shared by two high priests. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss sort them out in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The first succeeded Simon ben Boethus and was, unlike the other high priests named by Herod, a native of Jerusalem. On the eve of one Day of Atonement he became ritually unclean, and a kinsman had to perform the service in his place.

Suspected of sharing in the golden eagle revolt, the first Matthias was deposed after only a year or two, about 5 to 4 B.C. The second Matthias, apparently his descendant, was the last high priest but one. He held office in 65 C.E., when the war with Rome broke out. He was deposed as a member of the peace party. At last Simon ben Gioras put him to death, the very strongman he had invited into Jerusalem against the revolutionists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meisach-joshua-:
Joshua Meisach was a Russian Hebrew author of tireless output. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Sadi, in the government of Kovno, in 1848, and began publishing in 1861 in the weekly “Ha-Karmel.” He went on to write and edit more than one hundred works in Hebrew and Yiddish. By 1904 he was living at Warsaw, still at work.

The entry lists his wares. They include essays on faith and enlightenment, letters, criticism, a book on the theater, and novels. They also include the magazine “Gan Perahim,” Garden of Flowers, which he edited at Wilna and Warsaw from 1881 to 1893. His most characteristic book may be the “Ozar Hadash.” It is a treasury of anecdotes and stories from the Talmud and Midrash, arranged in alphabetical order and printed at Wilna in 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menz-abraham-jo:
Abraham Joseph ben Simon Wolf Menz was rabbi at Frankfort-on-the-Main. He served at the opening of the eighteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. J. Levinson enter him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They enter him not for a commentary but for a mathematics book. His "Reshit Limmudim," Beginning of Studies, was an elementary textbook in three parts. One part gives the rules of algebra. One gives the elements of geometry. One gives the elements of astronomy.

Only the first part ever reached print. It appeared at Berlin in 1775, decades after his time. It contains the first book of Euclid rearranged. It holds many examples of the author's own devising. The notice is brief. It rests on the standard bibliographies of Steinschneider, Fürst, Zeitlin, Fuenn, and Benjacob. Still, it preserves a small landmark. A Frankfurt rabbi taught his community algebra, geometry, and the sphere in Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mi-un-10888:
Mi'un is a Hebrew word meaning refusal or protest. It is the legal act by which a girl married off while still a minor could end that marriage. The Jewish Encyclopedia article appeared in 1906. Its authors were the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius H. Greenstone. It sets out the rabbinic rules in the Talmud, Maimonides, and the Shulḥan Aruk.

A marriage arranged by a father stood firm, the article explains. It needed a formal divorce. But a second minority marriage, arranged by a mother or brothers, could be undone at any time before she came of age. The girl simply declared before two witnesses that she would not live with her husband. No divorce writ was required. Even accepting betrothal money from another man set her free.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-ben-sha:
Michael ben Shabbethai Cohen Balbo, called Michael Cohen of Crete, was a Greek scholar, Hebrew poet, and preacher. He was born on March 27, 1411. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Almost everything in it rests on manuscripts kept in the Vatican. The article is candid about tangled identities.

One Vatican manuscript holds his poem of 1453 on the fall of Constantinople to Mohammed the Conqueror. It also holds a lament for his father from 1456 and a commentary on Psalm twenty-eight. Three sermons preached at Khania in the 1470s are there too. Another manuscript records his disputation with Moses Cohen Ashkenazi on the transmigration of souls. Zunz, Steinschneider, and Wolf all dispute which works are truly his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-isaac:
Moses ben Isaac Hanessiah was an English grammarian and lexicographer of the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His second name came from his mother, a Cambridge Jewess named Comitissa. Little else is known of his life.

In his youth he wrote a Hebrew grammar, the Leshon Limmudim, now lost. His surviving work is the Sefer ha-Shoham, the Onyx Book, whose title is an anagram of his name. It shows some knowledge of Arabic and of Joseph Kimhi's writings. Part of it was published at Oxford in 1882, and the entry closes by weighing whether a London tombstone was his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-motta-jacob-de-:
Jacob de la Motta was an American physician, the son of Emanuel de la Motta of Charleston. Cyrus Adler and L. Hühner wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born about 1789, he studied medicine and joined the South Carolina Medical Society in 1810. He served as an army surgeon in the War of 1812.

After the war Motta practised at Charleston and then at Savannah, where he helped build a synagogue and preached in it without pay. His 1820 discourse at its consecration drew letters of praise from Jefferson and Madison. He ended as a leading Charleston physician and a federal receiver under President Harrison. He died at Charleston in 1845.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahshon-11288:
Nahshon, son of Amminadab, was prince of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on him. Aaron was his brother-in-law, and through Boaz he became an ancestor of David. At the Tabernacle's dedication, though Judah ranked fourth, Nahshon offered first.

The rabbis explain that honor. At the Red Sea, they say, Nahshon sprang first into the water, and his name itself means stormy sea-waves. So all Israel pointed to him when Moses asked who should offer first. The letter vav in his offering's account, they add, marks him as ancestor of six great men, David and the Messiah among them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naumburg-louis-:
Louis Naumburg was a cantor from a long line of cantors. Cyrus Adler and Josiah Cohen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Treuchtlingen, Bavaria, in 1813. His family had sung in synagogues since 1612. Each generation held at least one cantor. He died in New York on March 4, 1902.

Naumburg reached America some time after 1848. Philadelphia's Keneseth Israel chose him as cantor in 1850. He held that Reform post for ten years. He also taught and read in the synagogue there. In 1865 he became minister at Rodeph Shalom, Pittsburg. He lived in Pittsburg until near his death. He also made a German verse version of Proverbs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-era-illustr:
The New Era Illustrated Magazine was a Boston-born Jewish monthly. Herman Rosenthal and Isidore Singer wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Raphael Lasker founded it in June 1902. It began as the New Era Jewish Magazine. In October 1903 its title changed as given here.

That year its office moved from Boston to New York. The New Era company took over the property then. It serves no class and speaks for no one person. Its pages cover all matters of Jewish interest. One prized feature reviews the Jewish reviews themselves. Isidor Lewi edits the magazine in New York. Contributors include Nordau, Montefiore, Kayserling, and Simon Wolf. Vogelstein, Geiger, and Berkowitz also write for it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nordheimer-isaa:
Isaac Nordheimer was an American scholar of Eastern tongues. Cyrus Adler and A. Rhine wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Bavaria in the year 1809. He died young, in 1842, in America. Memelsdorf, near Erlangen, was his birthplace.

He shone early as a Talmudic student. Presburg's school and Moses Sofer formed him first. Würzburg and Munich gave him his doctorate in 1834. New York called him across the sea in 1835. He taught Arabic and Hebrew at its university. Union Seminary also claimed him as an instructor. His Hebrew grammar rested on a philosophical basis. Its two volumes won great repute on appearing. A concordance from his hand stayed unfinished at death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oliveyra-solomo:
Solomon de Oliveyra was a hakam and author at Amsterdam. The board and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A hakam is a sage and teacher of the law. His father was David Israel de Oliveyra, a scholar. Solomon died at Amsterdam on May 23, 1708.

Oliveyra taught at the Keter Torah school in Amsterdam. He taught in place of Moses Raphael de Aguilar there. In time he led the rabbis' school of his flock. That flock was the Spanish and Portuguese group in the city. As a youth he turned to Hebrew verse and song. He put out a rhyming word book in Hebrew. He wrote word books in three tongues for school use. Those tongues were Hebrew, Aramaic, and Portuguese.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-osnabruck-11788:
Osnabrück is the chief town of its district in Hanover. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Hanover was then a province of Prussia, in Germany. A Jew named Jacob is named there in 1267. The text of a Jewish oath of that age has been kept.

In 1309 Bishop Engelbert the Second gave an order. His lay judges were to shield the Jewish homes there. Those homes then numbered about thirteen in the town. He set a cap on the gain Jews could take on loans. It was one pfennig per mark for each week. In 1327 Bishop Gottfried shielded fifteen Jewish homes by name. Each home paid a tax to him each year. In the Black Death years, Jews were slain at Osnabrück.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-papa-11888:
Papa was a Babylonian sage of the fifth group of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. An amora was a sage who taught the Mishnah's sense. Papa was born about the year 300 in Babylon. He died in the year 375, by the entry's count.

Papa read with Raba and with Abaye, two great sages. When both of his teachers died, he founded a school. That school stood at Neres, a town near Sura. His friend Huna ben Joshua worked at his side there. Papa's father seems to have been a man of wealth. That wealth let the son give his days to study. Papa grew rich in his own right by the brew of beer. He was a skilled hand at that trade in Babylon. His teacher once praised his rare lot in life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pehah-from-the-:
Peḥah was the title of a governor in ancient Palestine. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The office was copied from a Babylonian model. English Bibles render the word as governor. It lasted well into the Persian period.

The title is named as early as Solomon's reign. No details of the office survive from that age. Under Persia these governors drew a fixed income. Zerubbabel and Nehemiah held the post for the Jews. Nehemiah took pride in giving up the taxes owed him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pharpar-12088:
Pharpar is a river of Damascus named in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It flows down from Mount Hermon. South of Damascus it bends southeast toward the lakes. The entry is short, matching the river's brief mention.

The river owes its fame to one sharp speech. Naaman the Syrian scorned the Jordan at first. He asked if Abana and Pharpar were not better. He meant the rivers of his own Damascus. Scholars still dispute which modern stream is Pharpar. Thomson and Smith give two different answers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pisa-da-12188:
The Da Pisa were an Italian family named for Pisa. Four scholars shared this entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The line is traced back to the fifteenth century. Its members joined learning, banking, and public service.

Abraham da Pisa was a Talmudist at Bologna. Popes squeezed him as court banker in wartime. His responsa stayed in manuscript, unprinted. Daniel da Pisa later led Rome's whole community. He united Italian and foreign Jews in one congregation. A council of sixty governed the united body. He also stood by David Reubeni at Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prophet-false-1:
False prophet is a charge treated in Jewish law. Solomon Schechter and S. Mendelsohn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Deuteronomy is the one book with laws on the point. It calls the man a prophet or a dreamer of dreams. Those who tempt others to false gods fall under the same charge.

Talmudic law narrows who can bear the charge, though. The accused must be a true, hallowed prophet of God. A plain man who lures others is judged by another name. If he lures single persons, he is a mesit. If he lures a whole town, he is a maddiah. The article works out these fine lines of law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-shela-:
Rabbah bar Shela was a Babylonian teacher of the fourth set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was of an age with the great Raba. He sat as a judge, most likely at Pumbedita. His name stands for strict honesty in that office. One of his sayings lays down the rule for judges.

A judge must not borrow from men under his court, he said. He may do so only if he can lend in return. A loan that cannot be matched breeds soft thanks. That thanks may bend the judge like a bribe, he warned. The entry sets out that rule and its ground. It traces his rulings through the Talmud's pages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rathenau-walthe:
Walther Rathenau was a German scientist, banker, and writer born in Berlin. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born on September 29, 1867. He studied at Berlin and Strasburg, taking a degree in 1889.

The article follows his work in the aluminum industry in Switzerland. With director Kiliani he found a way to make chlorine and alkalis. In 1893 he founded electrochemical works at Bitterfeld. He devised methods for making sodium, magnesium, and other materials. In 1899 he joined the board of a large electric company. In 1902 he moved into banking in Berlin. That year he also published essays called Impressionen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-robles-antonio-:
Antonio Rodrigues da Robles was an English Marano merchant and shipper. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Fundão, Portugal, about 1620. He settled in London and traded with the West Indies.

The article tells of his ships seized in 1656. England and Spain were then at war. Two ships, Two Brothers and Tobias, were taken. Robles himself was arrested as a Spaniard. He claimed he belonged to the Jewish nation instead. He said he came to England fleeing Spanish tyranny. Commissioners found the balance of testimony favored that claim. The Privy Council ordered his release. After that, no Jew in England need deny his faith. The entry marks a turning point in English Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sadakah-ben-abu:
Sadakah ben Abu al-Faraj Munajja was a Samaritan physician and philosopher who died near Damascus in 1223. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as court physician to the Ayyubid prince Al-Malik al-Adil.

Sadakah's works survive, the entry says, in manuscript copies still extant. One comments on Hippocrates, the father of Greek medicine, for Arabic readers. Another treats the soul and the spirit in philosophical terms. Others take up the unity of God and the doctrines of faith. He is also said to have commented on the Pentateuch itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ibn-abun:
Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel ibn Abun ben Yaḥya, an Arabo-Jewish poet. He lived in the eleventh century. Samuel was the great-grandfather of Samuel ibn Nazar. He was also a contemporary of the poet Moses ibn Ezra.

Very little of Samuel's work survives. One poem of his, built on an acrostic, has been printed. Luzzatto edited it from the fourth section of the Oran Maḥzor. It appeared in the journal Kerem Ḥemed. Moses ibn Ezra wrote an elegy when Samuel died. That elegy was printed in the same journal. The entry preserves the trace of a poet known through two short pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saphir-moritz-g:
Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Moritz Gottlieb Saphir. He was a Hungarian humorist. Saphir was born at Lovas-Berény on February 8, 1795. He died at Baden, near Vienna, on September 5, 1858. He went to Prague in 1806 to study the Talmud. German literature drew him more, and he settled at Pesth in 1814.

At Berlin, Saphir edited the Schnellpost and the Courier from 1826 to 1829. His clever plays on words won the public. That style was then new in German writing. His success also made him enemies. Critics attacked him in a pamphlet called Saphir in Berlin. He answered with a witty pamphlet of his own. It ran through four large editions in a week. He later founded papers at Munich and Vienna. His comic writings filled many volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schnabel-isidor:
Isidor Schnabel, an Austrian physician of the eye, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman, published in 1906. Schnabel was born at Neubidschow, in Bohemia, on November 14, 1842. He studied at the University of Vienna. He took his medical degree there in 1865. He then assisted in the university's eye clinic.

Schnabel rose through a chain of university chairs. He became professor of ophthalmology at Innsbruck in 1877. Graz followed in 1887, Prague in 1892, and Vienna in 1896. He still lives at Vienna in 1905. His writings treat the causes of nearsightedness. Others cover the diseases that follow iritis and the nature of glaucoma. He also wrote on syphilitic eye disease and on curing myopia. Pagel's lexicon of physicians supplies the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shirah-perek-pi:
Perek Shirah, the Chapter of Song, gathers praise of God from all creation. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Heavenly bodies, plants, and dumb creatures each sing in it. Each singer gets one or two verses of Scripture.

The chapter divides into six parts for the six weekdays. Yet the whole chapter is repeated daily in morning prayer. On Sabbath a different hymn takes its place instead. Saying Perek Shirah is not a duty for all. Only very pious Jews keep the practice regularly. Strange bird names in it hint at great age. Traces of it appear in the Talmud itself. The entry presents a hymn where the whole world joins in worship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-eleaza:
Simeon ben Eleazar was a tanna of the fourth generation, probably Eleazar ben Shammua's son. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He learned from Rabbi Meir and transmitted his sayings. Those sayings cover both law and homiletic teaching.

A famous anecdote shows Simeon striving hard for perfection. Coming home joyful from the academy, he met an exceedingly ugly man. The man greeted him, but Simeon mocked his ugliness instead. Go tell the Master who made me, the man replied. Simeon fell to his knees and begged pardon at once. The man refused until townsfolk greeted Simeon as rabbi. Then his rebuke shamed the sage before his own people. The entry uses one story to teach humility.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sirkes-joel-b-s:
Joel ben Samuel Sirkes was a Polish rabbi born at Lublin in 1561. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Bernhard Friedberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. At fourteen he was sent to study under Solomon ben Judah. He later studied at Brest-Litovsk under Rabbi Phoebus. While still young he was called to the rabbinate of Pruszany.

Sirkes held rabbinates in many towns, ending at Cracow. He loved the Cabala and opposed both pilpul and philosophy. His chief work was Bayit Hadash, on the Turim of Jacob ben Asher. It set out the basic principles of the Law. He also wrote notes on the whole Babylonian Talmud. He died at Cracow in 1640.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-de-saba: Solomon de Sabalducchio was a physician who flourished in Perugia, Italy. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He lived in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries there. Pope Boniface IX appointed him his body-physician in 1392. The pope's bull of April 1402 granted Jews certain rights. That grant grew in part from Solomon's work at court, with another physician named Angelo.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stanislavski-si:
Simon Judah Stanislavski was a Russian author and journalist born in 1850. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Nikopol on December 18 of that year. His father was a wealthy Lithuanian merchant in that town. Simon was first meant for a commercial career in life.

He overcame his father's opposition and turned to study instead. His teacher Ilya Orshanski reshaped his ambitions toward journalism. Under Orshanski he read Buckle, Draper, Darwin, and Mill. He also studied Latin, mathematics, and other sciences with care. He began writing for St Petersburg journals as a young man. In 1881 he became assistant editor of the Voskhod periodical.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-struck-hermann-:
Hermann Struck was a German painter born at Berlin on March 6, 1876. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. His family first aimed him at a rabbinical career. His talent for drawing soon changed that plan. He studied five years at the Berlin Academy of Fine Arts.

Struck traveled through France, Italy, Belgium, England, and Holland. In 1901 Prussia bought three of his drawings for a Berlin museum. They show a Polish rabbi and two old men. Struck stayed a devout Jew and studied Talmud for pleasure. He signed his pictures with his Hebrew name. He illustrated a 1904 book of travel pictures from Palestine. The entry catches a young artist early in his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teixeira-teixey:
Teixeira was a noble Portuguese Marano family of merchants. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The family first bore the surname Sampayo. Spain's Philip the Fourth set their arms in its roll. A 1643 patent granted nobility to Diego Teixeira.

The patent blazons an eagle displayed in purple. Checkered gold and black fields complete the shield. Eight silver letters S mark its red border. Most of the family later swapped those arms. Marriage to the De Mattos line brought a fir tree design. Members grew rich in trade and gave generously. They lived in Hamburg, Holland, London, and Vienna. Diego left Portugal for Antwerp in 1643. He died at Hamburg in 1666. The entry traces hidden Jews raised to titled rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-unitarianism-14:
Unitarianism, the Christian movement rejecting the Trinity, is traced from the Reformation onward. Kaufmann Kohler and M. H. Harris wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It first appeared in Poland in the later 1500s. Transylvania followed soon after, and the sect still flourishes there. Its modern center lies in the English-speaking world.

Exclusion from Protestant synods made it a separate church in 1565. The two Socinuses framed its first theology. Francis David became its first martyr. Joseph Priestley, finder of oxygen, spread it in England. Milton, Locke, and Newton are claimed among its adherents. Emerson gave it a transcendental touch in America. Its wings split over whether Jesus was divine. Conservatives accept his miracles still.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-washington-d-c-:
Washington, D.C. is the capital of the United States. Cyrus Adler and Abram Simon wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1849 only six Jews lived in the city. They traded on Pennsylvania Avenue. For major holy days they traveled to Baltimore. On April 25, 1852, they organized a congregation.

The First Washington Hebrew Congregation began with twenty one members. Solomon Pribram was its first president. In 1855 Congress extended church rights to the congregation. That act incorporated the district's first Jewish body. In 1863 it bought an old Methodist church. President McKinley laid the cornerstone of its new home in 1897. The entry traces a small group's steady rise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolff-joseph-14:
Joseph Wolff (1795-1862) was a mission worker and a bold traveler in the East. Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born near Bamberg, he was the son of a rabbi. He left home young, drawn to the Christian faith.

He was baptized in 1812 near Prague. He then studied Arabic, Syriac, and Persian tongues. He read church thought at Vienna and at Tubingen. In 1816 he reached Rome and met the pope in person. He joined church schools there for a time. In 1818 he was cast out for a public attack. He had charged that papal claims of no error were false. The long entry tracks his wide trips and his work in the East.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yir-am-of-magdi:
Yiram of Magdiel was a Bible scholar who lived at Rome. Crawford Howell Toy and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the tenth century of this era. His town name comes from a verse in Genesis. Rabbis read that name, Magdiel, as a sign for Rome.

He was a young peer of the famed Saadia Gaon. He may have been a pupil of that great man. He wrote a work on the Book of Chronicles. Just three scraps of that work live on in print. One scrap is drawn from the work of Saadia. One gives a tale sense to hard words in the text. One treats the sense of the tale as a whole. The man who bound the scraps charged him with weak grasp.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zebedee-apparen: Zebedee was the sire of two of the twelve men of Christ. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His name seems to mean the gift of God in Hebrew. He was the mate of Salome in his house life. He was a man of Galilee who fished for his bread. His boat and his hired hands are named in the Gospels. Those marks show a man of some means in his trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zuckerkandl-emi:
Emil Zuckerkandl was an Austrian anatomist who taught in Vienna for most of his career. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Raab, Hungary, in 1849, he took his medical degree at the University of Vienna in 1874. A year later he was teaching anatomy at Utrecht as a privat-docent.

Vienna called him back as assistant professor in 1879, and Graz made him professor in 1882. From 1888 he held the Vienna chair of descriptive and topographical anatomy. His many journal studies cover the skull, glands, and the sense of smell. His largest book treats the normal and diseased anatomy of the nasal cavity and its air spaces.
judge-epitome-of-theosophy-1888:
William Q. Judge boiled his creed down to its bones in An Epitome of Theosophy, a brief tract of 1888. The word means a short sum of the whole. In a few pages he states what the creed holds on God, man, death, and the fate of the soul.

The tract is like a short creed card for the faith. New fans could learn it by heart. Groups gave it out at doors and talks. Judge had a gift for plain, brief speech. This tract is that gift at its most lean. Brief as it is, the tract packs in karma, planes, and Masters. A keen fan could grasp the whole creed's frame from these few pages.
kalevala-vol1-crawford-1888:
Elias Lonnrot, a Finnish doctor, built the Kalevala from the songs of the folk of Finland and Karelia. John Martin Crawford turned it into English in 1888, the first full English form of the epic. This book is the first part of his work; the second part stands in the library too.

The songs tell of Vainamoinen, the old singer sage, and of the forging of the Sampo, a mill of wealth. Charms, births of iron and fire, and quests fill the lines in the old runo metre. The epic gave Finland its voice as a nation, and Crawford gave it to English ears.
kingsford-dreams-and-dream-stories-1888:
Anna Kingsford kept a log of her dreams, and Dreams and Dream-Stories prints it in 1888. Her friend Edward Maitland set the notes in form past her death. In sleep she met guides, saw signs, and got creeds in tale form. She held these dreams bore true light.

Some dreams read as brief fables. Some gloss her war on cruel tests on beasts, a cause she led. The log is the chief source for her signs and lore. It shows how her creed grew from night sight, not books. Some dreams warn, some teach, and some read as pure signs. Maitland adds brief notes where a dream needs a key to grasp.
kipling-plain-tales-1888:
Rudyard Kipling was a teenage newspaper reporter in India when he wrote these stories. Plain Tales from the Hills, published in 1888, was his first book for a wide audience. He wrote it at Simla, the summer capital where British officials escaped the heat.

The forty short tales show Anglo-Indian society in miniature: flirtations, feuds, pranks, and sudden tragedies. Young officers and clever widows scheme through the season while disease and distance shadow everything. Kipling's style is quick, dry, and knowing far beyond his years. The book announced a major storyteller and remains a sharp picture of the British Raj at play.
knigge-philos-endliche-erklaerung-1788:
Adolph von Knigge gave the Illuminati its shape as a working order, recruiting members and building its grades. By 1788 his partnership with founder Adam Weishaupt had collapsed in anger and mistrust. Philo's endliche Erklärung und Antwort, printed at Hannover that year, is his final public word on the break.

Writing under his order name Philo, Knigge answers the charges and questions put to him about his role. He complains that private letters and small slips were dragged into print to ruin men in public. He gives his side of the quarrel and explains why he left. Students of the order read the pamphlet as the key record of its inner split.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-3-1888:
Henry Charles Lea closed his History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages with this third volume in 1888. It turns from the map of the tribunal to special subjects that cross all lands. Lea's calm, record-based method made the set the standard work in English.

The Knights Templar and their fall, the trial of Joan of Arc, and the crimes of Gilles de Rais fill the great case studies. Lea then anatomizes the Inquisition itself: its books, its prisons, its money, and its men. He ends with the intellectual price the system charged the church. The three volumes together remain the base on which all later study builds.
lempriere-classical-dictionary-1788:
John Lemprière published his Bibliotheca Classica in 1788, a dictionary of the Greek and Roman world. Lemprière was a schoolmaster and clergyman who wanted classical learning within reach of readers without Latin and Greek. The book is better known by its short name, Lemprière's Classical Dictionary.

Thousands of entries explain gods, heroes, places, and stories from ancient myth and history. The dictionary gave poets a ready store of classical material: Keats, Byron, and Shelley all drew on it for their verse. For about a century it was the English reader's standard gateway to antiquity. Later classical dictionaries replaced it in schools, but its entries still show what educated readers of the Romantic age knew and loved.
library-of-the-world-s-best-literature-a:
Volume Two of Warner's anthology appeared in 1896, dated on its own title page. Charles Dudley Warner served as editor, with Mabie, Runkle, and George Henry Warner as associates. Professors from leading American universities formed the advisory council behind the selections. The series promised the world's best literature, ancient and modern, between its covers.

Like its companion volumes, this one collects excerpts and whole pieces across many centuries. The range runs from early classics toward the literature of Warner's own century. Short introductions and careful editing helped general readers approach famous names. The volume preserves a snapshot of the shared reading culture of its time. Harvard's Crawford Toy, a professor of Hebrew, headed the council list. Princeton's William Sloane represented history and political science there.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Chapter Four opens Motley's third volume on Barneveld and his times. An insurrection at Utrecht had just been subdued by the States' army. Dutch embassies hurried to England and France seeking support. Henry IV prepared for war and longed for Barneveld's presence in Paris.

Then came the king's murder, which transformed French politics overnight. Sully fell, and Spanish influence triumphed at the French court. Negotiations over the India trade added strain to Dutch diplomacy. The volume shows one assassination redirecting the fate of nations. Conversations between Henry and the Dutch commissioners fill long central passages. Henry's coronation preparations for his queen proceed alongside his war plans.
lives-of-alchemystical-philosophers-base:
Arthur Edward Waite revived these alchemists' lives in 1888. His materials were collected in 1815 by Francis Barrett. Recent researches supplement Barrett's older biographies here. The Boston Medical Library copy reached the Internet Archive in 2011.

Waite adds a demonstration of the magnum opus's true principles. Alchemical re-construction, he argues, works as spiritual chemistry. The adepts' lives illustrate that hidden doctrine across centuries. Waite had already written on the Rosicrucians and magic's mysteries. Waite also digested Éliphas Lévi's writings on magic. The real history of the Rosicrucians preceded this volume. Plain readers can follow the lives without knowing the old art first.
lives-of-alchemystical-philosophers-to-w:
Waite's 1888 London edition adds a list of books to the alchemists' lives. George Redway published it from York Street, Covent Garden. The preface traces the foundation to Barrett's earlier Lives. A full list of alchemy writers came with that first book.

Waite adds fresh research to the 1815 materials. His account explains the great work of alchemy remade. Soul-side chemistry, not mere metal-making, frames his case. The new list covers alchemy and hermetic thought broadly. A critical catalogue of alchemical writers followed Barrett's lives. Waite's preface directs readers to that foundation explicitly. The lives run from old adepts down to men of Barrett's own day.
maine-international-law-1888:
Henry Sumner Maine's International Law was published in 1888 from his Cambridge lectures of 1887. Maine, the author of Ancient Law, was the great master of the historical method in legal study. In these late lectures he turned that method on the law between nations.

Maine traces how states slowly learned to live under rules: the growth of diplomacy, the laws of war, and the treatment of neutral nations. He treats international law as a real growth from custom and treaty rather than a code handed down at once. His skepticism about grand schemes keeps the lectures grounded in practice. They were his last lectures, printed after his death in 1888. The book shows the Victorian jurist viewing world order through history's lens, and it still rewards readers who doubt easy theories of global law.
mathers-tarot-1888:
S. L. MacGregor Mathers wrote his tarot tract, Book T, in 1888. It was made for the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. Mathers led that order and set its teach in print. The tract gives the sense the order laid on each card.

Hebrew marks, star signs, and grades of the order lock to the cards. Short fate senses for each card fill the last pages. The scheme in Book T lies at the root of the Waite-Smith pack. Most new occult packs since draw on its plan in some form.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette:
Volume five of Campan's memoirs opens book two at chapter one. The oath of the States General at the Tennis Court starts it. A royal sitting on June 23 follows that famed oath.

The King orders the Orders to vote apart, and threats follow. The Queen counts Necker's absence that day as treachery or cowardice. Then come the risings of July 11, 12, and 14, 1789. The Bastille falls, and Flesselles and Launay are killed by the crowd. The people still cried love for the King that July, she notes. The Queen and the Comte d'Artois drew the crowd's hate instead.
molinos-spiritual-guide-1688:
Miguel de Molinos was a Spanish priest in Rome whose Spiritual Guide, Englished in 1688, taught the quiet way of prayer to eager readers. The book won praise across Europe and, for a time, papal approval in high places. Then Rome condemned its propositions, and Molinos died in prison.

Molinos tells the soul to lay aside effort, images, and even anxious self-examination, resting in God without grasping. Critics charged that such quiet kills moral effort and the church's sacraments alike. His fall shaped European mysticism by warning it where the line of suspicion lay. Its short chapters made it a handbook readers could carry and reread.
monluc-commentaries-cotton-1688:
Blaise de Monluc, a Gascon soldier, wrote his Commentaires in 1592 about the wars he fought under King Henri II of France. Charles Cotton's English translation, first made in 1674, appears here in the printing of 1688. Monluc rose from common soldier to marshal by wounds, daring, and a fierce will to be remembered.

His memoir is all camp and battlefield: sieges, charges, feuds, and the raw talk of men at war. King Henry IV is said to have called the book the soldier's breviary, the handbook every fighter should keep. Monluc spares no one, least of all himself, in telling how war really felt. The Commentaries remain a classic soldier's memoir of the 1500s.
morris-dream-john-ball-1888:
William Morris, the designer and poet, had become a committed socialist by the 1880s. He published A Dream of John Ball in 1888, pairing it with a shorter prose piece, A King's Lesson. The dream tale first ran in a socialist newspaper, Commonweal, which Morris helped run.

A modern socialist narrator dreams himself back to 1381, during the Peasants' Revolt led by Wat Tyler. He talks through the night with John Ball, the rebel priest who preached that things would never be well while some were masters and others servants. Morris uses the rising to ask what his own movement must learn. The book blends history, hope, and warning.
most-die-anarchie-1888:
Johann Joseph Most published Die Anarchie in 1888, as number ten of the Internationale Bibliothek. Most was the era's most notorious German-American anarchist editor. The pamphlet argues that the public misunderstands the word anarchy. Anarchy, he writes, does not mean confusion; it means the absence of rule, or freedom.

All rule, he argues, arose from the evil will of the strong to subjugate the weak. Property owners hold power in every age, against the propertyless. He lists three stages: ownership of men, of land, and of property generally. Such works were later barred from American mails, and their editors jailed or deported.
nutt-studies-holy-grail-1888:
Alfred Nutt published Studies on the Legend of the Holy Grail in 1888, and it helped found modern Grail scholarship. Nutt was a folklorist, and he asked a bold question about the famous cup. Was the Grail a Christian relic, or something older?

Nutt pointed to Celtic tales of cauldrons of plenty that feed every guest and never empty. Behind the holy cup, he argued, stood these pagan wonders from Welsh and Irish story. His Celtic-origin case set the terms of debate for decades. Scholars still argue with this book, which is a sign of how much it started.
olympiodorus-alchemist-art-sacre-berthel:
Olympiodorus of Thebes, a scholar of the sixth century, wrote a long commentary on Zosimos and on the sayings of the old alchemists. His work On the Sacred Art is given here in the French version of Berthelot and Ruelle, from their 1888 edition of the Greek alchemists. Olympiodorus read the art through Neoplatonic thought.

He treats the metals, the egg of the philosophers, and the work of turning base stuff toward gold as signs of a deeper order. His pages carried the alchemy of Alexandria into the Byzantine world. Without such bridges, the Greek art would not have reached the Arabs or the Latin West. The commentary is dense, learned, and strange.
openalex-w1582174288:
Jon Paul Rodríguez, Garry Peterson, and six co-authors wrote this paper. It appeared in Ecology and Society in the year 2006. Ecosystem services are benefits people gain from nature. Management choices can raise one service while cutting another. Such losses are called trade-offs in the paper.

Trade-offs vary by place, by timing, and by reversibility, they write. Some choices are explicit, others happen without awareness. Across global scenarios, provisioning services won most often. Cultural services were almost never counted in the models. Supporting services were often taken for granted, they found. Good policy must track long-term, slow changes too.
openalex-w1951965788:

Managing soil to boost one service can harm another, they note. The paper examines how soil cycles and biodiversity interact. It asks how management shifts services for good or ill. Farms, climate policy, and nature protection all depend on soils. The authors urge care for soils as living systems. Their framework links soil science to ecosystem policy.
openalex-w2059874988:

The team tested seven products on stored patient samples. Samples came from South America. Lab kits proved more sensitive than rapid strip tests. All tests were highly specific overall. Most tests missed one dengue type more often. They also worked less well in repeat infections. Tests performed best on days three to four of illness. The data help clinics choose tests for early care.
openalex-w2067376788:

The program is one of the most used tools in the field. It sorts samples into genetic groups. Researchers needed up-to-date guidance on its use.

STRUCTURE detects allele frequency differences within data. It assigns each individual to likely subgroups. The review covers the program's main applications. It explains key parameter settings in plain terms. It also surveys extra software that supports STRUCTURE runs. Good settings matter for trustworthy group assignments. The guide serves both genetics and forensic users.
openalex-w2090628788:
Simon Delgado, Bobbie Erickson, Roberto Agudo and colleagues identified a new virus from a fatal fever case in Bolivia. Their paper appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2008. A small cluster of haemorrhagic fever cases struck near Cochabamba. Samples survived from only one patient. That patient died after severe bleeding signs.

Lab teams grew the virus from patient serum. Tests showed it was an arenavirus. Full gene sequences of both segments were read. It was closest to the Sabia virus of Brazil. Differences were large enough to mark a new virus. They named it the Chapare virus. Bolivia thus faces two arenaviruses that cause severe fever.
openalex-w2102456788:

Maps help show where malaria can spread. Few past maps rested on full evidence. The team built theirs from predicted species ranges.

They combined distribution maps for each major vector. The result shows how complex the picture is regionally. In Africa, three species share dominance widely. In Asia and the Pacific, many species coexist. Dominance shifts from place to place there. A large occurrence database underlies the maps. The authors discuss where the method may mislead. Control programmes can plan around local vectors.
openalex-w2114260388:
Christophe Monnin, Valerie Chavagnac, Cedric Boulart and colleagues studied unusual underwater springs in Prony Bay, New Caledonia. Their paper appeared in Biogeosciences in 2014. The springs release highly alkaline water. Such systems have been known on land since the 1800s. A recent survey found many similar vents underwater.

A research cruise sampled water, gases and rock deposits. Divers collected samples at vents up to fifty metres deep. One spring sits exposed at low tide. The fluids differ sharply from normal seawater. Their chemistry reflects reactions with deep rock types. Microbes living there were also characterised. High-pH systems interest scientists studying early Earth conditions. They may resemble habitats on other worlds too.
openalex-w2125198788:
Amy Buck, Gillian Coakley, Fabio Simbari, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2014. They asked whether worm parasites can send small RNA messages into the cells of the animal they infect. In mammals, RNA is known to travel between cells inside tiny sacs called exosomes.

The team studied a gut worm that infects mice and is related to human hookworm. They showed the worm releases sacs packed with small RNAs and a worm Argonaute protein. Mouse cells took these sacs in. Giving the worm sacs to mice through the nose calmed type-two immune responses and reduced swelling signs triggered by an allergen.
openalex-w2135648488:
Cosme Damião Cruz published this software paper alone in Acta Scientiarum Agronomy in 2013. He presents GENES, a free program for data analysis in experimental statistics and quantitative genetics. Plant and animal breeders use such tools to estimate traits and judge whether a selection plan is likely to succeed.

GENES runs many biometric models for processing breeding data. It is available online in Portuguese, English, and Spanish, with guide literature and sample files. The program works with Word, Excel, and Paint for moving data and results in and out. It also links with the free tools R and Matlab through supplied scripts for extra analyses like genome-wide selection.
openalex-w2318568688:
Saskia Keesstra, Johan Bouma, Jakob Wallinga, and colleagues published this forum paper in SOIL in 2016. They argue soil science is essential to reaching the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Soils quietly underpin food security, clean water, climate action, biodiversity, and health, yet soil experts often sit outside those debates.

The authors map soil functions and their ecosystem services onto several goals. Their advice to colleagues is direct. Embrace the goals as a platform proving the field's relevance. Show how modern soil information improves joint studies across disciplines. Lead whole-system analyses, spread the word on soil organic matter, and train knowledge brokers. The paper is a call for soil scientists to claim their seat at the policy table.
openalex-w2395026888:
Dorothée Bakker, Benjamin Pfeil, Camilla Landa, and colleagues published this data paper in Earth System Science Data in 2016. It presents version 3 of the Surface Ocean CO2 Atlas, the global collection of surface-ocean carbon dioxide measurements. These records anchor estimates of how much human carbon the ocean absorbs.

The atlas now holds over fourteen million quality-controlled values from more than thirty-six hundred datasets, spanning 1957 to 2014. This version adds over four million values and four recent years over its predecessor. Quality checks run automatically at upload, accuracy is defined for every quality grade, and a flag now marks data from newer sensors and platforms. An upgraded viewer and automated uploads promise faster future releases for climate researchers.
openalex-w2575837388:
The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network reported this study in Nature in 2017. It gives an extensive molecular portrait of cervical cancer, a leading cause of cancer death worldwide. The team analyzed two hundred twenty-eight primary tumors with many kinds of genomic tests. Few studies of this cancer had ever been so large or so complete.

The analysis found strong patterns of APOBEC mutagenesis, a process that scars DNA in a distinctive way. It named several newly confirmed mutated genes, including ERBB3, CASP8, and TGFBR2. Some tumors amplified immune targets PD-L1 and PD-L2, which matter for modern immunotherapy. Human papillomavirus DNA was built into the tumor genome in most samples. That integration was linked to structural changes and higher activity of nearby genes. Together the results map new routes toward understanding and treating this cancer.
openalex-w2964004288:
Regina Medina-Sauza, Marycruz Álvarez-Jiménez, Alix Delhal, and colleagues wrote this systematic review in Frontiers in Environmental Science in 2019. It examines how earthworms shape the microbe communities of the soil. Earthworms work in tight soil spaces, yet their effects spread to the whole soil layer they inhabit.

Feeding is the main route of influence, since earthworms eat soil and the microbes in it. Digestion can cut microbe numbers, above all fungi. At the same time, worms can favor or stir up certain microbes that help them digest soil organic matter. The review pulls together this evidence on how worms, meal by meal, build up the living community of the soil.
openalex-w3086687188:
Carolina Sansaloni, Jorge Franco, Bruno Santos, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It analyzes genetic diversity across eighty thousand wheat accessions held in seed collections. Wheat supplies about a fifth of the protein and calories in human diets worldwide.

Since farming began over ten thousand years ago, breeding raised yields but thinned the gene pool of elite wheat. That narrowing now limits the creation of new varieties for a changing world. By scanning the vast collection, the team traced the footprints that past selection left in the genome. Some footprints mark losses to repair; others mark chances to recover useful traits. The study turns a seed vault census into a breeding roadmap.
openalex-w3210397188:
Rosario Javier-Astete, Jorge Jiménez-Dávalos, and Gastón Zolla test a fast way to measure wood chemistry in two Amazonian trees. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2021. Capirona and Bolaina grow quickly and are in rising demand for timber. Breeders need the amounts of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin in young trees, but standard lab tests are slow.

The team scanned stem samples with infrared light, a method called FTIR, and built prediction models from the spectra. Wood makeup differed between the top and base of each stem, which helped the models learn. Lignin was predicted well in both species, and cellulose very well in Bolaina. The method could speed up breeding of better timber trees.
openalex-w4368363688:
Ahmed Osman, Eman Abd El-Monaem, Ahmed Elgarahy, and colleagues review how to prepare sorbents for cleaning water, in Environmental Chemistry Letters in 2023. Adsorption, trapping pollutants on a solid's surface, is a cheap and effective treatment. Classic adsorbents come from fossil fuels and can cause fresh pollution themselves. Sorbents made from living waste promise a cleaner alternative that also fits the circular economy.

The review covers biological sorbents, magnetic sorbents, and other low-cost options. Raw materials range from wood and farm waste to algae, bacteria, and animal waste. The authors explain preparation methods, the pollutants each type removes, and how the trapping works. They also cover how spent sorbents can be renewed, a key step for real-world use.
openalex-w4383105288:
A global team of seabird researchers maps where oceanic birds meet plastic pollution at sea, in Nature Communications in 2023. Plastic spreads unevenly across the oceans, and so do the birds at risk of eating it. Petrels, a wide-ranging seabird group, often swallow plastic and are already highly threatened. The team combined plastic density estimates with tracking data for more than seven thousand birds of seventy-seven petrel species.

High exposure areas emerged in the Mediterranean and Black seas and in parts of the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian oceans. Threatened species faced disproportionately high risk. Risk peaked mostly on the high seas and in the waters of the United States, Japan, and the United Kingdom. The authors call for international cooperation, since birds breed in one country and feed in many.
openalex-w4407468688:
Oliver Cornely, Rosanne Sprute, Matteo Bassetti, and colleagues present a global guideline for candidiasis. It appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2025. Candida fungi are the leading cause of fungal disease in hospital patients. They sicken and kill people worldwide.

Three international societies joined forces to write the guidance. The European Confederation of Medical Mycology led it, working with two partner societies. It covers how to diagnose this infection and how to treat it. It aims to give doctors everywhere one shared, evidence-based standard. Steady use of one standard should improve outcomes for a common and dangerous set of diseases.
openalex-w7129093688:
Naoya Murakami, a radiation oncologist at Juntendo University in Tokyo, wrote a 2026 review on treating lung cancer that is locally advanced and cannot be removed by surgery. This form of non-small cell lung cancer makes up a large share of cases and is hard to treat well.

Murakami traces three decades of change, from radiation alone to radiation combined with chemotherapy, and then to immune therapy or targeted drugs given afterward. A trial drug called durvalumab became standard care after combined treatment, and another drug helped patients whose tumors carry a specific gene change. He also warns that lung inflammation from radiation can be fatal, so dose limits and risk checks matter greatly.
openalex-w7137857988:
Leticia Pereira led a 2026 study in the Journal of Antibiotics proposing a new way to hunt for antibacterial drugs using Euglena gracilis, a single-celled organism with a plant-like chloroplast. Because that chloroplast keeps some bacterial features, antibiotics can bleach it white while the cell itself stays alive by eating organic carbon.

One test can therefore flag three things at once: antibacterial action, lack of poisoning to the cell, and whether a compound crosses several membranes. The team tuned the test and set simple light readings to sort results automatically. They tried it on a commercial compound library and on rare natural compounds from myxobacteria and fungi. The screen is cheap and broad, though some antibiotic classes will slip past it.
openalex-w7162264588:
Yu Takiguchi and Koji Nemoto published a 2026 mathematical study of two conflicting rumors spreading through the same population, such as fake news and its correction. Their model borrows from epidemic theory: people can catch and spread either rumor, lose interest, and become susceptible again. Unusually, each person's opinion feeds back on how easily each rumor infects them.

Working out every steady state and its stability, the authors find a surprising coexistence mechanism. Belief in one rumor can paradoxically help the opposing rumor spread, and a rumor with a lower infection rate can sometimes spread further. A majority advantage also emerges on its own, and a rumor dies out unless its starting share passes a critical threshold, which the authors derive.
openalex-w7204485688:
Ana Alice Gomes Damasceno and Débora Silva Santos released a Portuguese-language study in Brazil in 2026 on maker methodology in biology and chemistry teaching. Maker culture, learning by building, promises an exit from fragmented, lecture-only science classes. The research reads research papers on classroom applications of the approach, looking for convergences, successful experiences, and gaps in prior studies.

Maker work develops self-rule, creativity, critical thinking, and collaboration, the authors find. In biology, didactic model building, investigative experiments, and interdisciplinary projects stood out. In chemistry, experimentation in maker spaces, problem solving, and prototype creation led. The culture has great potential to improve science teaching, they conclude, though real adoption depends on infrastructure, teacher training, and deeper work.
openalex-w7204635388:
Marivalda Brandão Ramos de Sousa led a Portuguese-language qualitative study, published in Brazil in 2026, on the difficulties teachers face working with autistic students in the municipal schools of Dom Inocêncio, Piauí. Autism diagnoses have risen sharply, and schools must be ready to include these students fully. Five early-years teachers answered a form sent through WhatsApp, and the team analyzed responses by categorical content analysis.

The teachers reported great difficulty working with autistic children and made clear they do not feel pedagogically prepared. Inclusion, on their account, does not happen in practice. The authors point to an urgent need for continuing training across the municipal network, so that legal inclusion becomes classroom reality for autistic students.
openalex-w7204947088: Ana Júlia Ribeiro Almeida and eleven co-authors in Brazil released a Portuguese-language review in 2026 on the psychosocial impact of acne vulgaris on adolescents and young adults. Acne is one of the most visible skin problems of youth. Appearing on the face at exactly the age when appearance weighs most heavily on self-image and social life. The review gathers the work on what that burden does to teenagers and young adults psychologically and socially. A dimension of the disease that purely medical treatment can overlook.

These devices are used for primary prevention in selected patients, but their benefit, mainly on overall mortality, remains controversial. Using standard review guidelines, the team searched two sources in April 2026 for 2021 to early 2026 randomized and cohort studies, with two independent reviewers selecting and appraising the work.

Results were mixed, the authors report. Evidence generally favored the device for preventing sudden cardiac death and fatal arrhythmic events. Findings on death from all causes were not uniform, with some studies showing benefit and others no major reduction. Benefit magnitude seemed to vary with patient traits, making selection decisive.
openalex-w7205006988:

The film also reproduces subaltern positions, he argues, by tying its characters to clandestinity and illegality. Leaves underexplored themes such as married men living double lives and chemical sex among men who have sex with men. Despite its merits in exposing part of queer São Paulo, the review concludes, the film reinforces stereotypes that deserved more questioning.
openalex-w7211991188:

Graduates of distance programs also performed far worse on the national exam than classroom-trained peers. In the first admission cycle under the new norm, demand for distance courses fell sharply at the big listed education groups while blended formats grew. The rules, Silva concludes, make physical campuses a competitive asset again, though towns served only at a distance risk losing access.
openalex-w7211997288:

These centers are the community backbone of Brazilian mental health care. The researchers interviewed thirty users with depression and mapped the themes in their answers with text analysis software. Three themes organize the findings: improvement tied to symptoms easing, help as emotional support alongside medicine, and everyday coping strategies.

Medication matters to users, above all because it reduces symptoms, and they say so clearly. But they also value what pills cannot do: being welcomed, being heard, psychotherapy, and the routines of daily life. Drug treatment alone, users report, does not meet their needs, yet the care model stays centered on medication. The authors call for strengthening the non-drug practices users themselves praise.
openalex-w7213870788:
