Single cases like this stretch what is known about a disease. They also hint that some variants may leave enough copper transport working to change the outlook.
pmc-13236988:
Gaber and colleagues tailor a family of borate glasses for two jobs at once: bending light and blocking gamma rays. The glasses mix borate with a ceramic compound known as BCZT, made by the standard melt and quench route. Tests confirmed every sample stayed glassy, with no crystals, while density rose as the mix changed.

The team measured how the glasses handle light, including nonlinear effects prized in photonics, and how well they shield radiation. A cheap, lead-free glass that blocks gamma rays could serve in medical and nuclear settings. Showing that one recipe can be tuned for both optics and shielding widens where such glasses might be used.
pmc-13240188:
Huang and colleagues build a screening platform that makes prime editing, a precise DNA rewriting tool, fast enough to test many gene variants. Prime editing can fix single letters of DNA, but it edits too weakly for large screens that ask what thousands of variants do. Their platform, EvoPRIME, sharpens the process and enriches for cells that took the edit.

A processing protein trims the guide RNAs, and a glow-based sort keeps the successfully edited cells. The team reports efficiency matching the best current systems, without needing to disable the cell's repair guards. Sharp screens like this can finally sort harmful variants from harmless ones at scale.
pmc-13240988:
Berding's team in Georgia dissected the language of surgeons' posts sharing research on the platform formerly called Twitter. Eighty-four posts came from 17 of the most-followed surgeon accounts. Software scored each post for analytic style, clout, tone, and authenticity. Readership and citation counts supplied the impact measures.

The posts skewed highly analytic but low in warmth and authenticity. Formal, analytic wording tracked with fewer readers and citations, not more. Confident clout helped readership, and a negative tone surprisingly raised impact. Whether the linked article was open access made no significant difference.
pmc-13241488:
Sharkawy's team at Cairo built hybrid-mode cruise control for electric cars. Their smart controller switches among cruising, spacing, and braking modes. One software platform tunes settings and gains online in real time. A real electric vehicle on a test rig faced a lidar-spotted virtual leader.

The car held speed and gap through harsh test runs. Cruising tracked at 98 percent accuracy, spacing control close behind. Braking lagged at 55 percent, limited to coasting-only slowing. Sharkawy offers the unified scheme as relief from driveline math headaches. All three modes ran in one scheme.
pmc-13242588:
Yao Zhang and co-authors mapped how colorectal tumors build an immune-suppressing neighborhood, using single-cell data and large public datasets. Their study appeared in Cancer Informatics in 2026. They profiled nine tumor samples cell by cell, charted which cells signal to which, and layered in bulk gene data from public databases. Machine learning then distilled the patterns into a prognostic risk score built from seventeen genes.

Macrophages and fibroblasts emerged as the loudest communicators, speaking through chemokine channels. A network analysis pointed to the MAPK signaling pathway as the core module behind the suppressive state. The seventeen-gene score predicted patient survival on its own and split tumors into immune types. High-risk tumors looked stroma-rich and immunologically cold, yet possibly more sensitive to certain chemotherapy and targeted drugs. The authors offer the score as a step toward matching treatment to tumor ecology.
pmc-13245788:
Heirani Moghaddam, Cressman, and Manson tested how people adapt their reaching when vision is distorted, in this 2026 PLOS One experiment. Forty-two right-handed volunteers reached for targets with a robotic exoskeleton while a cursor showed their hand position. For half, the cursor was rotated slightly; for the others, it was mirror-flipped across the body's midline.

Everyone learned to reach under the rotation, and test trials without the cursor showed they had learned unconsciously, without trying. Under the mirror flip, only about half learned at all, and none showed that unconscious learning. The contrast suggests mirror reversals force a different, more deliberate strategy than rotations, a point that matters for rehabilitation and training design.
pmc-13246488:
Yilmaz and co-authors review a new direction for farm sensing in this 2026 Global Challenges article. Smart farming already uses buried probes to track soil moisture, temperature, acidity, and nutrients, but rigid probes cover little ground and can be fragile. The authors ask whether geotextiles, the fabric sheets already spread over fields, could carry flexible sensors across whole plots.

The review compares soil sensors by materials, fabrication, testing, power supply, and wireless links, then merges the lessons into one design framework. Their conclusion is that fabric-based, large-area sensing is plausible and could adapt as conditions change. Such platforms, they argue, would give precision agriculture denser, cheaper soil data for healthier soil management.
pmc-13247588:
van der Coelen, Sas, and Richter-Unruh followed hormone patterns in girls with Turner syndrome to foresee ovarian failure, in this 2026 Journal of the Endocrine Society study. Turner syndrome, a missing or altered X chromosome, often shuts the ovaries down early, and predicting which girls keep ovarian function matters for fertility counseling. The team reviewed records of three hundred sixty-five girls, tracking puberty milestones and repeated hormone measurements.

Girls who entered puberty spontaneously had shown lower FSH and higher AMH, the hormone marking egg reserve, already before age eight. In a joint statistical model, lower AMH significantly predicted earlier ovarian insufficiency, while FSH did not. Individual predictions stayed very uncertain, however. The authors say AMH informs counseling but a dependable personal prediction model needs more data.
pmc-13247788:
Ho, Chan, Lo, and co-authors asked whether diabetes medicines protect against depression, in this 2026 Psychological Medicine cohort study. People with type 2 diabetes develop depression at high rates, worsening their outcomes. The team used Hong Kong's territory-wide public health records. They followed more than six hundred eighty-six thousand people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2002 and 2021. Depression diagnoses were compared between patients exposed to each glucose-lowering drug and those not exposed.

Exposure to any antidiabetes agent was linked to substantially lower risk of a first depression diagnosis. Several individual drugs, starting with metformin, showed the same direction. Sensitivity analyses, including longer exposure windows and single-drug use, supported the pattern. The authors are careful: records cannot prove the drugs prevent depression, and mechanisms need dedicated research.
pmc-13248488:
Chen and Feng studied whether China's bulk drug-buying policy changed how drug firms innovate, reported in 2026. The policy trades lower prices for guaranteed sales volume, and critics feared squeezed profits would cut research. The authors tracked one hundred sixty listed Chinese pharmaceutical firms from 2015 through 2023 using a staggered comparison method.

Firms covered by the policy raised research spending intensity by about a fifth relative to its average, and gained more patents each year. Gains grew over the first four years and were strongest in large, private, and chemical drug firms. The authors read this as firms shifting money from marketing toward real research.
pmc-13249188: Boucher, Shamma, and Boubenec issued this correction in PLOS Biology in 2026. It concerns their paper on blood flow responses in the premotor cortex, the brain area that helps plan movement, during decision making. Some supporting figures were wrong: in one, the spots labeled T and R were swapped, and panels showing how brain positions were matched across images needed fixing. The notice supplies the corrected figures. The paper's main claim, that these responses track what the animal perceives more than how it moves, stands unchanged.
pmc-13250388: Awan writes a 2026 letter in Clinical Case Reports about watching children whose duodenum is blocked after seatbelt injuries. The blockage can come from a blood collection behind the abdominal lining, and careful non-surgical care may suit stable children. Awan argues that monitoring should not rest on stomach tube output alone. Teams should set escalation triggers in advance, combining tube output, the child's overall condition, inflammation markers, nutrition, and selective imaging, so worsening cases move to stronger treatment without delay.
pmc-13253788:
Prabesh Ojha and colleagues run computer tests on tiny silver wires in a 2026 study. They modeled two fivefold twinned nanowires crossed at 90 degrees and sintered, or heat-fused, at three temperatures and three heating rates. After cooling, the wires were pulled in virtual tensile tests at varied strain rates.

Wires fused at lower heat with faster heating kept higher yield strength, since limited atom movement preserved twin boundaries. Faster pulling also raised strength. Single-crystal wires, by contrast, showed about 18% lower yield strength but far greater stretch before breaking, with fracture strain 4.5 times that of the twinned wires.
pmc-13253888:
Eirini Sampson and Zen Makuch draw lessons from Denmark's heating system in a 2026 paper. District heating, where one network warms many buildings, covers two-thirds of Danish home heat demand. Over 90 percent of those networks are owned by towns or cooperatives, a setup the authors review for lessons.

They name three supports: a Heat Supply Act that gives towns planning power, steady finance for non-profit systems, and ownership models that let residents take part. Heating and cooling use over 60 percent of European Union energy, so the authors argue such public, shared governance can help other cities cut carbon fairly.
pmc-13253988:
Nikta Bazleh reviews substance use among school students in Iran in a 2026 systematic review. Databases in English and Persian were searched from 2003 onward. The review combined 35 cross-sectional studies covering about 45,000 students, comparing rates by province, gender, and substance type.

Lifetime use of any substance ranged widely, from 1.4 to 55.9 percent, with a median near 20 percent. Hookah use reached up to 59 percent, and rates were higher in boys than girls. Southeastern provinces near the Afghanistan border showed high rates. The author calls for prevention plans fitted to local culture and region.
pmc-13255388:
Alaa A Abdalla and colleagues link heavy internet use and self-injury in teens in a 2026 case-control study. The team recruited 110 teens from a university clinic in Egypt: 55 with major depression and 55 healthy peers. All filled in standard scales for mood, internet use, self-harm, and acting on impulse, and the team mapped links among them.

Teens with depression scored higher on self-injury, internet use, and rash action. Heavy internet use tied to self-injury through both low mood and rash action. The path from rash action to low mood was slightly stronger than the reverse. The authors call for joint screening and prevention aimed at rash action.
pmc-13256488:
Clara Cher Yi Tan leads a 2026 pilot study of the Sleep Memories app, a phone tool that tests how sleep helps memory in older adults. The app uses a 32-item word-pairs task done in the evening and again the next morning. Participants were patients aged fifty and over at a specialist brain health and memory clinic in Sydney, Australia, many with concerns about their thinking.

The clinic invited 141 people over eight months, and 76 agreed to take part. Sixty-eight finished at least one test, and 57 percent finished both the evening and morning recall tests. Willingness to join was lower in people with lower thinking scores and poorer sleep. Users mostly liked the app, though some reported minor technical problems.
pmc-13260688:
Hermann Yokolo and co-authors present a 2026 narrative review of the cholera epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Cholera is a waterborne diarrheal disease, and the Congo is among the worst-affected countries, with endemic foci in its eastern lake provinces since the 1970s. The review searched three databases for work from 2015 to 2025, plus grey literature from health agencies. It examines structural causes, public health responses, and persistent barriers.

As of August 2025, 46,800 cases and 1,362 deaths were recorded, despite a national elimination plan involving more than twenty-two ministries. Transmission is driven by unsafe drinking water, poor sanitation, conflict, displacement, and inequality. Death rates reached 11.1 percent in some provinces. Vaccination and water, sanitation, and hygiene campaigns help but fail in isolation, the authors say, calling for integrated long-term investment and community trust.
pmc-13260788:
Sadia Imran and co-authors present a 2026 look-back study of diet during treatment for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia at a specialist hospital in Pakistan. This leukemia is the most common childhood cancer, and survival lags in lower-income countries, partly because many children are underfed. Records for 332 patients treated between May 2022 and April 2023 were reviewed. Nutrition status was checked with World Health Organization growth measures for younger children and body mass index for older ones.

More than a third of patients, 38.5 percent, were malnourished, most of them underweight, some severely so. Weight changed a lot between the first check and the end of the intensive treatment phase. Being underfed was clearly linked to positive bacterial cultures and to repeated hospital stays. It was not linked to death in this sample. The authors call for longer forward-looking studies of diet and survival.
pmc-13260888:
Vatsal Siotia and co-authors present a 2026 engineering study of a stall detection and parachute recovery system for unmanned aerial vehicles, or drones. A stall can send a drone into an unrecoverable fall. Their system uses a flight controller that reads gyroscope and accelerometer data plus angular speed, vertical acceleration, and motor saturation to confirm a genuine stall. This multi-parameter, altitude-aware design differs from single-threshold pitch or roll triggers used in conventional systems.

Emergency response triggers within 1.1 seconds of stall confirmation. In simulations and hardware-in-the-loop tests, parachute deployment at twenty-five metres cut impact speed from 22.2 to 3.2 metres per second, with a ninety-five percent survival rate. Deployment at ten metres was largely ineffective, at about forty percent survival, highlighting the need for low-altitude protection below fifteen metres. The system also transmits GPS coordinates after landing to speed retrieval.
pmc-13261088:
Yutaro Okumura and co-authors report a 2026 study of CISP, a cold-induced barley protein that acts as a small RNA chaperone. Cold limits plant growth, and barley tolerates it well. CISP is switched on in barley roots at low temperature, but its role was uncharacterized. Part of the protein is intrinsically disordered, meaning it lacks a fixed shape.

Expressing CISP in E. coli bacteria improved their late growth at low temperature compared with the normal strain. Overexpressing it in Arabidopsis, a plant lacking a matching gene, also improved seedling growth in the cold. In RNA beacon tests, CISP reduced the formation of folded RNA structures and helped unfold them. That is chaperone-like activity. CISP lacks the usual RNA-binding domains, so the authors suggest it is a previously unrecognized type of RNA chaperone that may aid barley cold tolerance.
pmc-13262888:
Zhe Wang and co-authors propose a decision and control method for required lane changes by self-driving cars in a 2026 journal article. A mandatory lane change is forced by a lane ending, an obstacle, or a needed turn. Their framework uses game theory, which models how each driver reacts to others, with payoff scores for the self-driving car and vehicles behind it in the target lane.

The plan updates as nearby traffic responds, and a sliding mode controller, a robust steering method, tracks the planned path. Tracking error combines sideways drift and heading angle, held within preset limits. The team built a joint simulation platform with human drivers in the loop. Tests with three drivers of different styles gave early evidence on how the method behaves.
pmc-13263188:
Jie Yang and co-authors use computer modeling to test a pelvic fixation plate across fracture patterns in a 2026 journal article. Sacral fractures, breaks in the triangular bone at the spine's base, can leave the pelvis unstable. A plate across the back of the pelvis is a common fix, but its strength may depend on where the break sits, graded by the Denis zones.

Their 3D model simulated one-sided unstable fractures in all three Denis zones under seven loading postures. They compared the plate against a stronger two-sided construct as a reference. The gap between methods was largest for zone I fractures and shrank across zones II and III. Small movements at the break fell as the fracture line neared the midline, suggesting a better fit there.
pmc-13263488:
Zaid Elsabbagh and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on whether a past calf strain raises the risk of Achilles tendon rupture in NBA basketball players. The Achilles tendon links the calf to the heel, and a rupture is a career-threatening injury. The team compared 60 players with ruptures against 258 with calf strains only, using public records back to 1958.

A previous calf strain came with about two and a half times the odds of later rupture, and most paired injuries hit the same leg, on average about two years apart. Three quarters of injured players returned, but efficiency, wins, and playing time all fell sharply afterward. Video showed a consistent false-step mechanism in nearly all cases with footage.
pmc-13264588:
Isabela Maria Agustini da Silveira Bastos led a 2026 review of fungi in mangrove forests worldwide. Mangroves are coastal trees whose fungi break down litter, cycle nutrients, and store carbon. The team combined a review of DNA-based survey studies with a fresh joint analysis of raw sequence data.

The review covered 23 studies and 1,154 samples. A shared core set of fungi appeared in mangroves around the world, led by the Ascomycota group, with a second group close behind. Bare mud held the richest mix, while living plant parts held a narrower set with many possible plant pathogens. Soil near roots held wood-eating fungi. The authors note DNA surveys reveal far more fungi than old culture methods, but can miss some groups.
pmc-13264988:
Myriam Calle Rubio and co-authors present a 2026 Spanish study of therapeutic inertia in severe COPD, the failure to step up treatment when goals are unmet. Using records from nearly 5,000 patients with severe disease, they also compared doctors' sense of control against test-based control.

Disease was uncontrolled in 72.5 percent of patients, yet in 43.7 percent of those cases no treatment change was made. Inertia linked to traits like former smoking, fewer past flare-ups, and patient satisfaction with treatment. Doctors judged disease controlled in over two thirds of uncontrolled cases, a sharp perception gap, while the mismatch was small in truly controlled cases. Treatment satisfaction and lack of recent flare-ups most swayed doctors' views. The authors urge standard, structured follow-up for severe COPD.
pmc-13267488:
Yossarian Liebsch and a large team report a 2026 study of holes punched in atom-thin sheets by ion beams. The sheets are made of molybdenum disulfide, a layered material one molecule thick. Ion beams can shape such sheets for future devices, but how the surface beneath the sheet affects the damage is poorly known.

Using a scanning electron microscope, the team measured pore size and counts for sheets hanging free, doubled, or resting on two supports. Pores were largest and most common on silica supports. A gold support almost completely blocked pore formation. Both slow heavy ions and fast heavy ions showed the same pattern. The authors conclude that energy loss at the surface and support decides the damage.
pmc-13268488:
Inês Carvalho and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter on deventilation syndrome in COPD. Many patients with severe COPD sleep with a breathing machine that eases carbon dioxide buildup. Some wake with intense breathlessness the moment the mask comes off. This deventilation syndrome can bring racing shallow breathing, panic, and a need to sit upright, lasting for hours.

Studies cited in the letter found the syndrome in about a third to over half of ventilated COPD patients. Proposed causes include overinflated lungs after a night of machine pressure. The letter reports a 68-year-old man whose severe morning breathlessness lasted 60 to 90 minutes daily, with no other cause found. Simple steps helped frame his care, such as starting inhaler therapy right on waking and rising gradually while still on the machine. The authors urge clinicians to ask about mornings.
pmc-13269888:
Laila Nassef and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a lightweight security system for industrial internet devices, which face growing cyber attacks. Their design mixes a graph attention network, which weighs links between devices, with a memory network that reads traffic in both directions. Training is shared across devices without moving private data.

A wolf-inspired optimizer tuned the system faster than older methods. In a ten-node simulation, shared training cut communication load by 20 percent. Detection accuracy reached up to 95 percent across attack types, including denial-of-service floods and zero-day exploits. Best scores on three standard datasets reached 0.94 on a balanced accuracy measure. An explanation module shows why alerts fire.
pmc-13270888:
Ricarda S. Schulz led a 2026 cohort study on whether cognitive decline, a drop in thinking and memory performance, raises stroke risk in older women. Past work linked poor thinking scores to stroke, but change over time had rarely been studied as a moving process.

The analysis used 5,093 United States women health workers, average age 66, from the Women's Health Study, followed for an average of 11.6 years. In that time, 302 strokes occurred. Women were grouped by their four-year change in thinking scores, from most improved to most declined. Stroke risk did not rise in a clear pattern across those groups, with the greatest-decline group close to the most-improved group.
pmc-13272688:
Matthias Fink leads a 2026 study testing whether radiologists can re-identify patients from memory of chest X-rays alone. That risk matters when image sets are shared for research. The study was set up to favor memory, as a worst-case stress test across 38 centers.

Thirty-three readers first read ten chest films, then, at least 24 hours later, saw six repeats and six new films. They said they remembered 35.1 percent, but half of the repeats were caught and 20.2 percent of new films were wrongly claimed. Only 1.3 percent of all films yielded a correct name code or case position, so memory alone rarely identified anyone.
pmc-13273988:
Daniel Pfeifer, Markus Graf, and Clas Rurik introduce a 2026 journal article describing Genestrip, a computer tool for sorting DNA reads. Such tools match short DNA fragments, called reads, against reference genomes to name the organism they came from. Older tools need huge amounts of computer memory to do this.

Genestrip instead builds small databases for chosen groups of organisms, from a dozen to a few thousand species. The authors report results on par with a leading tool while using only a fraction of the memory. Example databases were built on a normal personal computer within hours. Uses they name include tick surveillance, medical testing, and farming.
pmc-13274588:
Hao Jia and a large team report a 2026 journal article mapping how gene activity in the human heart changes across the whole life span. They built an atlas from single-nucleus RNA sequencing of nonfailing heart tissue. The data cover 442,239 cell nuclei from fifty-four samples donated by twenty-nine people, from development through old age.

Across all major cell types, aging brought a progressive loss of orderly gene control plus rising stress and inflammation signals. Heart muscle cells showed distinct aged states rich in senescence markers. One regulator, PRDM16, faded with age; disturbing it aged lab-grown heart cells, while restoring balance in old mouse hearts improved function. Their age-prediction models tracked real age and flagged faster aging in diseased hearts.
pmc-13274888:
Mohsen Keramati, Mahdi Rostami Haji Abadi, and Saija Kontulainen present a 2026 feasibility trial of pole walking in retirement homes in Saskatoon, Canada. Pole walking, brisk walking with ski-like poles, can build balance and strength in older adults. The single-arm trial ran supervised group sessions three times a week for twelve weeks across four homes in summer 2022.

Of twenty-four residents assessed, nineteen consented and fifteen finished, with a mean age of 85.2 years and ninety-three percent women. Attendance averaged ninety percent, and participants and instructors alike rated the program above four out of five for acceptability and feasibility. No serious harms were recorded. Balance, leg strength, and self-rated physical function all improved over the twelve weeks.
pmc-13275188:
Kazuyoshi Okumura and a large team present a 2026 case report of emergency drainage for a newborn whose malformed lung cysts were crushing her normal lung. The baby girl's congenital lung lesion had already been shunted before birth, a tube to vent fluid. After delivery the cysts ballooned fast, shifting her chest organs and causing severe breathing failure.

Immediate full resection looked unsafe, so surgeons opened the chest and, watching directly, removed the old shunts and fixed drainage catheters securely into the cyst walls. Continuous drainage deflated the cysts, let the normal lung expand, and steadied her breathing. Once imaging clarified the lesion's extent, a delayed removal of the lower lobe was done safely, with a favorable recovery.
pmc-13275988:
Sehrish Khan and co-authors present a 2026 randomized trial on placing breathing tubes in heart surgery patients. Patients having coronary artery bypass surgery, which reroutes blood around blocked heart arteries, often have weak hearts. The tube placement itself can spike pulse and blood pressure, adding strain.

Eighty-six patients were assigned by chance to a standard curved blade tool or a video laryngoscope with a camera. Staff tracked pulse and blood pressure from before the procedure to ten minutes after. Both tools caused similar swings, with no clear difference between groups over time. The video tool gave a better view of the vocal cords and succeeded on the first try more often, though that gap was not clear-cut. No major complications occurred in either group.
pmc-13276588:
Yufei Qin and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a smart dye that reads tissue thickness, in the physical sense, to find and treat disease. Diseased tissue often turns more viscous, or syrupy, at the microscopic scale. Their molecule twists in a way that splits absorbed light energy between glowing and heating, governed by that local viscosity.

In thin surroundings the dye stays dark; in thick, diseased surroundings it glows faintly in the deep near-infrared band while still heating strongly. A large library of variants tuned the color and balance. One version imaged fatty liver disease and drug-induced liver injury in living animals. Packed into tiny carriers, it heated tumors under a deep-penetrating laser and killed them, even beneath tissue cover, with good safety in tests. The authors call the design dim-but-hot, favoring therapy with just enough glow to guide it.
pmc-13277188:
Sisi Deng leads a 2026 study testing whether a blood test can diagnose endometriosis without surgery. Endometriosis is a painful condition where tissue like the womb lining grows elsewhere. The team used a magnetic scanning method to profile small chemicals and fat particles in blood from patients, symptomatic controls, and healthy volunteers.

Against women with similar symptoms, the blood panel added nothing beyond age and body mass. Against healthy volunteers it looked very accurate at first, but that result failed in a later group. Clearer biological signals also came mostly from the healthy comparison. A reliable blood test for real clinic use remains out of reach, the study suggests.
pmc-13277388:
Ayalew Temesgen Wodajo leads a 2026 laboratory study of leaf extracts from Verbascum sinaiticum, a plant used in Ethiopian traditional medicine for wounds and other ills. The team screened extracts made with two solvents for plant chemicals and tested them against bacteria and in antioxidant assays, tests of power to block damaging oxygen reactions.

Both extracts held phenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, tannins, and other active plant compounds. The methanol extract showed stronger antioxidant action, closer to vitamin C in one test, than the chloroform extract. Extracts also slowed bacterial growth in dish tests, including Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. Dish results are early evidence only, and the authors frame them as support for the plant's traditional use.
pmc-13278388:
Lindsay Reese and colleagues wrote a 2026 editorial arguing that tobacco control should empower people who smoke rather than only press for abstinence. Global rules have cut smoking in some groups, but remaining smokers often face poverty, stress, stigma, and poor access to care. Abstinence-only rules and bans can widen those gaps, the authors argue.

Non-burning nicotine products cut exposure to smoke toxins, yet are often dismissed or prohibited despite growing evidence of value for people unlikely to quit outright. The authors propose a framework called EMPOWER, built on evidence, practicality, risk-based rules, and person-centered communication. Policy should prize autonomy and equity over moral judgment, they conclude.
pmc-13279488:
Daria Goriachun and colleagues report a 2026 study of how social contact shapes abstract word sense. Abstract words name ideas you cannot touch, like freedom or justice. Social talk is thought to ground such words, yet hard proof was scarce. Sixty French speakers sorted words by how social or how concrete they felt. Some worked alone and some worked in pairs.

Pairs beat solo workers when they judged the social side of abstract social words. Pairs did worse on the concrete side for the same words, as if talk made them feel more concrete. Gaze based checks split pairs by teamwork level. Gains came mostly from the more cooperative pairs, who looked and worked as one. Word sense shifts with company, not just with the mind alone.
pmc-13279688:
Martina Meciakova and colleagues report a 2026 study of an estrogen receptor gene and prostate cancer in Slovak men. Prostate cancer is the most diagnosed cancer in Slovak men and the third cause of their cancer death. The receptor, GPER1, passes fast estrogen signals and may serve as a drug target. Little was known on how gene variants in GPER1 shape cancer risk or traits.

Blood DNA came from seven hundred one patients and six hundred fifty nine healthy men. Three gene variants were typed by a targeted lab test. Gene use was also read in cancer tissue versus benign prostate tissue. One variant, rs3808350, went with higher cancer risk. The link ran strongest in patients with high Gleason scores, a grade of cancer vigour, and with spread to nodes or far sites. Other variants showed no clear link in the excerpt.
pmc-13280588:
Siren Eriksen and team give a 2026 qualitative study of staff priorities for a good death across care settings in Norway. End of life care runs in hospitals, nursing homes and municipal home care, with varied resources. Twenty two healthcare personnel from across Norway took part in virtual focus group interviews. They came from three distinct settings and diverse professional backgrounds. Interviews were audio recorded and transcribed verbatim. Qualitative content analysis was informed by theory on professional competence.

A good death was a shared focus for all participants. Across settings, priorities and concerns aligned. Staff likened their role to a pilot boat skipper, who guides the end of life process. Three focuses structured that guidance: offering support and information, providing symptom relief, and ensuring a presence at the bedside. Each theme marks a key priority in end of life work, in any setting.
pmc-13280688:
Yujie Song and colleagues published a 2026 brain scan study on post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD. PTSD can follow a frightening event and brings lasting fear and stress. The team scanned survivors of an earthquake. Sixty-one had PTSD and sixty-two did not, though all had lived through the quake. They measured how well brain wiring and brain activity matched in each area.

The PTSD group showed a changed match in many brain networks, for sight, movement, and deep thought. Some changes tracked with how bad symptoms were. Gene maps linked the changed areas to synapses, the links between brain cells, and to chemical signals in the brain. The authors say the work ties large brain changes to small cell-level clues.
pmc-13280788:
Frederic Meyer and colleagues reviewed trials of natural products for gum health in a 2026 study. Toothpastes and gels with plant extracts are sold as gentler options. The team searched for strict trials that tested such products against normal ones. Ten trials passed their checks, out of more than two hundred found. Products used aloe vera, a Chinese plant mix, or a mineral much like tooth itself.

Pooled results showed gums got healthier with the natural products than with the controls. Aloe vera and the tooth-like mineral helped in trial after trial. The authors say these products matched or beat standard pastes for gum health. They present them as sound options or add-ons for daily care. More and longer trials would firm up the proof, they note.
pmc-13281288:
Tobias Riet and colleagues reported a flaw in a cell therapy for blood cancers in a 2026 research letter. The therapy trains a patient's own immune cells to hunt cancer. One target, called CD86, also sits on the trained cells themselves. In lab and animal tests, the trained cells killed each other. This self-killing, the authors show, cut their survival and their power to kill tumors.

The team proposes a two-key design to dodge the trap. The cell fires fully only when it meets a second target found on cancer cells. The first target then acts as a helper switch, not the trigger. Tests of the paired design back the plan. The authors say such logic gates could make cell therapy safer for hard blood cancers, where good targets are scarce.
pmc-13281888:
Jian Huang and colleagues tested paired care for advanced liver cancer in a 2026 study. The cancers could not be cut out and had grown into the liver's main vein. Patients got a targeted pill, alone or with pinpoint radiation. The study read records of one hundred thirty-three patients treated from 2021 to 2023. To level the groups, patients were matched on their starting traits. Survival and time before growth were the main measures.

The paired group lived a median of close to twenty-five months, against about sixteen for pills alone. Time before growth ran thirteen months against about nine. Tumor shrinkage was far more common with the pairing. Gains held after matching. They were limited to patients with milder vein spread, vanishing in the worst spread class. More paired patients later reached surgery, which itself guarded survival. Harms were alike and manageable in both arms.
pmc-13282088:
Jongseo Kim wrote a 2026 study using artificial intelligence, computer software that spots patterns in images, to measure whether a skin treatment shrank large facial pores. Large pores are a common cosmetic worry, worsened by aging and overactive oil glands. Thirty subjects had three sessions of microneedling, where fine needles prick the skin, combined with a cream made from stem cell exosomes, tiny packets released by fat-derived stem cells.

Three separate tools checked the faces: three-dimensional imaging, surface roughness mapping, and AI pore counting. All agreed the skin grew smoother after treatment. Roughness fell sharply, and pore size dropped most on the forehead and nose, less on the cheeks. Pore scores improved across all six face zones measured. Kim argues that using several objective tools together gives firmer proof than photos alone. The results support the combined treatment for people seeking smoother skin texture.
pmc-13282288:
Ulrika Svenninghed and co-authors present a 2026 Swedish focus group study on quality of life in children born with a rare bladder malformation. In this condition, the bladder and related parts form abnormally, risking lifelong urine and genital problems. The team ran ten focus groups with fifteen children aged eight to eighteen and twenty-three parents, aiming to guide a condition-specific questionnaire.

Over seventeen hundred statements sorted into seven themes. Physical issues included urgency, leakage, smell, infections, and pain. Children weighed whether to tell others about their condition. Friendships could be supportive yet also exposed social vulnerability. Bladder care shaped nights, schedules, clothing, school, toilets, and leisure. Emotional effects and worries about appearance were common. Older children thought about sexuality, parenthood, and independence. The authors say the breadth of impact justifies a tailored questionnaire for this group.
pmc-13283388:
Seungsoo Rho and Pete A Williams present a 2026 review of nerve-protecting therapies for glaucoma. Glaucoma kills eye nerve cells and causes lasting vision loss. Pressure-lowering care is standard, but direct nerve protection still lacks a proven drug.

Past hope faded when a large late trial of memantine failed on endpoints. Lab work now favors targets such as cell energy failure and loss of growth support. Nicotinamide leads the field by boosting cell energy stores in nerve cells. Trials also test repurposed drugs, slow-release implants, and function boosters. New endpoints, imaging markers, and gene risk scores aim to sharpen trials. Proof in patients is the key next step.
pmc-13284388:
Wedad Sakran and colleagues examine a new drug carrier for cervical cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory study. The team loaded febuxostat, a drug used for other conditions, into chitosan-coated niosomes called chitosomes. Using a factorial design, they made eight versions and compared size, charge, and how much drug each one held.

The best version held about 91 percent of the drug and entered HeLa cancer cells about twice as well as free drug in lab tests. It also cut the dose needed to halve cell growth by about threefold, and cell studies pointed to death in the G1/S phase. The authors argue the carrier could make a reused drug more useful against cervical cancer, pending further work.
pmc-13284488:
Michael Hrdy and colleagues describe a 2026 pediatric emergency bootcamp built for graduating emergency medicine residents. Normal rotations do not cover the full range of child emergencies, which can leave new doctors less ready for very sick children. The one-day course used team simulations, skills stations, and talks based on a prior needs survey.

From 2022 to 2024, 98 residents from nine programs attended, and most who replied felt better prepared to manage child patients, steady airways, and do key procedures. At nine-month follow-up, most respondents said the day eased their move to solo practice. Breathing distress care and spotting heart disease were themes they planned to carry into practice.
pmc-13284888:
Andreea-Ramona Treteanu and co-authors survey telemedicine views among Romanian medical students in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Remote care now shapes access and workflow, yet student readiness in Romania was little known. A nationwide online survey ran in late 2024 across all university centers, with 608 students replying to 21 questions.

Most students knew the term telemedicine, but few had used it themselves and most had no formal training, the authors report. Large shares backed its place in medical schooling and felt it lifts care quality. Time saving and specialist access topped the gains, while limits on physical exams and weaker personal contact topped concerns. The authors link uptake to training and confidence.
pmc-13284988:
Clemens Rieder and co-authors report a 2026 project to extend a common health data model for life support research. Extracorporeal life support creates dense data, yet shared standards to store them across centers are lacking. Experts tested whether the OMOP common data model could hold circuit and treatment details for this care.

The standard model lacked many fitting concepts for circuit data, the team found. They built custom tables and new concepts, cutting needed database entries by up to ninety percent for test cases. The expansion, called the ECLS common data model, was released as open source in the public domain. The authors say shared structure should lift data quality and multi-center research.
pmc-13285088:
Svenja Jung and co-authors test a new 3D printed template system for skull surgery in a 2026 preclinical study. The retrosigmoid route reaches tumors and vessel lesions near the ear, but closing the bone gap afterward can be hard, above all if the opening must grow mid-surgery. The concept uses a printed stencil to mark implant edges on the skull first.

Nine senior surgeons tested the system on a printed model of the rear skull space, doing openings on both sides. The implant gap with the new concept was far smaller than with the standard method in the trials reported here. Timing for prep and closure was also logged. The authors call the fit gain promising, pending patient tests.
pmc-13285388:
Thinking skills nine months after intensive care lag for Spanish-speaking survivors next to English-speaking peers, Ana Lucia Fuentes and co-authors show in a 2026 study. Patients with weak English are often left out of big recovery studies, even though language gaps may shape delirium care. The team enrolled adults from two mixed intensive care units in 2024 and 2025.

Phone testing found lower scores for Spanish speakers, with over half classed as impaired versus about a third of English speakers in this small group. The gap shrank a bit once delirium and deep sedation entered the math. The authors point to care gaps, such as missed delirium and deeper sedation, as one path behind the split.
pmc-13285588:
A new gene-based family tree for bone marrow failure syndromes holds up in real-world data, Giulia Maggioni and co-authors test in a 2026 study. The taxonomy sorts myelodysplastic syndrome patients into sixteen groups by gene faults, chromosome quirks, and gene loss marks. The team checked it on 5,136 past cases plus RNA data from 477 fresh cases.

Groups showed clear gaps in traits and disease course, and RNA reads backed their biological separateness. Yet folding group links into a top risk score did not sharpen forecasts. Apart from one grim group, the labels failed to predict drug or transplant response, though they tracked survival. Non-gene factors may steer treatment response more.
pmc-13285988:
Gabriela Lipošćak and co-authors recount a rare valve clot case in a 2026 report from cardiology care. A 67-year-old man arrived with a heart attack, and imaging showed a floating clot in the main left coronary artery with no major plaque to blame. Doctors suspected a clot had formed on his own stiff aortic valve and broken loose into the heart's blood supply.

Suction tools cleared the clot twice after chest pain returned the next day, and ultrasound inside the artery ruled out hidden plaque. A heart valve narrowed by calcium, plus a rhythm problem found later, fit the suspected source well. After three months of blood thinners, surgeons replaced the valve with a tissue one. Later scans found a small new channel between two heart chambers, a rare surgical side effect, but tests showed it carried little flow, so watchful care was chosen.
pmc-13286088:
Haochen Zhou and colleagues report scope surgery to free a fish bone buried in the food pipe wall in a case report published in 2026. The patient, a 63-year-old woman, came in four days after swallowing the bone by accident, and a scan showed it lodged upright deep in the wall. The scope alone showed only swelling and a sore patch, with no bone in sight to grab.

Sound imaging through the scope pinpointed bright traces of the bone under the surface lining. Doctors then cut along the sore with a fine electric knife, a tuned version of a tumor removal method, and lifted the bone out with small forceps under direct view. Clips closed the cut, and a scan one week later showed no leftover bone or harm. A month on she ate normally with no complaints, spared the open chest surgery such cases can demand.
pmc-13287288:
Jinglong Chen and co-authors fed a chromium supplement in 2026 to yellow-feathered chickens kept under repeated daily heat for two weeks. One hundred eighty birds were split into a cool control group, a heated group on plain feed, and a heated group given the supplement in feed.

Heated birds grew more slowly and converted feed poorly. Supplemented birds partly recovered that loss. Heat shortened the gut and raised stress hormone and toxin levels in blood, while the supplement eased those changes and strengthened gut lining genes. Gut microbe patterns also shifted back toward the cool group. The authors link protection mainly to a healthier intestine.
pmc-13287588:
Xianmang Xu and co-authors introduce in 2026 a special issue gathering nine studies on cleaning heavy metal pollution with living systems instead of harsh chemical methods. Metals reach food, tap water, and daily products, and older clean-up routes can be costly and rough on ecosystems.

Collected work spans microbe-based cleaning, plant and microbe pairings, metal recovery by leaching, and soil additives. One strand weighs the toxic effects of tiny particles themselves. The editors frame the set as a step from lab proof toward field use. They argue that living clean-up must prove itself at scale before it can guide real sites.
pmc-13287688:
Yasemin Utkueri and colleagues present a method in 2026 for aligning whole-body magnetic resonance scans from different UK Biobank volunteers onto a common frame. Alignment used fat and muscle outline maps, drawn by an automated tool, on top of standard brightness matching, with men and women handled separately.

On 4000 volunteers the mask-guided method folded tissue far less often than brightness-only alignment. Overlap scores for body regions rose by several points against three rival methods. Age maps for fat and tissue volume also came out cleaner and better aligned. The authors say standardised scans will sharpen studies linking body measures to health records at population scale.
pmc-13288388:
Adam J Devall and co-authors set out a Cochrane review plan in 2026. The plan covers the diabetes drug metformin for women with polycystic ovary syndrome. The drug would start before pregnancy and continue through the first three months. The condition raises risks of infertility and pregnancy loss, and metformin is already widely used around conception.

As a plan, the document states the question, the comparison against dummy pills or no drug, and the outcomes the finished review will weigh for benefit and harm. No results are reported yet. The authors frame the review as a check on a common practice whose balance of gain and risk in early pregnancy remains unsettled.
pmc-13288888:
Karl-Hermann S Kamgang and colleagues track antipsychotic use in Swedish youth in 2026. Their register study covers everyone under age 18. It follows first prescriptions from 2008 to 2021. It also guesses the likely reason for each drug. Most use was off label, the team reports.

Use rose from 0.48 to 1.28 per 1,000 youths. The rise was steepest in teen girls. Quetiapine and aripiprazole grew the most. Autism was the top likely reason. ADHD and anxiety came next. Among cases with a clear reason, 81 percent were off label. The authors urge long-term safety checks. They also urge care with first prescriptions.
pmc-13289188:
Afifah Rahman-Shepherd and colleagues issue a 2026 call to action for public health schools. The first such school opened in 1916. Now over 150 exist worldwide. Health systems face deep reform calls. The authors ask what role schools should play.

Forty deans and leaders met in Bangkok. They were pressed to name their role. Four pillars frame the new mandate. One is close ties with policy bodies. Such ties can guide long-term choices. Short-term politics often harms health, they warn. Other pillars ground teaching and service locally. Schools must act as stewards, not bystanders.
pmc-13289788:
Michael P. Moghadasnia and colleagues report a 2026 breakthrough: a halogen-bonded organic framework that stays porous after drying. Halogen bonds can order light molecular solids by design, yet no such solid had proven lasting pores before. A threefold-symmetric building block ending in iodine-bearing rings assembled itself into a low-density crystal held by stacked layers and helical bond chains.

Gas uptake tests at very low temperature confirmed lasting pores after full solvent removal, and X-ray checks tracked the open structure. Slight twisting disorder inside the chains could still be resolved in the crystal data. A hydrogen-bonded twin solid collapsed on solvent exchange instead, showing the halogen version holds together better. New porous materials may follow.
pmc-13289888:
Ahmad Rifai Sarraj and coauthors ran a 2026 randomized trial on adding brain stimulation to a recruitment therapy for chronic paraplegia after spinal cord injury. Recovery is usually seen as limited once early spontaneous gains end. The base method pairs motor imagery with intense peripheral sensory input, and the add-on uses gentle direct current stimulation to the head, called tDCS.

Fifty participants with injury averaging 15.4 months earlier were split into standard care, base therapy, or combined therapy over ten days. Standard care showed no clear recovery in the trial. Both active groups gained sensory function equally, suggesting peripheral input alone restores feeling. Motor scores rose more with stimulation added, at 18 points versus 14 points as reported.
pmc-13290088:
Writing in 2026, Nolan Dvorak and Jeffrey Noebels describe a signaling pathway that makes brain cells overactive early in Alzheimer's disease. Their study links the protein complex mTORC2 to the sodium channel Nav1.2 in a mouse model of the disease.

The authors show that overactive mTOR signaling boosts Nav1.2 channel function, and that this effect needs mTORC2 and does not extend to other major brain sodium channels. In the mouse model, cortical pyramidal neurons showed the same raised channel activity and excess firing. Because overactivity appears before heavy damage and speeds later decline, the mTORC2 and Nav1.2 pairing is put forward as a drug target for early treatment.
pmc-13290388:
Family empowerment is widely preached for preventing stunting in babies and toddlers, yet the idea itself stays fuzzy, Titin Sutini and colleagues argue in a 2026 concept analysis. Stunting in children aged 0 to 2 years carries lasting effects on growth and development, especially in poorer countries.

Using the Walker and Avant framework, the authors searched PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar and synthesized 27 studies. Across the literature, empowerment came out as a process with five linked attributes: families deciding reflectively, confidence in their own ability, active participation, putting health knowledge to use, and pulling resources together. Families appear as active agents who monitor growth, provide stimulation, and act early in the first 1000 days. Sutini and colleagues propose measuring empowerment alongside growth so programs can target it directly.
pmc-13290588:
More than a third of young children in vulnerable Yemeni communities had acute watery diarrhea recently, Mansour Abdu Al-Taj reports in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Diarrhea still kills large numbers of small children, and what mothers know shapes how an episode ends.

Al-Taj interviewed 895 mothers from displaced and host communities face-to-face. The share of children with diarrhea was 36.4%, yet good knowledge of spread and prevention reached only 39.3% of mothers, and just 15.9% gave oral rehydration solution in the last episode. Older mothers and those with secondary schooling knew more, and knowledgeable mothers were nearly twice as likely to use the solution. The author calls for targeted teaching in these communities.
pmc-13290688:
Adding blood-flow restriction to electrical muscle stimulation helps over weeks but hurts acutely, Xin Shu and colleagues find in a systematic review from 2026. The review compares the combined method against stimulation alone for building muscle size and strength in healthy adults.

Seven studies with 124 adults met the criteria. In single-session studies, the combined method caused bigger immediate strength drops and fatigue, plus more swelling, favoring plain stimulation. In longer programs the pattern flipped, with trends favoring the combination for strength and muscle growth. Pooled numbers, though, showed no significant overall difference, and the authors note a confound: long studies all used fixed pressure while acute ones individualized it. Shu and colleagues read duration, not just the method, as the real divider and ask for cleaner trials.
pmc-13290788:
Laser and needling finish in a near tie for acne scar repair, Asia Batool and colleagues conclude in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026. Fractional CO₂ laser and microneedling are both standard for atrophic facial scars, yet direct comparisons have been scattered across small trials.

Seventeen head-to-head studies in adults were pooled under PRISMA rules. Average scar-score improvement did not differ significantly between the approaches, though categorical treatment success tilted modestly toward the laser. Safety split by comparison: laser carried about triple the risk of post-treatment darkening versus plain microneedling, yet hurt less than radiofrequency microneedling. Redness, crusting, and swelling were alike. Batool and colleagues advise matching the tool to skin type and scar type rather than declaring a universal winner.
pmc-13291288:
Many Pakistani children miss shots despite clinic visits. Areesh Fatmee leads a 2026 study of these missed chances. Mothers bring children in for other care needs. Staff fail to give due vaccines at that same visit.

Data came from a huge national household survey. It covered 195,000 homes and over 100,000 children. About one quarter of young children missed a dose. Miss rates were alike for first and later doses. Rural homes and uneducated mothers saw more misses. Private clinic visits linked to more missed shots, above all in cities. Maps showed sharp district gaps. Simple visit checks could close much of this loss.
pmc-13292388:
Fotini Mitropoulou and co-authors follow a 2026 cohort of 150 atrial fibrillation patients through recovery after cryoablation, asking who bounces back fastest. Quality of life was measured with the SF-36 survey before the procedure and at three and six months after it. The team looked for age and sex patterns in physical and mental component scores.

Overall scores climbed from a baseline of 57.5 to reach 77.1 at three months and 80.1 at six months in the group's results. Patients aged 65 and younger gained more function than older adults at both check-ins. Men seemed to improve a touch faster, but that sex gap faded after statistical correction. Younger age stood as the strongest independent predictor of recovery, ahead of paroxysmal AF type and starting ejection fraction. The authors advise tailoring follow-up talks to demographic recovery profiles.
pmc-13292688:
Zhongcheng Sun and co-authors investigate a 2026 duck farm scourge in China: red skin and bristle feather syndrome, which reddens backs and wrecks feather growth in meat ducks. They collected 300 samples from sick and healthy birds across eight major producing provinces between February and July 2025. Quantitative PCR screened multiple pathogens, followed by family-tree analysis of the main hits.

Duck circovirus led detections at 66.44 percent of tested samples, then novel duck reovirus at 32.33 percent and waterfowl parvovirus at 19.18 percent in the screening. Solo parvovirus infection, mostly the novel goose type, carried nearly tenfold odds of the syndrome. Neither other virus hurt alone, but pairing either with parvovirus sharply worsened disease. Shandong province was the hotspot, and three-to-five-week-old ducks were most vulnerable. The authors call for targeted vaccines.
pmc-13292788:
Minho Kim, Walid G Al Hakeem, and Michael J Rothrock used machine learning in a 2026 study of Campylobacter in pastured chickens. This gut bacterium is a food safety risk, yet what drives its spread from farm to final product is unclear.

Data came from 11 farms in the US southeast, gathered between 2014 and 2017, with 1,942 broiler samples of soil, feces, gut contents, and rinsed carcasses. Random forest models pointed to the farm itself as the strongest guide to whether the bacterium was present. Bird age and season also mattered, with summer peaks noted. Weather played a role too, as strong wind and rain on sampling day linked to lower levels in feces.
pmc-13293388:
Han Gong and colleagues trace cell lineages, in a 2026 study, to watch how the fruit fly gut ages from the inside. Stem cell upkeep shapes tissue aging, and the team followed gut clones across adult life with an improved labeling system.

Across days 3 to 33 of adult life, clone variety peaked right after emergence from the pupa, then fell sooner than expected. Later tracking to day 63 showed steady loss in the rear gut. Lineages born in the first 10 days lasted best, with one clone passing 63% of sampled cells by day 63, a share the authors report. Models could forecast which clones would endure.
pmc-13293788:
Ananda L. Roy, Ranjan Sen, and Dinah S. Singer introduce, in a 2026 editorial, a research collection on gene control in lymphocyte growth and response. Lymphocytes, the B and T cells of adaptive immunity, must switch genes on and off precisely as they mature and meet germs.

The editors frame the stakes: innate defenses act fast and broadly, while adaptive cells give slower, targeted clearance, with some cells bridging both arms. Gene control needs hundreds of factors meeting at one gene in the right cell at the right moment. The collection gathers work on those pathways in B and T cells, aiming to deepen a still incomplete picture of immune regulation.
pmc-13293988:
Midhun Krishnan Vasanthakrishnan, Marion Hogg, and Kif Liakath-Ali review RNA detection methods in 2026 through the lens of reproducibility. Offerings now span hybridization, amplification, imaging, and sequencing, and each rests on a different core principle. The authors trace growth from basic assays through PCR variants, microarrays, and single-molecule imaging to spatial and sequencing approaches.

Later parts cover bulk, single-cell, long-read, direct RNA, and spatial transcriptomics, plus CRISPR tests and metabolic labeling for RNA dynamics. Mature tools benefit from shared standards, while newer ones still need study-specific controls. Choosing well means matching the question, resolution, sample limits, and method maturity.
pmc-13295788:
Philipp Sewerin and colleagues compare heart tracings in psoriatic arthritis in a 2026 study. The joint and skin disease raises heart risk, including rhythm problems, yet structured tracing-based screening was missing. Records from 2014 to 2022 supplied patients and a matched comparison group.

Each group held 725 people of similar age and sex mix. Simple heart block rates matched between groups overall, at roughly one person in ten. Signs of atrial strain and a stretched heart recovery interval ran clearly higher in the arthritis group. Among patients, male sex and longer illness tied to conduction delay, supporting routine tracing checks.
pmc-13297188:
Tuba Dilay Kökenek Ünal and colleagues measure, in 2026, a gene family tied to stem cells in bladder lining cancers from eighty-four patients. Ten family genes were read in tumour tissue split by grade and invasiveness, against normal lining controls.

Five genes ran higher in tumours and three ran lower. Low levels of five genes, including some raised overall, tracked with poorer survival. The authors say the family had not been charted in this cancer before. Their pattern hints at both forecasting value and possible treatment targets, pending wider study.
pmc-13297488:
Two rival maps of the developing hypothalamus get a head-to-head comparison in a 2026 review by Marika Kapsimali. One map, the prosomeric model, treats the region as an anterior unit split into two prosomeres. The newer tripartite model, built from gene expression, single-cell sequencing, fate mapping, and functional tests, places most of the hypothalamus within the diencephalon and sets its rear boundary at the retromammillary area. pmc-13298988:
Speakers adjust their pronunciation after hearing their own voice distorted, even when the distorted voice arrives on a trial where they never actually spoke. Benjamin Parrell and colleagues demonstrate that result in a 2026 speech experiment testing what drives motor learning.

Participants were cued to say a word or, on some trials, to stop themselves. On stop trials they heard a recording of their earlier speech with its first formant shifted, timed as if live. They still adapted their vowels on later trials, countering the shift. Passive listening without intent to speak produced no adaptation. The authors conclude prediction errors, not corrective commands, drive speech adaptation.
pmc-13299488:
Specks small past sight can find a tumor, show it on a scan, and treat it in one trip. Junaid Ali and his team review such specks in a 2026 paper. They set three kinds side by side: zinc oxide, iron oxide, and gold.

Each kind brings its own gift. Zinc oxide wakes up in acid and can haul drugs. Iron oxide answers to magnets, fits MRI scans, and can heat a tumor. Gold gives a firm base to fix hot atoms and adds heat and ray boosts of its own. The team weigh how each is made, coated, and tagged with a hot atom. Most sets prove scan strength well. Proof on cure, long-run harm, and how the body clears the specks lags far back.
pmc-13299888:
Plans that let nurses pull urine tubes by their own call stall on pecking rank and sheer load in Saudi top-tier wards. Nader E Alotaibi and Ahmed S Alsadoun found why in a 2026 talk study. They spoke with 23 nurses, germ-guard nurses, and nurse chiefs at two big Riyadh care sites.

Talk across trades, years on the job, and pride in the work all helped the plans land. Load and short staff hurt them. So did the sway of doctors, which made nurses hold back. Thin know-how, shaky notes, and plain lack of note that a tube was still in hurt too. The team urge more say for nurses, tight notes, and fresh rounds of school for staff, so the plans stick and sick folks stay safe.
pmc-13302688:
Which pulp-cap cement glues best to which glass ionomer filling depends on the pairing, Mehmet Salık and Elif Pınar Bakır test in a 2026 laboratory study. Ninety-six acrylic blocks received one of four calcium silicate biomaterials, including ProRoot MTA and Biodentine, then one of three glass ionomer restoratives, making twelve combinations. A testing machine sheared the joints apart after a day of storage.

Both material choices significantly shifted bond strength. The TheraCal LC base under Fuji II LC held tightest, while MTA BioRep beneath Equia Forte HT let go easiest. Because these layers meet in everyday vital pulp therapy, the authors say the pairing deserves deliberate selection rather than habit.
pmc-13303688:
Manar-Aleslam M Mattar leads a 2026 metagenomic study of viruses in rural groundwater near Toukh in Qalyubia, Egypt. Groundwater holds rich microbe communities, yet the viruses living alongside them have rarely been described.

Water from three hand pumps with different surroundings was analyzed with paired detection tools and quality checks. The team recovered 9,534 distinct viral pieces, mostly tailed viruses that infect bacteria. One pump held a clearly richer and different viral mix, while the other two grouped together. Predicted hosts, dormant versus active viral lifestyles, and extra metabolic genes also differed by pump, hinting at local viral roles.
pmc-13303988:
Zhicheng Zhu heads a 2026 meta-analysis of exercise for lung function and quality of life in asthma. Activity is promoted as a drug-free extra treatment, but past reviews covered narrow ages, single exercise types, or mixed lung measures.

Six databases were searched for randomized trials lasting at least six weeks, yielding 22 trials with 1,280 patients. Pooled results showed gains in a key breathing measure, peak flow, lung volume, and a child asthma quality-of-life score. Some other lung measures did not move. Program length, weekly count, session length, and exercise type failed to explain the mixed results.
pmc-13304188:
Caio Santos Bonilha argues in a 2026 review that where immune activity sits inside tissue matters as much as which molecules are involved. Immune drugs are usually judged cell by cell, yet inflammation gathers in lasting pockets within diseased organs.

Cell mix, tissue compartments, and the staying power of contact zones shape where signals concentrate and persist. Reading these interaction zones as working units helps explain why the same drug engages its target well in one patient and poorly in another. Aligning drug plans with the immune layout that dominates a tissue may sharpen treatment choices.
pmc-13304588:
Donghong Lai, Yuehong Peng, Han Wu, and Qiangqiang Xiong review colored rice as a health food in a 2026 synthesis. Pigmented grains carry more protective compounds than white rice, including the purple pigments called anthocyanins.

Gene switches and growing conditions such as light, heat, and feeding shape pigment building. Colored rice also offers more resistant starch, fiber, protein quality, minerals, and calming compounds. Benefits for sugar, fats, gut germs, and inflammation are traced through several pathways. Keeping nutrients through milling without losing taste, and winning buyer trust, remain industry hurdles for wider use.
pmc-13305288:
Chien-Tung Yang leads a 2026 nationwide Taiwan study of blood-thinning choices after ischemic stroke in East Asian patients. Western guidelines dominate, yet East Asian patients far more often carry a gene variant that weakens one common drug, clopidogrel.

Insurance records for 5,746 adults treated within two days of stroke imaging were tracked for 100 days. Two-drug therapy tied to a sharply higher heart attack rate than aspirin alone, with harm seen in few treated patients. Many bias checks supported the signal. A new risk score blending age, sex, illnesses, and drug plan was built for this population.
pmc-13306188:
Torben Rogge used quantum chemistry in 2026 to explain a palladium reaction that can follow two rival paths. Coupling of protected diazene partners with aryl partners can keep nitrogen to form azo dyes or lose nitrogen to form biaryl products instead.

pmc-13306288:

One channel follows change over time while the second follows each variable on its own, and the pair together read tangled patterns better than single-path rivals. Tests beat several standard time-series classifiers on accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score in reported results. The authors present simulation plus dual reading as a scalable route for solar monitoring.
pmc-13307188:

Good outcome was forecast when albumin stayed above 31.8 g/L in reported thresholds, alongside coma score above eleven and bleed volume at or under 23.6 mL in the given figures. Albumin also rose steadily across coma score bands.
pmc-13309388:
Naeem and co-authors review processed animal proteins as feed for poultry in a 2026 review article. These proteins come from animal by-products that are rendered or broken down with water and heat. Interest has grown as farms seek cheaper and less wasteful protein than soybean meal.

Corrected here is panel E of figure 3: the method text and scoring math did not match, so the team reran the analysis with the stated product method and replaced the panel. pmc-13310388:

Patients skewed old, with a median age of 79 years in the cohort, and diabetes appeared in 21 patients. Escherichia coli was the most frequent germ, found in 21 cases, including drug-resistant strains. The authors set out the typical route from scan surprise to care.
pmc-13310788:

pmc-13310988:

pmc-13311088:
Kehinde Alare and colleagues review whole brain radiation for brain spread cancer in Nigeria in a 2026 study. pmc-13311188:

pmc-13311288:

pmc-13312088:

pmc-13312788:

pmc-13312888:

pmc-13314288:

pmc-13314388:

pmc-13314488:

pmc-13315088:

pmc-13315188:

pmc-13315888:

pmc-13316188:

pmc-13316288:

pmc-13316388:

pmc-13316688:

pmc-13316788:

pmc-13317488:

pmc-13317588:

pmc-13318888:

pmc-13319088:

pmc-13319388:

pmc-13319488:

pmc-13319888:

pmc-13320288:

pmc-13320388:

pmc-13320488:

pmc-13322188:
