Affected adults carried far more other illnesses, with a comorbidity score of 1.43 against 0.34 for matched peers in the study. Depression, anxiety, and quality of life scores were all worse. Care use was much higher too, with about 13 provider visits on average against about 3 for the comparison group in the past period.
pmc-13322488:
Victor Goiris Calderaro and co-authors follow new hearing aid users through their first year in a 2026 study. The group included 24 adults with moderate or severe sensorineural hearing loss. Brain response tests, speech sentence tests, and handicap questionnaires were run before fitting and again at six and twelve months.

Brain wave timing and size did not shift across the year for either tone or speech stimuli. Speech understanding still improved across the three stages, above all in moderate loss, and fitted thresholds opened access to speech sounds. Users also reported fewer social and emotional limits. Benefit in daily life can thus grow even when lab brain measures stay flat.
pmc-13322888:
Linfei Yu and co-authors show that the enzyme OTUD7B worsens atherosclerosis by driving a form of cell death, in a 2026 mouse and cell study. They built artery disease in mice with a high-fat diet and partial carotid tying, then studied human aortic smooth muscle cells in culture.

OTUD7B rose in plaques alongside necroptosis markers RIPK1, RIPK3 and phosphorylated MLKL, with more inflammation present. Lowering OTUD7B eased cell injury, cut inflammatory signals and reduced plaque build-up and fat deposits in animals. Restoring RIPK1 reversed that protection, which places the effect on the RIPK1 path. The authors nominate OTUD7B as a possible treatment target for artery disease.
pmc-13323488:
Ni Luh Suriani and co-authors test black turmeric extract on male fertility in mice, in a 2026 study of Curcuma caesia. This traditional medicinal plant carries antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compounds, yet its effects on male reproduction were poorly documented.

Twenty-four male mice split into four groups received extract at three doses or none, in a randomised design. Chemical analysis found flavonoids, phenolics, tannins and alkaloids. The top dose raised sperm concentration sharply against controls in their measures, while the middle dose gave the best sperm viability, movement and normal shape, plus healthier testicle tissue structure. Testosterone levels were tracked by blood assay, and the authors judge the middle dose most balanced overall.
pmc-13323688:
Xin Wan and co-authors compare two antibody-based chemotherapy backbones in slow-growing B-cell lymphoma with heavy tumour burden, in a 2026 real-world study at the First Hospital of Jilin University. They reviewed 186 untreated follicular or marginal zone lymphoma patients treated between 2016 and 2025.

Complete response after induction ran far higher with obinutuzumab than with rituximab in the weighted comparison, and three-year survival without progression and overall survival also favoured obinutuzumab. Early progression within two years was less common in that group. Side effect profiles looked similar across arms. The authors used overlap weighting to balance the groups, and they present obinutuzumab as the stronger option for this high-risk set.
pmc-13325088:
Margherita Gazzotti and colleagues compute the acid strength of a new family of chiral phosphoric acid catalysts in a 2026 chemistry study. These acids steer many mirror-selective reactions, and their power depends on fine scaffold details.

The family rests on a decahydroquinoxaline frame with two-fold symmetry, and 34 new members were modeled with density functional theory. Two calculation routes estimated acidity in DMSO and acetonitrile, first checked against known BINOL-based acids. Substituent effects on the scaffold shifted acidity in clear trends. Bench titration then confirmed the forecasts, mostly within 1 pKa unit of measured values. The map gives catalyst designers a guide for picking acid strength before synthesis.
pmc-13325388:
Bruna Cristina Corcino Carneiro and colleagues simulate a water pair under an electric field in a 2026 study. Two linked water molecules form the smallest test case for the hydrogen bond quirks behind liquid water behavior.

Density functional runs raised the field step by step until the dimer snapped into a new shape. Past a threshold strength, the pair swung into a cis-like layout as the donor hydrogen shifted to one side. Vibration checks confirmed the new form sits at a stable energy dip. The switched shape kept a high dipole even after the field was removed, showing memory of the push. A simple dipole and torque picture explains the flip.
pmc-13327788:
Tadeg Quillien offers a causal account of luck and intentional action in a 2026 article. People often deny that a lucky success was done on purpose, as when a poor shot hits a target by chance. Quillien argues that judgments hinge on how strongly a person's desire caused the outcome.

When chance dominates, desire looks like a weak cause, so purpose ratings fall. Experiments back the link: where purpose is denied, people also refuse to credit the agent's desire as the cause. Purpose judgments tracked cause judgments more closely than rival factors offered before. A firm desire-to-outcome link thus sits at the heart of the everyday idea of acting on purpose.
pmc-13327888:
Nabil Mohammad Azmi, Mohd Firdaus Mohd Hayati, and Zairul Azwan Mohd Azwan write a 2026 letter on botulinum toxin shots for urge fecal incontinence. They comment on a study of injections into the rectal wall for patients who had failed sacral nerve stimulation, a group with few gentle options left. The study reported durable score gains over a median 22.5 months with no adverse events.

The letter praises the work, then raises points needing care: a backward-looking, single-center design, a small sample, and reinjection left to physician judgment could all sway results. Only women were included, though anatomy and rectal behavior differ by sex. Repeat outpatient treatment still looks attractive before major diversion surgery, the writers agree.
pmc-13328188:
Xiaoxu Li and co-authors chart auxin hormone rewiring during bacterial wilt in a 2026 article. Ralstonia solanacearum clogs plant water pipes and devastates solanaceous crops, and auxin, a growth hormone, keeps surfacing as a regulator of the infection. The authors gather findings across model plants and crops over space and time.

Infected roots shift hormone patterns, raise indole-3-acetic acid, and switch on auxin programs in set tissues, while primary roots shorten, root hairs surge, and side roots grow late in infection. Root hair formation needs working auxin signaling, and susceptible plant types fire the pathway harder than resistant ones, while blocking auxin sensing raises resistance. Breeding or treating for calmer auxin responses may slow wilt.
pmc-13328488:
Yoon Sang Cho and co-authors test scan-based forecasting of inherited BRCA mutations in breast cancer in a 2026 multicenter study. Gene testing guides personal treatment but costs money, so flagging likely carriers from MRI could focus spending. High-risk patients from two centers who had both scans and gene tests supplied the data.

Three predictor families were tried alone and combined: clinic and pathology facts, radiologist-read scan traits, and computer-extracted radiomics from tumor outlines. Six learning models were checked by repeated splits inside one center and by cross-center validation. The multimodal design tests whether images add real signal beyond the chart, a question the authors put to strict outside checking before any clinic use.
pmc-13328788:
Namsu Kim, Sam-Jun Lee, and Jinseok Lee study memory and thinking problems in older women living at home in South Korea in a 2026 report. The group included 1,065 women aged 65 or older from 13 cities. Thinking was screened with a standard dementia test, while mood, muscle weakness, frailty, and long-term illness were also recorded.

Women with impaired thinking showed more depression, weaker muscles, more frailty, and more chronic illness than peers with normal scores. After adjusting for age and other factors, depression, diabetes, arthritis, weak muscles, and frailty each stayed linked to impairment. The authors argue that care should tackle mood, strength, and frailty together, since each may be open to change.
pmc-13329388:
Wei Yao and co-authors review materials that could keep brain implants working longer in a 2026 article. Electrodes placed in the brain lose stability over time as the body reacts to a foreign object. That reaction changes across phases, from early swelling to lasting scar tissue and fouling.

The review gathers bio-inspired and active material designs matched to each phase. Some calm early immune attack and limit scar growth. Others form barriers against fouling and infection, or resist wear from tiny movements and breakdown. By sorting designs by phase and by how they act, the authors map a path toward tougher brain-computer electrodes. Lasting, stable contact is the goal for clinical use.
pmc-13330688:
Zeng-Jin Huang and colleagues design a gel that eats wound glucose and returns oxygen for diabetic wounds in a 2026 study. Starving microbes of glucose can aid healing, yet the reaction drains oxygen and worsens low-oxygen stalls. The gel holds glucose oxidase plus a copper peptide, GHK-Cu, in a linked cascade.

The enzyme first turns glucose into peroxide while lowering local sugar. Copper then splits peroxide in a catalase-like step, freeing oxygen back into the wound. The peptide also supports skin repair on its own. Tests showed germ killing, tissue repair support, antioxidant action, and new vessel growth in the reported checks. The gel tackles sugar, oxygen, and repair at once.
pmc-13330788:
Musbahu Adam Ahmad and colleagues test coated carbon dots against breathing viruses in a 2026 study. Influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and human metapneumovirus burden health systems, while current drugs face toxicity and resistance limits. Tiny carbon dots with tunable surfaces offer a fresh scaffold, building on earlier work against HIV entry.

The team made dots by heating, covering them densely with boronic acid and boroxine groups. The dots proved non-toxic and showed strong action against all three viruses in lab tests in the reported results. Blocking tests and docking models point to binding at sugar-rich virus surfaces, though firm proof awaits direct checks. The platform merits further study, the authors conclude.
pmc-13333388:
Chiara Martinello and colleagues updated the numbers on a scan finding in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026: unexpected tracer uptake in the prostate during PET/CT scans done for other reasons. Such incidental uptake is turning up more often as molecular imaging spreads, and teams must decide who needs a prostate workup.

Twenty-four studies met the criteria, 23 using the FDG tracer and one using somatostatin-style tracers. Pooled prevalence was 1.7 percent of FDG scans in men, while the other-tracer study saw 4.5 percent. Among uptake cases that went on to checks or biopsy, malignancy rates were 21.3 percent for FDG and 59.7 percent for the evaluated subset in the other study, with no cancers found in the somatostatin study itself. Cancer cases skewed older, with hotter uptake values, and uptake at the gland's edge predicted malignancy. The authors advise individual follow-up, above all for focal, edge-located uptake.
pmc-13333588:
Quang Tam Nguyen and colleagues overturn a suspicion in a 2026 melanoma study: nitric oxide, long blamed for poor outcomes, turns out to be required for anti-PD-1 immunotherapy to work. The gas, made by the enzyme iNOS, had a split reputation, harmful in some settings and immune-friendly in others, and the team tested its role directly.

In mice carrying melanoma tumors, animals lacking iNOS grew tumors faster and gained nothing from anti-PD-1 treatment, while normal mice responded. Nitric oxide donors in dishes slowed melanoma growth and pushed cells into death, and gene profiling showed the drug switched on interferon pathways, STAT1, IRF1, IFNB1, only when iNOS was present. In blood from 27 treated patients, a nitric-oxide-producing dendritic cell subset tracked with longer progression-free survival, at a hazard ratio of 0.453. The authors propose iNOS activity as both a response biomarker and a treatment partner worth developing.
pmc-13333688:
Oluwatosin Babasola and co-authors built a 2026 math model of a hypothetical human outbreak of H5Nx, a highly pathogenic avian influenza. Their model asks how vaccine timing and how the public acts shape an epidemic curve.

Unlike simpler models, theirs builds in three delays: incubation, vaccine rollout, and the lag before vaccination protects. The population splits into vaccine-accepting and vaccine-hesitant groups, and non-drug measures enter as well. Simulations showed that slow rollout and slow immune protection blunted vaccination's effect on peak infections, while earlier delivery cut early growth. Reproduction number and stability analyses frame the conditions for control. The results warn planners that speed of rollout matters as much as eventual coverage.
pmc-13334388:
Qian Shi and co-authors identified the fungus behind sugarcane white rash disease in coastal Guangxi, China, and screened fungicides against it in a 2026 plant pathology study. The disease has become endemic in the region's cane fields.

A fungus repeatedly isolated from diseased leaves reproduced the field symptoms in inoculation tests and was identified as Elsinoë sacchari from host range, symptoms, and form. It grew fastest on potato dextrose agar at pH 6.0 and 25 degrees Celsius, favoring oat as a carbon source. Lab assays found difenoconazole best at stopping mycelial growth and a pyraclostrobin-boscalid mix best against spore germination. Field trials singled out a trifloxystrobin-tebuconazole product for lowest disease severity and top cane yield.
pmc-13334888:
Başak Günay, Narmin Soylu, and Merve Bayram compared two stainless steel crown systems for children's molars in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. These crowns restore badly decayed baby teeth, but head-to-head evidence between commercial systems is scarce.

The study covered 65 children aged 2 to 8 who received at least one crown under general anesthesia. They were followed for at least six months, totaling 246 crowns from Kids Crown and NuSmile. A single calibrated examiner scored retention, fit, bite, contact, gum health, and complications, while parents rated satisfaction on a five-point scale. Both systems succeeded well, with retention above 97 percent overall and good marginal adaptation in 98.3 percent of crowns, slightly favoring Kids Crown on that measure.
pmc-13336388:
Ziwen Gan and co-authors made an underwater sound-absorbing material whose performance is set chemically rather than carved in shape in a 2026 study. Acoustic metamaterials usually obey a shape-sets-performance rule, which narrows bandwidth and complicates making them.

MXene nanosheets were coaxed to self-assemble with polyvinyl alcohol into a film of nano-thin layered structure, then laminated with styrene-butadiene rubber. Stable cross-links plus dynamic hydrogen bonds form a tunable constraint network. Raising or lowering crosslinker levels works like chemical scissors, sliding the local resonance bands without steps. At only 10 mm thick, deep below the wavelength, the material absorbed an average coefficient of 0.90 across 1000 to 4000 hertz in testing. Film thickness and layer count add physical tuning on top.
pmc-13336888:
Ronglong Chen and a large team overload tumor power units with calcium in a 2026 nanomedicine study. Flooding mitochondria with calcium can destroy tumors, but cancer cells pump and gate calcium tightly to protect themselves. Acid inside tumor cells breaks the cluster open. Released signals suppress mitochondrial fusion and add hydrogen sulfide, jointly forcing the calcium gate open. Calcium surge and rising harmful oxygen species then feed each other, driving cell suicide from the power unit outward. The therapy worked strongly in mouth cancer models, including patient-derived grafts. Rewiring calcium self-control could sharpen this treatment class.
pmc-13337388:
Zesong Jiang and colleagues review testis macrophages, immune cells that guard sperm making, in a 2026 article on sperm production disorders. The testis is shielded from normal immune attack, and its macrophages keep that calm, tame swelling, and support hormone balance, all of which help sperm form. When sperm making fails, their numbers, placement, and behavior shift.

Wrongly switched-on macrophages feed lasting low-grade swelling that wrecks the sperm-forming setting. New single-cell gene tools have sharpened the picture of these cells' types and origins. The review pulls scattered work into one account, from how the cells arise to their roles across male infertility types. It closes by weighing treatments aimed at these cells, a target long missed in male fertility care.
pmc-13339588:
Alex Lloyd and colleagues map social and emotional profiles in at-risk teenagers in a 2026 study. Early adolescence is when many mental health problems start or worsen. Risk factors that cross diagnosis lines may matter more than single-disorder signs.

A total of 559 youths aged 12 to 14 at higher risk took part as reported, with average age 13.26 years. Questionnaires and tasks covered emotion reading, control, body sensing, and peer and family ties. A neural network projected profiles onto a flat map, and clustering found zones of similar functioning. Zones linked differently to broad symptoms, suggesting tailored support by profile rather than label.
pmc-13339688:
Ayla Yildiz, Süleyman Yazici, and Zülfiye Yildiz test a mitochondrion regulator as a heart ischemia marker in bypass surgery in a 2026 study. PGC-1 alpha was measured around aortic clamping in 44 adults having open-heart surgery between June and December 2024. Diabetes links received special attention.

Levels before and after surgery did not differ clearly, at 2.06 versus 1.43 in the reported means, while troponin rose sharply as expected. Starting levels tracked moderately with diabetes at r equal to 0.366 as reported. Diabetes and intensive care stay independently tied to the marker in adjusted models. The regulator looks more like a metabolic signal than an ischemia gauge.
pmc-13339888:
Zeliang Yang and colleagues optimize tongue swab culture for tuberculosis diagnosis in a 2026 study. Many patients cannot produce sputum, and tongue swabs offer a painless alternative. Swab samples spiked with a vaccine strain tested digestion times in growth tubes.

A 10-minute treatment with 4 percent sodium hydroxide gave the best balance of low contamination and growth as reported. Among 119 people with suspected tuberculosis, tongue culture matched sputum culture with sensitivity near 81.43 percent in the reported estimate. Against a combined standard, specificity reached 94.12 percent as reported. The method could widen testing for patients without sputum.
pmc-13340288:
Two bacterial strains that lock up cadmium are examined in a 2026 study by Yu Tao and colleagues. Achromobacter insuavis SL8 tolerated cadmium up to 600 mg/L and Enterobacter cancerogenus SL12 up to 400 mg/L, and each removed about 70% of the metal from a 100 mg/L solution.

Spectroscopy, metabolomics, and proteomics showed raised activity in metal transport, binding, energy production, and antioxidant defense. Pot trials removed 13% of cadmium from soil and 20% from Chinese cabbage, pointing toward farm use of such consortia.
pmc-1334188:

They removed parts of older standard vectors that got in the way, making the new set cleaner to use. With them, researchers can measure how active a gene switch is and test gene silencing in days rather than months. Faster plant tests speed work on crops, resistance, and basic gene function.
pmc-13342188:
Lab-grown human microglia respond to a brain protein, in a 2026 study by Daniel Navin Olschewski and colleagues. Rodent microglia and cell lines translate poorly to humans, so the team grew microglia from induced pluripotent stem cells of two healthy donors.

Identity and the phagocytic marker CD68 were checked by staining, viability by dye exclusion, shape change by branching analysis, and inflammatory genes by PCR. pmc-13343488:
Jill Ashey and co-authors catalog noncoding RNAs in reef-building corals in 2026, the first broad survey of its kind. pmc-13346088:
Hayato Miyasaka and co-authors probe why ankles stay stiff and sore at the front after fracture surgery in 2026. Blame usually falls on front-side impingement. Rear tissue change, the authors suggest, deserves a place in post-fracture ankle assessment.
pmc-13346788:
Gayoung Kim and Hae Won Kim review teaching studies on digital sexual media literacy. Their scoping review was published in 2026. It covers work from 2015 to 2025. pmc-13347288:
Rihab Akasha and colleagues compare infections in kidney failure patients by dialysis type in the Hail region, in a study from 2026. pmc-13348188:
Julian Hörndl, Jakub Zalesak, Franky E. Bedoya-Lora, Sophia Haussener, and Simone Pokrant test how heat and light levels wear solar water-splitting electrodes, in a study from 2026. Warmer baths cut output by 52 percent and life by 8 percent. While stronger light lifted early output by up to 77 percent yet cut life by 38 percent in the reported runs. pmc-13349988:
Christian Aalborg and colleagues measured observer variation in kidney MRI readings in a 2026 prospective study. Seventy-two patients awaiting a diagnostic kidney biopsy underwent a full multiparametric scan covering volume, tissue mapping, diffusion, blood flow, and oxygen measures.

Manual outlining is common but depends on who draws it, and small shifts can move the numbers. pmc-13350188:

The best coating killed about 60 percent of one species. It killed about 80 percent of the other. The coating stayed gentle to cultured cells and kept the plastic strong. Such coatings could make long aligner treatment safer for teeth.
pmc-13353088:

Patients used the system repeatedly at home so brain signals and thinking scores could be tracked over time in daily life. The study asks whether such remote, frequent checks are workable for people with mild dementia. Day-to-day swings become visible instead of hidden between clinic visits. Workable home tracking could sharpen how new disease-slowing drugs are judged.
pmc-13355488:
Yilin Zheng and co-authors tested tiny platinum-copper-sulfur clusters in 2026 as a treatment for gut injury from radiation therapy. In their tests, the clusters boosted a protective chemical pathway, shifted gut immune cells toward a healing mode, and helped restore gut bacteria after radiation. Gut injury eased without weakening the cancer treatment itself. The authors present the clusters as a possible way to improve life for patients during radiation care.
pmc-13355788:
Ahmed Sami Raihane and co-authors present a 2026 case of a 36-year-old woman with a birthmark that follows the lines of Blaschko, the hidden pattern skin cells take as a baby grows. In a few cases, the tissue shows a pattern called epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, tied to keratin gene changes.

Her lesions stayed stable through childhood, then spread over two years to trunk, armpit, and limbs, with a new growth on the vulva in the past year. The bumps sit on hair follicles rather than forming flat plaques, an unusual look that prompted biopsy. The pattern matters for genetic counseling.
pmc-13357088:
Long Chen and co-authors compared treatments for vestibular schwannoma in 2026 using a large United States registry. These benign ear-nerve tumors can be watched, removed by surgery, or treated with radiation, and the best choice per patient is debated. Surgery patients had the highest five-year survival, about 94 percent, versus 78 percent with no treatment, with combined therapy and radiation in between. No approach clearly raised treatment-related death risk. The authors caution that healthier patients likely got surgery, so choices should fit age, tumor size, and symptoms.
pmc-13358488:
Xiaoxing Bian and co-authors compare two drug plans for HER2-positive breast cancer in a 2026 study from Tianjin, China. Both plans pair a taxane drug with two targeted antibodies before surgery. One plan adds carboplatin, a harsh drug that raises side effects. The team asked if some patients can safely skip it.

They reviewed patients with stage II or III disease who finished six cycles of one plan or the other between 2019 and 2022. By comparing how well tumors shrank and how patients fared over time, the study looks for traits that mark who still needs the full plan. That could spare some women heavy side effects without losing ground against the cancer.
pmc-13361688:
Yahya Faruk Karatas and co-authors studied diet and muscle loss in dialysis patients in a 2026 paper. Muscle wasting, called sarcopenia, is very common in people on long-term hemodialysis, above all when diabetes is also present. The sugar and insulin load of a diet may feed the metabolic trouble behind muscle loss. The team enrolled 92 patients, 43 with diabetes and 49 without.

Three-day food records let them score each diet's glycemic and insulin index and load. Muscle status was checked with grip strength, body composition scans, walking speed, and a screening questionnaire. Blood and body measures added clinical context. The team compared patterns between the diabetic and non-diabetic groups. Findings like these can guide diet advice that protects muscle in a fragile group.
pmc-13362188:
Tao-An Chen and co-authors review a stubborn hospital germ in intensive care in a 2026 paper. The authors trace how the germ persists in sinks and equipment, builds biofilms that shrug off drugs and cleaning, and picks up resistance. Gene tracking now lets hospitals spot outbreak strains early and separate look-alike cases. Infection control tactics, from device care to environmental cleaning, are weighed. The synthesis aims to help ICU teams break the cycle of repeated outbreaks.
pmc-13362988:
Fathima Zahraa Ozeer and Jemila Caplan Kester present a 2026 review on whether lab-grown 3D tumor models can stand in for flat cell cultures and animal tests in pancreatic cancer research. Microbes living in these tumors seem to blunt treatment, yet flat cultures miss the tumor's structure, stroma, and immune mix. The review asks what a good model must hold: cancer cells, support tissue, immune cells, and the microbes themselves.

The authors survey 3D culture work in other cancers, where organ-like models already host this microbe-tumor-immune interplay, and map how to adapt those designs to pancreatic tumors. Such models could speed drug screening and cut animal use. Gaps in realism and shared standards remain the chief barriers.
pmc-13363088:
Cynthia T Brewer, Greg Brewer, and Raymond J Butcher present a 2026 chemistry study on how handedness passes through a family of nickel complexes. They reacted left- and right-handed forms of three sulfur-bearing amino acids with an imidazole aldehyde and nickel salts. Each reaction closed a new ring, thiazolidine or thiazine, and yielded just one mirror form of product, which they confirmed with crystal structures and standard spectra.

The starting amino acid kept its handedness, and the two new centers formed with matched settings in the five-membered rings. In the six-membered ring case, the new centers matched each other but opposed the old one, yet all key hydrogen atoms stayed on the same face. The authors credit the fused ring frame for this strict order.
pmc-13363988:
Alessia D'Andrea and colleagues present a 2026 study on 3D-printed skull implants that also deliver medicine. A base wash before coating made the mineral layer even and firmly held. Coated scaffolds raised cell survival and bone-forming behavior in dishes, and the drug beads released their load in a controlled way without poisoning cells. The authors present the combined implant as a step toward one-piece cranial repair with local therapy built in.
pmc-13369888:
Brendonas Stakauskas and Paweł Górecki test in 2026 if the deep codes that protein learn mods build hold the marks of kin trees. Such mods learn shape and work from code with no kin rules built in. The pair checks if gaps in code space can rebuild trees in a no train pass.

One code lump per protein loses most kin marks, they find: tree shape and limb spans come back poor. Stack gaps by each code spot in line, in mods that read the line whole, lifts shape truth to par with trained tools. Limb spans stay shaky. Kin use of such codes needs the stack route.
pmc-13370788:
Peter Olsén and Elena Subbotina map in 2026 the path from lignin, the tough glue of wood, to plastic build bits. Work on the path runs in three worlds, wood chem, bond craft, and stuff science, each with own marks. That split slows the whole, they hold.

Rough counts say waste lignin streams could fill a big share of scent bit needs for plastics. The pair back mill plans that use the mix as it comes, keep its built in traits, and pick bits by end use need, not by copy of oil bits. Use first design is the call.
pmc-13376788:
Sajeela Akbar and co-authors read drug pump genes in a ward germ in Peshawar, Pakistan, in a 2026 study. The germ can shrug off many drugs, and a cell pump that throws drugs out is one cause. A total of 200 case samples were drawn for tests.

A full 120 held germs proof to many drugs. Nine held all three pump parts, while pump switch genes showed in all 120. Small code shifts, some mute and some sense-shifts, laced the pump genes. Such pumps help germs live through care, so to track them is to track a key drug-proof path.
pmc-13378888:
Benjamin Moya-Leal and colleagues present a 2026 case of blocked and damaged bowel in a one-year-old boy. The cause was a birth defect in which the gut did not settle into its normal position before birth. Bands of tissue linked to that defect pressed on the bowel from outside.

The previously healthy child arrived with vomiting, a swelling belly, pain, and refusal to feed. A scan showed a blockage near the end of the small bowel. As his condition worsened, surgeons operated at once and found about a metre of bowel starved of blood by the pressure. The case shows that this defect can appear late, not only in newborn babies.
pmc-13381088:
Hae-In Jo, Jin-Uk Park, and Yeon-Kyeng Lee describe a 2026 account of World Allergy Week activities in Korea. Allergic diseases are long-lasting and recurring, and they can seriously limit daily life. The World Allergy Organization runs the annual campaign to raise awareness and promote early diagnosis and steady care.

For 2026 the global theme was that allergy care is essential care. Korea's disease control agency adopted its own slogan stating that allergy management is a necessity, not an option. Planned activities with local governments include quiz events, promotion booths, and hands-on education. The article sets out the campaign's aims and the messages behind the planned outreach.
pmc-13382688:
Chrysttian M S Garcia and co-authors published a 2026 study on why ethanol fuel becomes acidic on its own and corrodes fuel injectors. Acids in fuel ethanol attack metal parts, and stainless steel injector valves are a known victim. The team soaked samples for ninety days at high temperature to speed the process.

Dry ethanol caused no visible corrosion, while water-containing ethanol corroded steel severely and built up high levels of acetic acid. Even initially acid-free mixtures formed acid through contact with metal. Two ion-exchange resins were then tested for removing the acid. One resin worked faster and held more, pointing to a practical way to clean fuel and protect injectors.
pmc-13382988:
Capucine Januel traces her route into veterinary brain research in a 2026 interview in Biology Open. She is a veterinary student in Christine Charvet's lab at a national veterinary school in Toulouse, France. Her featured study compared brain aging in cats and humans using MRI scans.

Januel explains how time at Auburn University in the United States let her join veterinary medicine with brain imaging. Work across fields showed her how natural disease in pets can inform human health. She plans to specialize in veterinary neurology while keeping a research role, drawn by questions about how brains age across species.
pmc-13386588:
Fengxia Yang and colleagues review kesterite-based devices that act like synapses and store data in 2026 work. These devices, called memristors, can merge memory with computing in a single part. That merger could cut the energy cost of classic designs, where memory and processing sit apart and data must shuttle between them.

Kesterite drew interest because it responds well to light, uses common elements, and costs little to make. The review weighs design choices such as layer depth, element mix, joined layers, and contact metals. It also covers test settings and run modes that shape how the devices mimic synapses, and it closes with open problems for builders of brain-like hardware.
pmc-13387688:
Manman Sun and colleagues assess stress symptoms in caregivers of burn-injured children in a 2026 study. The work covered 240 main caregivers of children treated in hospital for burns between January 2024 and June 2025. A standard checklist scored three symptom groups: reliving the event, feeling on edge, and avoiding reminders of it.

Reliving symptoms were most common, then feeling on edge, with avoidance last in this group. Risk rose with burn severity, having seen the injury happen, home area, schooling, marital status, and household income. The authors say caregiver checks belong in burn care for children, since family stress can shape how a child heals.
pmc-13390488:
Faith Ye and a large team examine, in 2026, how the purity of bacterial spores changes their heat resistance and readiness to germinate. Earlier work found that less purified spores of Bacillus cereus and Bacillus subtilis survived wet heat better than cleaner preparations, a surprising result for food safety.

The new work widened the purity gap, used spores grown on plates and in liquid, and included a different Bacillus cereus strain and a plasmid-free Bacillus subtilis. The team measured resistance, germination, and the spore core's calcium compound and water content. Food scientists gain a warning. How spores are made in the lab can shift the heat score a test gives. That shift affects how heat rules are set and matched across labs. Cleaner is not always truer, this work warns.
pmc-13392288:
Aamir Lal and co-authors model, in 2026, how protein and DNA interactions may explain why the genome segments of nanoviruses accumulate at unequal levels. These multipartite plant viruses carry several genome pieces whose copy numbers form shifting formulas during infection, though all rely on one replication protein.

Focusing on a regulatory region of one segment of milk vetch dwarf virus, the team used structure-based computation to compare binding by replication and movement proteins from two nanoviruses under consistent conditions. Plant virus teams gain a clear claim to test. It may show how these split-genome viruses keep each part at its own level, year in and year out. The two source viruses share one host crop, which makes the match-up fair.
pmc-13393288:
Andrés Fuentes-Ramírez and four colleagues returned to fire-scorched monkey puzzle tree forests in the southern Andes eight years after severe wildfire to test whether surviving trees again produce sound seed. These ancient conifers carry deep ecological and cultural weight in south-central Chile, and post-fire germination data were almost absent. Seeds gathered from the same mother trees first surveyed after the 2015 reserve fire were sprouted under greenhouse care.

Germination climbed from sixty-five percent one year after the fire to ninety percent at eight years, with faster sprouting and higher seed viability in the later collection. The team suspects heat during early seed development depressed the first crop. Provided no new disturbance intervenes, surviving trees show strong maternal recovery, and the authors plead for shielding burned landscapes from grazing and human pressure while that recovery runs.
pmc-13393588:
Jaakob Semken and seven colleagues counted deaths from anaphylaxis across Finland from 2014 to 2023. Anaphylaxis is the most severe allergic reaction. The count used the national cause-of-death database, which is cross-checked against the population register and backed by a high autopsy rate. Certificates were re-read against standard clinical criteria to confirm true anaphylaxis. The backdrop matters: hospitalisations for anaphylaxis have been climbing in Finland and many other countries.

Across the decade, forty-three adults died of anaphylaxis and no children did, with yearly deaths ranging from none to eight. Rates per million people stayed low and variable year to year. The headline contrast is the empty paediatric column despite rising case numbers in children. The authors set out the main triggering agents and causes behind the fatal adult cases to guide prevention, noting the register's completeness as a strength of the count.
pmc-13393788:
Nicole Billias leads a fifteen-author scoping review mapping every reported route by which highly pathogenic bird flu H5N1 reaches humans, together with the body doors it likely uses. Older summaries were outdated or thin on pathway detail, a gap that matters for pandemic readiness. Searches across six databases plus grey literature to late October 2025, with duplicate screening, yielded one hundred twenty sources.

Animal-to-human spread dominated the reports, overwhelmingly from poultry, with cattle appearing in a small share after the recent dairy outbreaks. Environment-to-human routes featured in about a quarter of sources and human-to-human spread in about a tenth. Pathways divided into direct and indirect contact, linked to plausible entry through mucous membranes, inhaled droplets, swallowing, or skin breaks. The authors stress plausibility is not proof, and call for work pinning down causal mechanisms and risk factors.
pmc-13394788:
Moulignier and team report, in 2026, a case of encephalitis that advanced slowly in a person whose HIV was well controlled, traced to human pegivirus, a virus rarely blamed for brain disease. Roughly half of encephalitis cases never get a cause despite wide testing. A test that reads all genetic material in a sample found pegivirus RNA in the patient's spinal fluid and brain tissue, and no other pathogen turned up.

The patient's spinal fluid showed inflammatory changes, including 21 white cells per microliter and raised protein, alongside white matter abnormalities on imaging. Doctors treated off-label with sofosbuvir/ledipasvir, a hepatitis C drug combination, and the patient improved in a sustained way. Spinal fluid normalized and the virus became undetectable after treatment. The authors argue pegivirus deserves a place on the suspect list for unexplained encephalitis in patients with weak immune systems, and that antiviral therapy merits formal study.
pmc-13394888:
Lumin Liu and a large team link, in 2026, screen time with poor sleep in women treated for breast cancer. Sleeplessness hits this group harder than most cancer patients. The study enrolled 778 women at a hospital in Shanghai, China. Phone-based records gave daily screen time for some, and all reported screen use before bed plus sleep quality.

Each extra half hour of screen time came with higher odds of sleeplessness. The link was stronger for screen use right before bed. Women above the middle level of use faced odds two to three times higher. Felt stigma sharpened the harm, with the highest odds in women high on both counts. The authors urge sleep advice that covers screens.
pmc-13395388:
Jing Yang and co-authors find, in 2026, a gene axis that helps prostate cancer shrug off radiation. A hormone receiver named NR3C1 ran high in resistant tumours and tracked with poor outlook. It switches on an enzyme, ACSL4, that loads fats into cell skins. Those fats can either feed growth or, under the right push, rust and kill the cell.

A plant-derived drug, dihydroartemisinin, gave that push. With ACSL4 high, the drug sparked ferroptosis, a rust-like cell death, and made radiation work again in cells and mouse tumours. A blocker of that death path undid the gain. The authors back ACSL4 as a marker for the paired cure.
pmc-13396188:
Maha I. K. Ali and co-authors baked lower-fat cakes by swapping part of the fat for ground wheat germ, pumpkin seeds, or rice bran, and compared the results in a 2026 food study. Each powder is rich in fiber and nutrients that plain fat lacks, so the swap could raise a cake's food value.

The mixes used 60 percent wheat germ, 60 percent pumpkin seed, or 40 percent rice bran as the fat stand-in. Wheat germ cakes came out highest in protein, fiber, protective plant compounds, and several vitamins and minerals, though they were also firmer. All versions were checked for texture, color, microbe growth over time, and how tasters rated them.
pmc-13397688:
Dehao Luan and colleagues compare platelet-rich plasma alone against plasma paired with other injections for worn knee joints. Their 2026 network analysis pools randomised trials found in twelve databases through April 2026. Plasma shots are widely offered for knee osteoarthritis, yet whether adding partners truly helps was unsettled.

Eighteen trials with 1,376 people compared plasma alone against plasma plus hyaluronic acid, stem cells or ozone. Two reviewers picked studies and judged bias with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, focusing on total WOMAC scores and pain ratings. Ranking methods then ordered the four options, letting clinics see which pairing, if any, earns its extra cost and effort.
pmc-13398188:
Bomonyo Fente and co-authors present a man whose heart pain came from tiny vessels, not blocked arteries. Their 2026 case report covers a man in his sixties with repeated night-time chest pain and test signs of ischaemia, the state where heart muscle starves for blood. Angiography found no obstruction, a pattern now named INOCA that leaves many patients without an answer.

An invasive microvascular study then measured how his smallest coronary vessels behave, confirming clear microvascular dysfunction behind the attacks. Spasm in the large or small vessels can produce the same picture, so the added testing separates causes that plain angiography cannot. The authors use the case to argue that a clean angiogram should start, not end, the search.
pmc-13398288:
Kamel Mouloudj and co-authors survey what makes Algerian doctors and nurses willing to use telemedicine for older patients. Their 2026 study questions 130 health professionals with a structured questionnaire built on the Technology Acceptance Model, extended with self-confidence and workplace support. Remote care could widen access for elderly patients where resources run thin, but only if staff intend to use it.

The extended model explained 48.7 percent of the differences in intention to adopt the systems. Institutional support stood among the added factors that lifted the model's reach beyond plain usefulness and ease. Findings give Algerian health planners a ranked set of levers (training, backing, tools) to pull before expecting telemedicine to take hold.
pmc-13399088:
Moses C Odoeke and co-authors published a 2026 study of why patients with heart failure return to hospital soon after discharge. Working from the MIMIC-IV intensive care database, they focused on social factors such as insurance type, marital status, and race alongside clinical severity. The outcome they tracked was readmission within 30 days of leaving hospital.

The cohort held 16,324 adults treated in intensive care, and 17.6 percent were readmitted within 30 days. After adjustment, Black patients had higher readmission odds than White patients at 1.37, and Hispanic patients also faced higher odds at 1.31, while private insurance carried lower odds than Medicare at 0.83 in the same models. More chronic illness and longer stays raised the odds further. The authors argue that discharge planning should weigh a patient's social situation together with medical risk.
pmc-13399288:
Nongiwe Linette Mhlanga and co-authors scoped the evidence on digital tools that help non-physician health workers prevent and manage chronic diseases in Africa, in a 2026 review. Africa faces a rising load of heart disease, diabetes, and cancer alongside a severe shortage of health workers. Sharing tasks with community health workers has become a central strategy. The review asked which technologies are used, what they do, and what helps or hinders them.

The team searched PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar for work published up to August 2025. They sifted 4,857 citations down to 15 studies from eight African countries. South Africa contributed the largest share. Mobile health tools appeared in 46.7 percent of the studies, and community health workers were the main users. Low digital literacy, patchy internet, and unreliable electricity limited use. The authors say wider benefit will require governance, steady funding, infrastructure, and training shaped to each country's context.
pmc-13399788:
Neil Patel and colleagues share practical tips for reconstructing the posterior cruciate ligament with a single graft bundle through the arthroscope, in a 2026 technical note. The authors refine the simpler single-bundle, all-inside route.

Their preparation uses a donated peroneus longus tendon folded to a graft 10 to 12 millimeters thick and 90 millimeters long. Adjustable loop devices at both ends let the surgeon tension femur and tibia sides in sequence. On the table, the knee rests at ninety degrees of bend with a foot bump and hip post, and pulses in the foot are checked by Doppler before starting. Afterward, rehabilitation restrains active hamstring work for four to six months to protect the graft. The authors frame these details as the difference between a stable knee and a failed graft.
pmc-13400088:
Tiffany Chu and colleagues review strokes caused by carotid plaques that barely narrow the artery, in this 2026 article with case discussions. The condition is called symptomatic non-stenotic carotid disease. The review assembles what is known about proposed definitions, plaque danger features on imaging, and how these patients are currently managed.

Guidelines do not recommend surgery for this disease. The authors note a growing literature suggesting endarterectomy and stenting can be safe and effective in selected patients. Their institutional contribution is a case treated with transcarotid artery revascularization, a hybrid procedure. It reaches the carotid through a small neck incision and reverses blood flow during stenting to protect the brain. They report it as, to their knowledge, the first use of that technique for this indication. The review's thrust is definitional: without a standard definition for the condition, trials cannot settle who benefits from intervention.
pmc-13400188:
Merijn Braams and colleagues introduce ABO, a three-dimensional culture system that carries human blood stem cells through the complete development of B cells, in a 2026 study. ABO aggregates human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells with mouse bone marrow stromal cells. The structure shepherds the cells through pro-B, pre-B, immature, and transitional stages in order.

The decisive test was disease modeling. Stem cells from a patient with RAG1-deficient severe combined immunodeficiency reproduced their developmental arrest inside ABO, and a RAG1 gene therapy lentiviral vector corrected it in the dish. The authors offer the platform as a clinically relevant bench for diagnosing B cell immunodeficiencies and for pre-screening gene therapy products before they reach patients.
pmc-13400388:
Cesar A Speck-Hernandez heads a team reporting in 2026 how a protective factor called Nrf2 shapes osteoclasts, the cells that resorb bone. A signal named RANKL drives their formation and raises reactive oxygen, which helps them develop but can also cause damage. Cells must balance that stress to keep working.

Using gene data and engineered mice, the team found RANKL weakens one defense system while switching Nrf2 on. Osteoclasts without Nrf2 formed more readily yet resorbed poorly, with lower activity of the main bone-cutting enzyme, cathepsin K. They also showed fat damage, faulty power stations and unstable storage sacs. Nrf2, in short, keeps resorption working safely.
pmc-13400588:
Julien Gotchac and colleagues test, in 2026, a bedside heart ultrasound measure in babies with severe bronchiolitis, a viral chest infection of infancy. The right side of the heart can struggle under breathing strain. The team measured how far a heart valve ring moves with each beat, a simple index of right heart function, at intensive care admission.

Forty-six infants, from two weeks to about nine months old, were scanned during one bronchiolitis season. The measure sat in the normal range for most and above normal for the rest, suggesting right heart failure is uncommon here. Higher values still linked to shorter stays and fewer days of breathing support. Other ultrasound measures showed no such links.
pmc-13400688:
Joao Pedro Santos Nascimento and colleagues map, in 2026, how spirituality is defined in cancer research, in a scoping review of 104 studies. Spiritual care matters in oncology, yet the word spirituality is used in shifting ways. Without shared language, comparing studies and designing care is difficult.

Searching five databases plus gray literature, the team extracted definitions and sorted them into themes. Six core themes emerged, led by the search for meaning and purpose, then transcendence, connection with others, inner peace, faith in the sacred and coping resources. Older work leaned on religious frames, while newer work favors broader existential readings. Definitions also varied by region, underlining the need for culturally sensitive spiritual care.
pmc-13400988:
Vishal Vennu examines, in 2026, what factors track with physiological dysregulation in United States adults aged forty-five and older, using nationally representative survey data. Dysregulation here means combined strain across heart-metabolic, kidney and liver systems. Eight biomarkers were blended into a single index, with higher scores meaning worse overall function.

The analysis sample held 496 people representing about seventeen million adults. Women scored significantly lower on dysregulation than men, and physically active people scored lower than inactive peers. Overweight and obesity both tracked with higher dysregulation than normal weight. The author highlights sex differences and activity as levers, while noting the cross-sectional design cannot show which factor drives which.
pmc-13401088:
Meredith M Howley and co-authors examine whether a mother's stress and social support around early pregnancy affect stillbirth risk when the fetus has a birth defect. Their 2026 study pools data from two large United States birth defects studies, covering exposures from three months before conception and across the first trimester.

Using statistical models adjusted for age and race or ethnicity, the team found neither high stress nor low social support was linked to stillbirth among fetuses with birth defects. Patterns by race were nevertheless striking. Compared with non-Hispanic White women reporting low stress, non-Hispanic Black women had elevated stillbirth risk at both low and high stress levels. Hispanic women showed a smaller elevation at low stress. A similar pattern appeared for low social support. The authors conclude Black women faced higher risk regardless of stress or support levels.
pmc-13401288:
Alina Peluso and colleagues published a 2026 matched-cohort study of how health care use changed before and after a COVID-19 diagnosis, using electronic health records from MedStar Health. They compared patients who tested positive with similar patients who tested negative.

Records ran from March 25, 2019 to June 30, 2021, and a difference-in-differences design compared the six months before testing with the six months after. The team counted outpatient, inpatient, emergency, and virtual visits, overall and within groups defined by earlier conditions such as heart failure, diabetes, kidney disease, and cancer, and by sociodemographic factors. The aim was to see whether a positive diagnosis changed care patterns unevenly across diseases and patient groups.
pmc-13401688:
Abdiftah Mohamud Abdi, Saralees Nadarajah, and Abdisalam Hassan Muse compared dengue fever forecasting models for Somalia in a 2026 retrospective time series analysis. Dengue is a growing threat in a climate-stressed country with a weak health system, and planners need forecasts that work with sparse data.

The team used annual reported incidence from 1990 to 2021, drawn from Our World in Data, training models on 1990 to 2016 and testing them on 2017 to 2021. They stress that forecasts project the reported burden, not true infections, because case definitions are unstandardized and under-reporting is heavy. A mechanistic SIR model, eight single time series models such as ARIMA and neural network autoregression, and twelve hybrid ensembles were compared. Individual statistical models gave basic predictive power, and a hybrid blending ARIMA with TBATS performed best of all.
pmc-13403088:
Esin Diremsizoglu and colleagues mine 43,954 YouTube comments to map how the public talks about managing skin changes in midlife and menopause. Menopause reshapes skin and self-image, yet clinics under-address it, pushing women toward video platforms for guidance. From 342 videos gathered through the YouTube API in March 2026, they sorted content types and built a 13-category management subset of 10,861 comments for closer reading.

Overall sentiment leaned positive at 59.6 percent. Hormone replacement therapy dominated discussion at 54.8 percent of management comments yet drew the lowest sentiment of any category. Alternative approaches and supplements scored highest praise despite thinner evidence. Personal lifestyle creators drew warmer responses than clinicians. A slight warming toward hormone therapy followed the FDA November 2025 warning removal. The authors urge skin doctors to counter safety misconceptions online.
pmc-13403288:
Kerr and colleagues follow the daily side of leaving the military, asking twelve Australian Defence Force members how their days changed when service ended. Transition research tracks jobs and identity, but occupation in the therapy sense, everything a person does with their time, shapes both. Their 2026 study uses narrative inquiry, two rounds of interviews that let participants check the researchers' reading, and reads the stories thematically.

Two themes frame the accounts. Inside service, life sat in a bubble: work crowded out leisure, and the routine supplied purpose, mateship, and structure in one package. Discharge popped the bubble. Losing occupations and the peer culture around them knocked confidence and competence in civilian life, and most participants worked, with mixed success, to build a balanced week again. Services that rebuild participation early, the authors argue, through community and leisure engagement, would soften a landing that is left to chance.
pmc-13403488:
Wenyu Jiao and a large transplant team traced immune cells in 2026 after human lung transplants. Lung grafts face a lasting tug between rejection and infection, both steered by T cells. The team sampled lung wash fluid and blood over time and read each cell's receptor code.

Recipient cells slowly built a lasting home in the graft lung. During infections, cells matched to the germ at hand grew in number there. A higher share of host-attacking clones in lung fluid tied to early rejection and poor lung function. The small early study names receptor traits that larger work should test as warning signs.
pmc-13403588:
Jacob Bethel, Asma Eslami, and Amgad S. Hanna shared a 2026 surgical case where milky lymph fluid leaked on the right side of the neck. Such leaks are rare and usually strike the left side, where the main lymph duct runs. The leak appeared during an operation to reach arm nerves for a nerve transfer.

The patient needed the transfer because one side of the diaphragm was paralyzed. Surgeons spotted the leak near a lymph node bed and tied it off with stitches. Recovery went smoothly with no further trouble. Odd lymph routes on the right side likely explain the surprise.
pmc-13404088:
Chandini Bhaskar Naidu, Javier Vera Lillo, and many colleagues found in 2026 that outside pulling forces can speed up shipping from the cell's Golgi hub. The Golgi sorts new proteins and sends them to the cell surface in small carriers. Cell sticking and spreading had hinted at a two-way link with that shipping line.

Their work ties grip strength to Golgi membrane tension, track stiffening, and fat plus enzyme signals. Those links shape how many carriers form and leave the hub. More export then feeds back to help the cell spread and adapt to force. The loop joins touch sensing to supply control.
pmc-13404488:
Rocio Martin-Cañavate headed a 2026 cost study of three child stunting plans run inside a trial in southern Angola. Stunting from long-term underfeeding blights growth across the region. The arms paired standard care alone, standard care plus cash, and standard care plus food supplements with a family ration.

Over the first year the plans reached 1,423 pregnant women and their children. Monthly cost per person ran about 12.85 dollars for standard care, 27.07 dollars with cash, and 33.51 dollars with supplements. Staff pay and training drove the plain arm's costs. Supplies drove the richer arms, where cash and food made the largest shares.
pmc-13404788:
Raissa Rafidhinar and co-authors look for catheter-based warning signs in rheumatic heart disease, reporting in 2026. Their patients showed a mismatch on ultrasound between the right heart chamber and its artery, a pattern called RV-PA uncoupling. Which pressure measures predict death or other bad outcomes in that group was unclear.

The single-centre review covered 56 adults who had a first right heart catheter test for risk grading before treatment. Fourteen patients, 25 percent, died during the hospital-record follow-up, and 23 had the combined bad outcome. Higher pulmonary vascular resistance, meaning tighter lung vessels, stayed linked to worse outcomes after adjustment. The authors use the results to sharpen risk grading before intervention.
pmc-13405088:
Ali Khadivi and colleagues measure wild Persian iris plants across Markazi Province, Iran, in 2026 work. The ornamental species grows naturally in mountain regions, but its variation between sites was little documented. Knowing that diversity helps conservation and breeding for gardens.

Seventy-eight single plants from seven regions were scored on 39 shape and colour traits. Flower width ranged widely, from 34.52 to 80.56 millimetres in the reported measurements. Ten main components captured 82.46 percent of all variation, led by flower size traits. Grouping placed the plants into four clear types, showing strong differences between mountain populations that collectors and breeders can use.
pmc-13405688:
Sangyoon Jang and co-authors study how travel memories steer online shopping across borders, in a 2026 survey of Chinese consumers. Shoppers had visited Korea and met Korean cosmetics in person. The question was whether that hands-on familiarity lowers the uncertainty that blocks cross-border orders.

Data from 325 travellers, gathered over four weeks in March 2026, were modelled with partial least squares methods. Tourism-derived information raised product familiarity and judged usefulness, and directly cut product uncertainty. Lower uncertainty then lifted intention to buy across borders. When transaction risk felt high, the negative pull of uncertainty on buying grew stronger, the model shows.
pmc-13406488:
Dimitris Chatzopoulos and colleagues test a five-minute music and movement break for preschoolers, in a 2026 classroom study. Fifty-three children aged five to six were split into an active break group of twenty-five and a seated control group of twenty-eight. Tests before and after measured self-control, memory, flexibility and maths.

The music-movement group performed significantly better on inhibitory control after the break, the headline finding states. Engagement in later classroom activities also seemed to rise. Other executive skills and maths scores were tracked for comparison, giving a fuller picture of what one short break can shift. The authors suggest brief active breaks as a cheap classroom tool worth wider testing.
pmc-13407788:
Lili Qin, Shasha Wang, and Haifeng Qin comment, in 2026, on claims that chest radiotherapy extends life in lung cancer that has already spread. A study by Xue and colleagues reported better survival with added chest radiotherapy. It joined targeted therapy or chemoimmunotherapy for spread lung cancer. The commentators urge a careful reading.

Their concerns are methodological. The compared groups may have differed in how far cancer had spread. Key prognostic factors entered the analysis unevenly. Survival data also remain immature. Each point invites residual confounding. Overlapping definitions of lung toxicity, side effects that unfold over time, and unadjusted subgroup claims add further doubt. Carefully chosen patients may still benefit, they conclude, but prospective trials and stronger real-world methods must define who those patients are.
pmc-13408188:
Ming Geng and colleagues report in 2026 the discovery of an unusual immune receptor in the lamprey Lethenteron reissneri. Lampreys are jawless fish whose adaptive immunity runs on variable lymphocyte receptors rather than the antibodies and T-cell receptors of jawed animals. Whether single cells juggle several receptor types was unresolved.

Single-cell gene profiling revealed a receptor that stays fixed rather than diversifying, sits anchored on T-like cells, and responds to stimulation with growth signals typical of those cells. The cells carrying it did not behave like B-like cells. Some also carried a second, diversified receptor, and the two appear to interact. Readers in evolutionary immunology get a refined picture of how lamprey T-like cells may pair a constant coordinator with a variable partner.
pmc-13408488:
Mohamed Ahmed Abdelhay, Abdel Nasser Helal, Abdel Aleem Elessawy, and Amir Lala build in 2026 a three-dimensional map of underground pressure for the Sapphire gas field offshore Egypt. The Nile Delta is one of the world's high-pressure basins, and guessing formation pressure wrong endangers drilling. Their workflow starts from seismic data rather than from wells alone.

Pre-stack seismic inversion produced cubes of rock properties that were converted into a detailed interval-velocity volume, the key input for pressure estimation. Standard pressure equations were retuned for Nile Delta conditions instead of borrowing Gulf of Mexico constants. Four wells built the model and a fifth checked it, and predicted pressures matched the measurements logged during drilling closely. The method is offered for well planning and exploration in similarly pressured basins.
pmc-13408688:
Patrick Binder and colleagues explain in 2026 why the malaria parasite's nuclei fall out of step while multiplying inside a red blood cell. One parasite becomes roughly twenty daughters in two days, and its nuclei divide inside a shared soup of cytoplasm, desynchronising within a few rounds. Live imaging paired with biophysical modelling tested what could produce that drift.

Independent clock-like cycles could not reproduce the data, so the nuclei must be coupled. The winning explanation is competition: nuclei draw sequentially on a scarce pool of DNA-copying proteins, grabbing them one at a time through stable attachment to DNA. Far from being sloppy, the resulting asynchrony speeds the whole brood by keeping the shared machinery busy instead of idle. The authors suggest resource rationing may be a general trick for fast growth in poor conditions.
pmc-13408788:
Junta Sugiyama, Akira Hashimoto, Kyung-Ok Nam, Yosuke Degawa, and Tsuyoshi Hosoya describe a new sooty mould fungus in 2026 from the highlands of central Japan. The species, named Capnofrasera abieticola, grew on living twigs and needles of a fir tree, tangled into the dark felt of a second, dominant sooty mould. Fresh specimens from Sugadaira supplied the description.

Its spores are shorter and narrower than those of its closest relative, a Swedish species living on elm, and its host choice differs as well. A single spore from the type specimen grew into a sterile culture. A three-gene family tree then placed the newcomer in the family Neoantennariellaceae, rather than the family its genus was assumed to occupy. Taxonomists gain both a species and a corrected address for its lineage.
pmc-13409088:
María Victoria Martínez-López and a large Spanish team listen in 2026 to forty-seven relatives who lived through a family member's organ donation. Spain leads the world in donation rates, yet the family's experience decides much about consent and about how grief unfolds afterwards. Many relatives described donation as meaningful, bringing comfort and a steadier grief, as if something of the death had been redeemed. pmc-13416488:

pmc-13418188:

pmc-13419288:

pmc-13419688:

pmc-13420488:

pmc-13420588:

pmc-13421788:

pmc-13425088:

pmc-13425588:

pmc-13425788:

pmc-13436088:

pmc-13436688:

pmc-13437288:

pmc-13437988:

pmc-13441288:

pmc-13442388:

pmc-13443488:

pmc-13444188:

pmc-13444488:

pmc-13445188:

pmc-13446988:

pmc-13467388:

pmc-13467788:

pmc-13468388:

pmc-13468788:

pmc-13469288:

pmc-13469688:

pmc-13470888:

pmc-13471288:

pmc-13471388:

pmc-13471588:

pmc-13472288:

pmc-13474388:

pmc-13474488:

pmc-13474688:

pmc-13477088:

pmc-13477588:

pmc-13478388:

pmc-13483188:

pmc-13487388:

pmc-13487988:

pmc-13488588:

pmc-13491688:

pmc-13491788:

pmc-13492288:

pmc-13493188:

pmc-13493788:

pmc-13493988:
